articles.title: California DMV bars Waymo AVs from operating on the state’s freeways
articles.snippet: Waymo said the DMV order only applies to freeways and will not affect its operations on city streets. | Source: Waymo The California Department of Motor Vehicles has barred Waymo autonomous vehicles (AVs) from operating on the state’s freeways. The DMV issued the order on Nov. 11, following a number of incidents in the state, it confirmed to The Robot Report . Waymo said it will restrict freeway operations across all of its operating areas, as part of its safety-first approach. The ban comes “following an incident in which three Waymo autonomous vehicles entered an active construction closure on U.S. Route 101 near Burlingame and another incident involving CHP vehicles on Highway 280 in San Francisco,” the DMV said. In the second incident, a Waymo vehicle can be seen attempting to drive past California Highway Patrol officers while they’re conducting a traffic stop. You can watch the incidents below. The DMV determined that Waymo’s freeway operations “pose an imminent hazard to public safety due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present.” The action prevents Waymo from operating or testing its driverless vehicles on all California freeways. The restrictions will remain in place until Waymo demonstrates to the DMV that it has “taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies that precipitated the restrictions.” This includes providing evidence that its AVs can safely detect and respond to construction zones, emergency vehicles, and other roadway situations within the vehicles’ operational design domain. “Safety is at the foundation of everything we do. Following recent freeway construction zone encounters on U.S. 101 in California that did not involve any injuries or collisions, the California DMV has implemented an operating restriction on freeway operations in the state. In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance. Our ride-hailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week. We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations,” a Waymo spokesperson told The Robot Report . Waymo AVs struggle with construction zones This isn’t Waymo’s first time running into issues with the California DMV this year. The DMV noted that Waymo AVs still posed a safety threat “despite a prior restriction and corrective actions implemented following similar incidents that occurred on May 18, 2026.” The incidents the DMV is referring to occurred when seven Waymo vehicles drove between construction cones and into closed lanes in San Francisco. This incident resulted in Waymo issuing a safety recall with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) in June. In the recall report, Waymo said that “under certain circumstances, the AV may enter and drive at speed in freeway construction zones due to inappropriately prioritizing the avoidance of other freeway hazards and/or failing to recognize the construction zone.” The recall was supposed to enhance Waymo AVs’ performance in and around freeway construction zones. Waymo said it plans to continue freeway testing with trained autonomous specialists in the vehicles. It noted that its vehicles had been driving fully autonomously on California freeways for several years and began offering public riders trips using freeways last November. Emergency vehicles, stopped school buses , and now construction zones have been some of the biggest challenges for Waymo since it began rolling out its robotaxis in 2018. Waymo now operates commercial services in over 15 cities in the U.S., including Austin, Las Vegas, and Atlanta. It has plans to expand to 17 more cities, including in London and Tokyo, in the coming years. Waymo vehicles and hit-and-runs in Arizona The robotaxis have also been involved in a growing number of hit-and-run incidents in Arizona, according to a local CBS channel. Almost half of all police-reported crashes involving Waymo robotaxis in the Phoenix metro area end with the human driver fleeing the scene—a hit-and-run rate per mile more than double that of the general public, according to a 10-month review of crash reports and body-camera footage. articles.title: External sandboxes for coding agents
articles.snippet: External sandboxes for coding agents I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine. I worked on this project with Prime Radiant , the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects . My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox. To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations: external-sandbox-v86 runs a Node.js server which then uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly. external-sandbox-container is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance. external-sandbox-quicksand is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's Quicksand sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package! Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code. The sandboxes also include an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy, so you can control exactly which hosts your agent's code is allowed to communicate with - plus a credential replacement mechanism to make authenticated API calls without sharing a secret with the agent. Here's the UI you can use to reconfigure that proxy while the sandbox is still running: I continue to be fascinated by the challenge of safely running untrusted code. This external sandbox pattern provides a neat way to experiment with different approaches. Tags: sandboxing , security , ai , webassembly , generative-ai , llms , coding-agents , claude-code , codex , pi

articles.title: GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol
articles.snippet: GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol OpenAI: We’re introducing GPT‑6.2 Astra, our new frontier model for your hardest projects, and GPT‑6.2 Sol, our efficient, versatile model for everyday work. They're available in the API as gpt-6.2-astra and gpt-6.2-sol . I shipped LLM 0.38 with support for the new models. 6.2 Astra is 80% of the price of 6 Astra - $8/MTok input and $40/MTok output, the same price as Claude Fable 5.2 (which was also 80% of its predecessor). 6 Astra and Fable 5 were both $10/$50. The cached price is an even bigger discount - $0.40/million compared to $1/million for the older model. This is great news for longer running agentic sessions. GPT-6.2 Sol is the same $2/$10 price as 6.1 Sol and 6 Sol - which are half the price of GPT-5.6 Sol ($4/$20). Here are the pelicans for GPT-6.2 Sol and for GPT-6.2 Astra . The 6.2 Astra max pelican looks like this: I have a full comparison grid here , but here's how the high/xhigh/max pelicans compare with the previous Sol and Astra releases: I also ran my most recent benchmark prompt against the two models, using "Ultra' effort levels in the Codex CLI: Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data Here's Sol and here's Astra . Neither of them did a good enough job of morphing Yonkers into a big mech, at least in comparison to Claude Fable 5.2 and Gemini 4 Carbon . This video showing the Astra and Sol animations playing out at the same time: I created that video using GPT-6.2 Astra (Ultra) in the Codex desktop app by prompting: https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/yonkers-gpt-6.2-astra-ultra/index.html and https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/yonkers-gpt-6.2-sol-ultra/index.html are two videos of the same thing by two different models I need a video of the first 10 seconds where the top half of the video plays the first and the bottom half plays the second I need an overlaid label of "GPT-6.2 Astra" on the top half and "GPT-6.2 Sol" on the bottom half. These labels should be tastefully positioned. Make the video square and 2000x2000 pixels Then later: OK make it 20s Here's the exported transcript . The buzz around these new models is mixed at the moment. Astra 6.2 isn't scoring quite as high as Fable 5.2 on various benchmarks, and I've seen a few complaints that its communication style can be confusing. Theo Browne's review (in the form of a feedback letter he sent OpenAI during pre-release) has this useful example: When this model is working on long tasks, it can pull in a lot of subagents and manage them pretty well. It will then proceed to randomly ask you some weird internal implementation detail bullshit that you could not under any earthly circumstance understand, much less have input on . I sent "/goal make a new level for Outer Wilds". 2 hours in, it's "blocked" because it wanted to ask me "does r24's reviewer write it's clips to 24_g521.mp4 or 24_p11.mp4?" articles.title: Learn how AI is changing supply chain robotics
articles.snippet: From left to right: Lior Elazary, the co-founder and CEO of inVia Robotics, Josip Cesic, the co-founder and CEO of Gideon, and Jeff Mahler, the co-founder and CTO of Ambi Robotics. Supply chain robotics is undergoing rapid transformation. Companies hope to address labor shortages, improve efficiency, and build resilience against disruptions. Increasingly, they’re turning to robotics to solve these challenges. Currently, available technologies include warehouse automation, picking and packing systems, autonomous mobile robots for material handling, and AI-powered inventory management. These systems can work together and help organizations adapt to changing demand patterns and product variations. Now, the integration of artificial intelligence is enabling predictive analytics, demand forecasting, and dynamic routing optimization. With AI, robots can learn from operational data to improve performance, reduce errors, and optimize energy consumption. Even manufacturers already using robots stand to gain from these advancements, achieving higher quality, reduced downtime, better predictability, and cost optimization. This transition is a strategic necessity, supporting the shift towards high-volume, high-mix production and resilient supply chains. Learn about all of the latest advancements in the webinar , “Robots in the Supply Chain.” The live webinar will take place Wednesday, November 18, 2026, at 12 P.M. ET. If you can’t attend live, registered attendees will be able to watch a recording of the webinar at their convenience. The webinar will feature insights from three robotics experts: Lior Elazary, co-founder and CEO of InVia Robotics; Josip Cesic, co-founder and CEO of Gideon; and Jeff Mahler, co-founder and CTO of Ambi Robotics. In this webinar, attendees will learn how: Integrated automation solutions combine warehouse robotics, AI, and predictive analytics for end-to-end supply chain optimization. AI-powered systems enable adaptive operations that respond to changing demand patterns and disruptions. High-volume, high-mix production requirements drive adoption of flexible robotic solutions. Real-time visibility and predictive capabilities improve decision-making and operational resilience. Meet the speakers Lior Elazary is the co-founder and CEO of inVia Robotics . At inVia, he leads the company’s vision for applying AI, software, and robotics to improve warehouse operations. With more than 20 years of experience in technology and entrepreneurship, he has built and scaled companies across robotics, software, networking, and enterprise technology. Josip Cesic is the co-founder and CEO of Gideon , a pioneering robotics and AI company. Gideon revolutionizes supply chains with their Physical-AI platform, automating some of the hardest automation problems such as loading and unloading truck trailers with autonomous forklifts. Cesic holds a PhD in autonomy technologies from the University of Zagreb (FER), Croatia, and completed with the University of Waterloo, Canada. His accolades include the Dean’s Award, Special Dean’s Award, Rector’s Award, Special Rector’s Award, and the Silver Plaque for his outstanding doctoral dissertation. He holds several patents and has published over 20 research papers on robotics and AI. Josip also serves on the Board of Alumni at FER. Jeff Mahler is a co-founder and the CTO for Ambi Robotics , previously serving as CEO of the company. Mahler is responsible for guiding the vision and execution of the company’s advanced operating system, AmbiOS, to power highly dexterous robotic systems in commercial production. Mahler obtained his Ph.D. from UC Berkeley as a member of the AUTOLAB and Berkeley Artificial Intelligence Research Lab. His dissertation research is on the Dexterity-Network (Dex-Net), and he has also published on deep learning from demonstration and control for surgical robots. His research papers have been nominated for numerous awards, including Best Manipulation Paper (ICRA 2016) and Best Human-Robot Interaction Paper (ICRA 2016). Mahler’s open-source code, training datasets, and neural network weights receive hundreds of downloads per month. Along with Prof. Ruzena Bajcsy, he helped start EE 106B, the UC Berkeley course on mathematical models for robot manipulation. Previously, he co-founded the 3D scanning startup Lynx Laboratories in 2012, which was acquired by Occipital, Inc., and he received the National Defense Science and Engineering Fellowship in 2015. articles.title: Chart Crimes: HELOC Edition
articles.snippet: Got home last night at midnight cause the Amtrak from Philly was a disaster (I’ll ignore the coincidences for now)1. So the longer discussion on Biases, Filter Bubbles ,and Investing Errors will have to wait. Right on cue, this beauty popped up. The problem is less about the chart itself than it is about the accompanying headline: These Charts Show How More People Are Pulling Cash Out of Their Homes . The Journal noted that “ Home equity lines of credit are becoming popular again as people try to avoid giving up their low-rate primary mortgages.” I beg to differ. That chart above was what the Journal began the piece with. To my eye, it looks like Home Equity has ~tracked the underlying value of mortgage debt, which we know tracks the value of residential real estate. If Equity is ~72% of total value now, that is where it was at the 2022 peak ($32T of $44T). It was 63% in 2019, 46% at the 2012 trough, and about 60% in 2000 and 2006-07. Mortgage debt is up from roughly $12T to $14T since 2022, about 14%, and total housing value rose about the same 14%. So debt is growing in line with values, and the loan-to-value ratio is flat at around 28%. How is that evidence of owners extracting more equity? Yes, more on an ABSOLUTE basis, but that’s not newsworthy; it’s GDP growth and inflation. This reminds me of the NYSE Margin panic we see from time to time. Contrary to some innumerate claims, record rising NYSE margin was nothing to worry about; this was back in 2015. Show me that the percentage of home equity is increasing faster than the underlying value of homes — and you have something. But rising more or less in line with Home values just means the entire RRE pie is getting bigger — mortgages AND home equity? Nothing to see there. One question that came up in Philly about How Not to Invest involved bad charts. My answer was: “ If a picture is worth a 1000 words, a Chart Crime equals 1000 lies.. .” Source : These Charts Show How More People Are Pulling Cash Out of Their Homes By Terell Wright and Veronica Dagher WSJ, Nov. 17, 2026 Previously : Margin Debt Hits an All-Time High . . . So What? (April 29, 2015) Why Do People Fear the Hindenburg Omen? (June 4, 2013) __________ 1. I don’t believe in coincidences, but I would rather not add to the noise until we know what this is and who is behind it. With this post, we add the Category “Chart Crimes” The post Chart Crimes: HELOC Edition appeared first on The Big Picture .

articles.title: Running the full server-side Datasette Python app in the browser with service workers and Pyodide
articles.snippet: Datasette Lite is my port of the Datasette Python application to run directly in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide . I've released a complete rewrite of Datasette Lite using service workers, and it's now almost indistinguishable from the real server-side application. You can now do all of the following, using a carefully crafted URL to lite.datasette.io : Load client-side Datasette to browse any SQLite database, JSON file, CSV file or SQL script Select a released version of Datasette to load from PyPI Load a specific commit, tag, or branch name from the Datasette GitHub repository Pick from over 100 versions of SQLite to use with Datasette Install additional Datasette plugins from PyPI or URLs to wheel files, including JavaScript visualization tools The ability to load specific Datasette references, plugins, and SQLite versions makes this a fantastic tool for linking to demos of work-in-progress features or bug reproductions, without needing to spin up a full web server to serve that demo. As an example, consider the following URL: https://lite.datasette.io/?install=datasette-maplibre&url=https://gist.githubusercontent.com/simonw/39fa5d399465766039549912e2b3d291/raw/f6dfba99a75cbb8b5d9386223220eb52272767ee/demo.db&metadata=https://gist.githubusercontent.com/simonw/39fa5d399465766039549912e2b3d291/raw/f6dfba99a75cbb8b5d9386223220eb52272767ee/metadata.yml#/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent Follow that link and, after a short loading screen, you'll find yourself on a page that looks like this: That's Datasette running the new datasette-maplibre plugin, loading up a database of GeoJSON shapes of countries and displaying both a combined map and individual boundary maps in a table. Let's break down that URL to see what it's doing: https://lite.datasette.io/ ?install=datasette-maplibre &url=https://.../demo.db &metadata=https://.../metadata.yml #/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent The ?install=datasette-maplibre installs that additional plugin from PyPI. You can pass &install=... as many times as you like to load more plugins. &url=https://.../demo.db loads that SQLite database from the provided URL. These URLs need to have open CORS headers - I host files like this in Gists , because they provide an easy way to get open CORS headers on a web-hosted file. &metadata=https://.../metadata.yml loads this metadata.yml file . The metadata file adds HTML descriptions to various tables, and to the Datasette homepage. Visit that homepage here for a guided tour of the other features of that plugin, all defined in the metadata file. #/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent is a fragment hash that turns into a location within Datasette - here it's loading the /demo/capitals_and_countries SQL view, then appending another fragment hash to it ( %23 is a URL-encoded # ) which tells the map plugin to zoom to a certain location and to set the color of the shapes on the map based on the continent column in the data. That URL is doing a lot of work! I wrote more about this trick for building URL-addressable software in URL-addressable Pyodide Python environments last year. The full set of supported URL arguments is described in the Datasette Lite README . I've already started using Datasette Lite as part of the Datasette development process. Here's a recent issue describing a pagination bug - I posted a comment there demonstrating the old, broken behavior and the new fix using links to Datasette Lite: Demo of the bug: https://lite.datasette.io/?ref=1.0a42&sql=https://gist.github.com/simonw/75ececf61d50e6e8d50f0c150150ee81#/data/scores?_size=2&_sort=score - click next and the second page is empty. Here's that same page with the bug fixed (running on 1.0a43): https://lite.datasette.io/?ref=1.0a43&sql=https://gist.github.com/simonw/75ececf61d50e6e8d50f0c150150ee81#/data/scores?_size=2&_sort=score How this works, using service workers Datasette Lite is not a new project. I launched the first version back in 2022 , originally as a bit of a joke (running server-side apps in the browser is pretty funny) but one that quickly started proving its value. The problem with that initial version is that it was a hack . It worked by running Datasette in a Pyodide web worker, simulating requests through that stack, then injecting the resulting HTML back into the top level page using innerHTML . This worked for basic Datasette, but meant that any feature that used JavaScript failed to work, because script tags in innerHTML don't execute, and the web worker tricks it used failed to load additional JavaScript or CSS files. The new version takes a completely different approach based on Service Workers . These allow JavaScript to intercept HTTP requests for new pages and resources and serve them from client-side code instead. Datasette Lite registers a service worker for the entire lite.datasette.io domain. The parent page then creates an iframe that sends requests for Datasette pages to URLs that look like this: /app/aa94e6851595/ # the homepage (HTML) /app/aa94e6851595/data/places # a table page (HTML) /app/aa94e6851595/-/static/navigation-search.js # (JavaScript) /app/aa94e6851595/-/static/app.css # (CSS) Those are regular Datasette URLs, but with a /app/aa94e6851595/ prefix. What's that about? The /app/<session>/ prefix is necessary because of multiple tabs. Consider the URL above, which loads the demo instance with the datasette-maplibre plugin. That URL defines a full, custom Datasette instance. You might have that one running in a tab, then one of my other demo links running in another. The service worker for lite.datasette.io is shared between all of those tabs. If it routed to a single instance of Datasette then every tab would share that underlying instance, no matter what plugins or other settings their URL attempted to configure. Instead, the parent page generates a random session ID and uses it as a prefix for all of the subsequent hidden asset

articles.title: Cloudflare Joins the Jevolution and Labels Itself a Neolab
articles.snippet: Cloudflare has been one of the essential infrastructure companies of the web for the past decade and a half. But now, it’s turning into a neolab — at least according to a presentation at AI Engineer Code Summit by Michelle Chen , who runs Cloudflare’s AI Platform on the product side. We’ll get into what exactly a neolab is in a minute (the short version: they build models and they’re not called OpenAI or Anthropic). Cloudflare is claiming to be one because it too has begun to launch models. Two System One models , to be precise: Clef and Clairic. As Chen explained in her talk, Clef is a decision model directly inspired by TypeSafe AI’s revolutionary Jev model , while Clairic is a new type of system one model that Cloudflare calls an “extract” model . In an interview with Latent Space after her presentation, Chen hinted that Cloudflare won’t just be producing system one models. There will be large language models, too. “We're not being a neolab [to] only launch system one models, even though it makes sense for our infrastructure. We've kind of entered this Pandora's box now, right? We opened it, now the possibilities are endless.” Chen said it’s “not just system one models, but potentially reasoning models that we've been experimenting with, and other LLMs and whatnot.” However, she added that these probably won’t be pre-trained models built from scratch, like the frontier labs produce. “I don't think that's our focus, but I think we can take existing resources out there and make [them] a lot more efficient and effective.” She noted that “most of our team really just does post-training,” so that will be the focus in model development. What is a neolab and is Cloudflare really one? The term neolab literally means a ‘new lab’ and it was coined last November by Stephanie Palazzolo from The Information, who defined it as “a new generation of research-focused AI startups.” Deedy Das , a partner at Menlo Ventures and an AI influencer, runs a big list of neolabs . It includes companies like Thinking Machines Lab, Poolside, and TypeSafe AI itself. According to Das, neolabs employ elite researchers, spend a lot of compute (“usually to train its own AI model”), don't have significant revenue traction, and they’re typically startups that have raised a lot of money. Deedy Das’ list of neolabs — note that TypeSafe is among the top 20. Cloudflare doesn’t tick at least half of those boxes, since it’s a public company with significant revenue traction . In fact, earlier this month Cloudflare announced record earnings . “The third quarter was Cloudflare's best quarter ever,” said CEO Matthew Prince . “We crossed $3 billion in annualized revenue with revenue of $782 million, up 39% year over year.” So Cloudflare as a “neolab” is pushing the accepted definition. However, as Chen argued in her presentation, building models is part of a natural progression for the company : from infrastructure, to compute (e.g. the Workers platform, including now for agents), to storage, to serving open weight models like Kimi, GLM and DeepSeek (on Workers AI), to now building its own models. Jev as the “east wind” Chen readily admits that Jev inspired Cloudflare’s pivot to building models. Referencing a Chinese proverb, she framed Jev’s arrival in September as “the east wind” that unexpectedly changed how Cloudflare viewed AI models. “And so when the system one and Jev paradigm started coming on board,” Chen said in her presentation, “we were like, this makes so much sense for us to adopt, right? We don't have to send every request to an LLM. We can send some of it to a System One model.” In our conversation, Chen commented on how it took only two weeks for them to build Clef — which is a copy of Jev — whereas it took TypeSafe AI two years to build Jev. She meant that as a compliment for how hard TypeSafe AI worked to create this new type of model. “All credit to TypeSafe, really, for actually attacking this space and inventing something new here , that people could relate to so strongly and be able to use it. And, yeah, we came up with a model super quickly, but they put in a lot of legwork and we knew exactly what the API schema should look like and whatnot.” Cloudflare is, at its core, still an infrastructure company — speed and low latency is its meat and potatoes. The main benefit of System One models, Chen remarked, is that they allow more work to be done by smaller, faster models , where output is measured in milliseconds rather than seconds. Clairic and what extraction models do While Clef was a clone of Jev, Cloudflare soon came up with an original twist on System One with Clairic , launched last month as “the first model in a new class: System One extraction models.” “What Clairic does is it can take unstructured input, and it can extract, compute, estimate and forecast values from those inputs,” Chen explained in her presentation. In our interview, Chen said that her team wanted to use System One principles to find other areas where LLMs were “overkill” and didn’t always return the right answer. One of the problems they settled on was that LLMs don’t always deal well with unstructured input. Because LLMs are autoregressive, Chen explained, they are prone to hallucinate and they sometimes return malformed JSON. “So we used the same System One principles [as Jev/Clef] there, and decided on extraction.” Some examples of system one use cases at Cloudflare. She used the example of an invoice, where an LLM will sometimes get an important detail wrong — like the order number. “When you send it [the order] to an LLM, they're like, wait, I think the order number's three, maybe it's four, maybe it's five. But it's like, the number's right there, you just have to read it! ” So the idea with Clairic is that it will extract a typed value — like a number — from unstructured data, in one forward pass. Why Cloudflare is in the lab now Using the label “neolab” sounds a bit like a marketing gimmick, but it also makes a ton of sense

articles.title: Boston Dynamics’ Atlas humanoid lands first non-automotive trial
articles.snippet: GlobalFoundries will test Boston Dynamics’ Atlas humanoid (right) in semiconductor manufacturing tasks in 2027. | Credit: Boston Dynamics GlobalFoundries, a leading semiconductor manufacturer, will become the first customer outside of the automotive industry to test Boston Dynamics’ Atlas humanoid. Atlas testing will begin in early 2027, marking a key step in Boston Dynamics’ efforts to commercialize its humanoid. GlobalFoundries is already a customer of Boston Dynamics , having deployed its Spot quadruped for industrial inspections for several years. The companies are expanding that relationship to include additional Spot deployments across GlobalFoundries’ global manufacturing network. Since April 2026, two Spot robots at its Singapore facility have collectively traveled nearly 900 km (559 mi.) and completed more than 90,000 inspections in sub-fab areas, achieving a 99% mission success rate, according to the companies. Boston Dynamics and GlobalFoundries will identify potential humanoid applications in semiconductor manufacturing, assess integration requirements and customer readiness, and begin training Atlas to perform specific tasks. The companies did not disclose how many Atlas robots will be involved, which facilities will host the humanoids, or what initial tasks they will perform. The Robot Report has reached out to Boston Dynamics for additional information. This story will be updated if we learn new information. The agreement gives Boston Dynamics an opportunity to validate Atlas in a manufacturing environment outside of that of its parent company, Hyundai Motor Group. While automotive manufacturing has emerged as an early proving ground for humanoids, semiconductor manufacturing could present a different set of technical and operational requirements. “Spot has helped us shift from reactive to predictive maintenance, collecting data across thousands of inspection points to prevent downtime and keep our fabs running more efficiently,” said Pradip Singh, chief manufacturing officer at GlobalFoundries. “Scaling Spot and testing Atlas are the next steps in our journey to AI-enabled manufacturing, putting physical AI to work across our operations worldwide.” Boston Dynamics expands Atlas beyond Hyundai When Boston Dynamics unveiled the product version of its electric Atlas humanoid at CES 2026 , it said its initial production run for the year was fully committed. The humanoids were earmarked for Hyundai and Google DeepMind, the latter of which is working with Boston Dynamics to integrate its Gemini Robotics foundation models into Atlas . Boston Dynamics said at the time it planned to begin working with additional customers in early 2027. GlobalFoundries represents the first publicly announced manufacturing customer outside of Hyundai Motor Group. In September, Boston Dynamics opened its Robotics Metaplant Application Center (RMAC) at Hyundai Motor Group Metaplant America near Savannah, Ga. The facility serves as a training and testing ground for Atlas ahead of its integration into Hyundai’s automotive manufacturing operations. Atlas is initially being trained to perform parts sequencing and material handling tasks, with Hyundai targeting component assembly applications by 2030. Boston Dynamics plans to move the RMAC into a facility approximately 10 times its current size in 2027. Hyundai has outlined plans to deploy 25,000 Atlas humanoids across Hyundai Motor and Kia manufacturing facilities over the next several years. It also plans to establish a U.S. factory capable of producing 30,000 robots annually. Boston Dynamics has ambitions for Atlas well beyond automotive manufacturing. In September, the company said it was in discussions with existing Spot and Stretch customers across several industries, including aerospace, semiconductors, logistics, food and beverage, and life sciences. Boston Dynamics’ installed base of mobile robots could provide it with an advantage over humanoid developers that are still establishing relationships with industrial customers. Those existing relationships give Boston Dynamics access to facilities, operational data, and customers that already have experience integrating autonomous robots into their workflows. Atlas continues to evolve Despite entering early production, Atlas continues to undergo hardware and software development. Boston Dynamics unveiled in October a redesigned hand for Atlas featuring four fingers and 13 degrees of freedom (DoF), up from seven DoF in its previous three-fingered design. Boston Dynamics designed the new hand with directly actuated joints and with simulation-based reinforcement learning in mind. The redesign is intended to improve the robot’s dexterity while balancing the reliability and manufacturability requirements of an industrial robot. Boston Dynamics also demonstrated an experimental version of Atlas equipped with wheels in place of its feet. Rather than signaling the development of a new commercial product, the experiment served as a testbed for whole-body control and demonstrated the ability of reinforcement learning-based control policies to adapt to changes in the robot’s hardware. The GlobalFoundries announcement comes just over a month after Boston Dynamics appointed former Amazon executive Rohit Prasad as CEO . Prasad previously served as senior vice president and head scientist for Alexa and artificial general intelligence at Amazon, where he helped build Alexa and led the development of the Amazon Nova family of foundation models. His appointment comes as Boston Dynamics looks to accelerate the integration of AI into its robots. articles.title: Ian Buck Kicks Off NVIDIA’s Week at SC26 as Science Enters the Age of Agents
articles.snippet: NVIDIA’s Ian Buck kicked off the company’s week at SC26 in Chicago on Monday with new tools for AI agents, software that can plan experiments, run code and check results on researchers’ own systems. In NVIDIA’s special address, Buck announced Nemotron for Science , the Rubin HPC GPU and an expanded Vera CPU platform for high-performance computing . He also detailed a new collaboration in quantum computing with IBM and Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory . “The frontier of computing and the new scientific stack is going to be simulation, as always, but combined with AI and the future of quantum,” said Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. Buck opened the talk by looking back to his first public talk on CUDA, at an SC06 tutorial in Tampa, Florida, 20 years ago. NVIDIA now offers more than 1,000 CUDA-X libraries , he said. Open Models for Science Agents “[Agents] have been just a game changer in how we interface with our supercomputers, with our devices, our instruments and how we can do the research,” Buck said. Simulation remains the foundation of scientific computing, “which will always be on the top,” Buck said, with AI, quantum and now agents working alongside it. Nemotron for Science combines the Nemotron 3.5 Super VL open model with a new open chemistry dataset and post-training recipes for life sciences and chemistry, Buck explained. Researchers can run it locally on a DGX Spark, a workstation or their own supercomputer. At Argonne National Laboratory, Buck said, an agent built with the toolkit took a single prompt, planned and tested hypotheses, chose which simulations to run and identified two new binding sites. “You own your data. You own the model,” Buck said. Buck highlighted other agents already in use: GROMACS: An agent from KTH Royal Institute of Technology repairs broken GROMACS setups on its own. In one overnight run on a single DGX Spark, it fixed 81% of test cases. SETI Institute: At the Allen Telescope Array, an agent took a one-line prompt to plot a methanol line. Buck explained that it then retuned for Doppler shift on its own [NGC 869 vs. 896, check slide]. Nsight AI Porting Agent: NVIDIA’s new agent ported a routine from the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model to GPUs, Buck said, speeding it up more than 5x using about 150 million tokens. CPUs for the Agent Loop Agents lean on CPUs to run tool calls between model steps, Buck explained. “That’s exactly what agents need,” he said. “They need a CPU that can run, evaluate, run the tool, perform the operations, gather the results.” DKRZ, the German Climate Computing Center, has selected Vera CPUs for its HLRE-5 supercomputer, expected in early 2028. Buck said it joins Vera systems already announced at Texas Advanced Computing Center. A New GPU for Science Rubin HPC is a new GPU in the Vera Rubin platform, built for science, engineering, analytics and AI, Buck said. It supports precisions from FP64 to FP4, adds sparse-data acceleration and connects over seventh-generation NVIDIA NVLink. With more than 50,000 CUDA cores, it has about three times as many as Hopper, Buck said. It is expected in 2028. Quantum Error Correction Buck said a simulation on Jülich’s JUPITER supercomputer showed that a technique called magic state cultivation can cut the operations needed for one logical step tenfold. The work is being added to CUDA-Q. NVIDIA, IBM and Fermilab announced plans today for a quantum computing co-design platform to support error-correction and applications research. NVIDIA and IBM are pairing NVIDIA DGX B200 systems with IBM quantum computers, including those powered by IBM Quantum Nighthawk. Buck also introduced a new breakthrough for quantum decoding. The goal, Buck explained, is to cut decoding latency from about 300 microseconds to 10. A new CUDA-Q decoding algorithm, TCBP-JOBS, cuts error-correction research computation from 12 weeks to 45 minutes, he said. Networking Buck also showed one of the first deployments of NVIDIA Photonics co-packaged optics switches, at Lambda . He said they are 15x more reliable on bit errors and link flaps. articles.title: Selling to friends
articles.snippet: There are two versions, very different: FAVOR: This is what multi-level marketing preys on. You ask a family member or a friend to buy something, not because they need it, but because you do. This doesn’t always end well. Someone might want to further their relationship with you by doing you this favor, but if the unspoken promise is that the item or service is worthwhile, the disappointment that ensues hurts everyone. Real estate brokers or middlemen in a bind often seek to build friendly relationships at the club or community meetings, but then try to leverage this friendship into a significant sale without doing the hard work of actually being the best choice. TRUST: This is the sort of sale that happens when you begin with the benefit of the doubt but actually deliver a great outcome. You’ll know this is the case when the person who trusted you ends up testifying on your behalf to others. “No pressure” is something that’s showing up more and more in the pitches I’m seeing. Of course, there’s no pressure! Just saying it implies that you wish there were. If you’re asking for a favor, you’re not serving and you’re not selling. You’re trading. And if you’re asking for trust, be prepared to honor the obligation it creates.

articles.title: Your Brain on Grief, Your Heart on Healing
articles.snippet: “Grief is a heart-wrenchingly painful problem for the brain to solve… to live in the world with the absence of someone… ingrained in your understanding of the world… For the brain, [they are] simultaneously gone and also everlasting, and you are walking through two worlds at the same time.” “‘Tis good — the looking back on Grief,” Emily Dickinson wrote as she calibrated love and loss . But she did not mean that it is good to ruminate and wallow — Dickinson so deftly played with the surface of meaning, so delighted in startling us into a flinch or furrow before plunging us into the deeper truths she fathomed. She meant, I think, that a love lost is grieved forever, whatever the nature of the loss — this she knew , and turned the ongoingness of it into a lifetime of art — but by looking back, we are reminded over and over that the sharp edge of grief does smooth over time, that today’s blunt ache is worlds apart from the first stabs, until grief becomes, as Abraham Lincoln wrote in his stirring letter of consolation to a bereaved young woman, “a sad sweet feeling in your heart, of a purer and holier sort than you have known before.” Art by Sophie Blackall for “Dirge Without Music” from The Universe in Verse . And besides, what does it mean to lose a love anyway? We never lose people, not really. I don’t mean this in some mystical sense — let there be no confusion about what actually happens when we die . I don’t even mean it in the poetic sense . I am speaking strictly from the point of view of the mind emerging from the dazzling materiality of the brain — that majestic cathedral of cortex and synapse shaping every thought we have and every feeling we tremble with. I am speaking of the paradox inside the brain: On the one hand, we lose people all the time — to death, to distance, to differences; from the brain’s point of view, these varieties of loss differ not by kind but only by degree, triggering the same neural circuitry, producing sorrow along a spectrum of intensity shaped by the level of closeness and the finality of the loss. On the other hand, no person we have loved is ever fully gone. When they die or vanish, they are physically no longer present, but their personhood permeates our synapses with memories and habits of mind, saturates an all-pervading atmosphere of feeling we don’t just carry with us all the time but live and breathe inside. Or the opposite happens, which is its own devastation — the physical body remains present, but the person we have known and loved, that safehouse of shared memories and trust, is gone — lost to mental illness, to addiction, to neurodegenerative disease. Art by Sophie Blackall for “Dirge Without Music” from The Universe in Verse . In both cases, the brain is tasked with the slow, painful work of reconstituting its map of the world, so that the world makes sense again without the beloved person in it. Mapping, in fact, is not a mere metaphor but what is actually going on in the brain, since our orientation in spacetime and our autonoeic consciousness — the capacity for mental self-representation — share a cortical region . Where the missed and missing person goes on the map, how the remapping actually unfolds, and what it takes to redraw the map in such a way that the world feels whole again are the questions coursing through The Grieving Brain: The Surprising Science of How We Learn from Love and Loss ( public library ) by neuroscientist Mary-Frances O’Connor — a pioneer in fMRI research since the technology first became available, who has devoted a quarter century to studying the particular neurophysiology of grief. She writes: The brain devotes lots of effort to mapping where our loved ones are while they are alive, so that we can find them when we need them. And the brain often prefers habits and predictions over new information. But it struggles to learn new information that cannot be ignored, like the absence of our loved one. […] Grief is a heart-wrenchingly painful problem for the brain to solve, and grieving necessitates learning to live in the world with the absence of someone you love deeply, who is ingrained in your understanding of the world. This means that for the brain, your loved one is simultaneously gone and also everlasting, and you are walking through two worlds at the same time. You are navigating your life despite the fact that they have been stolen from you, a premise that makes no sense, and that is both confusing and upsetting. Making an important distinction between grief (“the intense emotion that crashes over you like a wave, completely overwhelming, unable to be ignored”) and grieving (an ongoing process punctuated by recurring moments of grief but stringing the moments into a larger trajectory), O’Connor adds: Grieving requires the difficult task of throwing out the map we have used to navigate our lives together and transforming our relationship with this person who has died. Grieving, or learning to live a meaningful life without our loved one, is ultimately a type of learning. Because learning is something we do our whole lives, seeing grieving as a type of learning may make it feel more familiar and understandable and give us the patience to allow this remarkable process to unfold. […] Grief never ends, and it is a natural response to loss. You will experience pangs of grief over this specific person forever. You will have discrete moments that overwhelm you, even years after the death when you have restored your life to a meaningful, fulfilling experience. But… even if the feeling of grief is the same, your relationship to the feeling changes. Feeling grief years after your loss may make you doubt whether you have really adapted. If you think of the emotion and the process of adaptation as two different things, however, then it isn’t a problem that you experience grief even when you have been grieving for a long time. articles.snippet: Release: llm 0.37.3 A bug fix release for LLM , mainly to cover a problem with the most recent Homebrew package of the software. Homebrew now ships the latest SQLite, 3.54.1 , which includes a fix that broke LLM's logging code . Short version: in SQLite 3.54.0 the following SQL: select json_object('a', (select json_array(1))) Returns this: {"a":[1]} But in 3.54.1 the same query returns this: {"a":"[1]"} According to D. Richard Hipp : That was a bug fix. Per the documentation, (SELECT json_array(...)) returns SQL text, not JSON. Hence the 3.54.1 behavior is correct and 3.54.0 was a bug. The workaround looks like this: select json_object('a', json((select json_array(1)))) Tags: llm , webassembly , sqlite , generative-ai , ai , llms , d-richard-hipp

articles.title: NVIDIA DGX Spark Developer Kit Turns a Desk Into a Supercomputing Lab
articles.snippet: At SC26, an annual supercomputing conference taking place this week in Chicago, NVIDIA is introducing the DGX Spark HPC Developer Kit for researchers, academics and developers. The kit is a four-node cluster of NVIDIA DGX Spark systems , each connected directly to its two neighbors in a ring, with an NVIDIA HPC SDK installation playbook coming soon. Researchers get a place at their desk to run multi-node scientific workloads, AI models and agents, instead of waiting for time on a shared GPU cluster. The kit puts the GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip on researchers’ desks. A Supercomputing Lab on Any Desk The DGX Spark Developer Kit changes how researchers work. Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26 It scales from one system, or node, to four — linked directly to one another over NVIDIA ConnectX-7 networking, with no network switch to buy or set up. At four nodes, it provides 512GB of combined memory and 16TB of NVMe storage that provides researchers more capacity to distribute models and scientific workloads across the cluster. With NVFP4, researchers can deploy models with up to 700B parameters locally across the four DGX Spark clusters, such as DeepSeek V4.1. With that much power at the desk, researchers with a fixed compute and server allocation no longer have to wait in a queue for every job. Teams can develop and debug on their own, saving server hours for production runs and keeping unpublished results, and proprietary datasets on premises. The playbook for NVIDIA HPC SDK is coming soon, bringing GPU-accelerated C, C++ and Fortran compilers, libraries and message passing interface tools to the DGX Spark cluster — the same development tools used on NVIDIA-powered supercomputers. Teams can build and test scientific applications across four nodes, check how computation and data are distributed, and debug communication issues before scaling to larger systems. The kit brings scientific simulation and AI models and agents to the desktop, with demonstrated four-system workloads including LAMMPS with Kokkos for materials simulation and NAMD for molecular dynamics. The broader DGX Spark community has validated GROMACS for molecular dynamics, OpenFOAM for fluid dynamics, WRF for weather modeling and NVIDIA NIM microservices such as OpenFold3 and Boltz-2 for predicting biomolecular structures. Running on DGX Spark, new open dataset and post-training recipes for Nemotron 3.5 Super VL help researchers adapt the model for life sciences and chemistry, enabling secure scientific workflows on infrastructure organizations control. What Researchers Can Do With It The kit opens up new possibilities for researchers. Researchers can explore agent-assisted workflows that prepare simulation inputs, launch runs and summarize results, while the scientists validate the setup and conclusions. Researchers can also train AI models that approximate slow simulations, then use them to refine wing designs toward minimum drag. Before committing supercomputer time, a team can narrow a 10-million-cell simulation to the 50-500 dimensions that matter. Kvantify is using NVIDIA cuQuantum, and reports running tensor-network simulations of quantum-chemistry circuits with up to 70 qubits and 975 gates on a single DGX Spark, benchmarking circuits generated for penicillin ground-state energy calculations. CYRAN AI , an IIT Delhi spin-out, uses DGX Spark and its PixelFlux library to accelerate JPEG 2000 decoding for large satellite images, supporting local geospatial analysis. OpenFold shows how researchers can fine-tune OpenFold3 on NVIDIA DGX Spark to improve protein-ligand structure predictions for drug discovery. The Rubin Lab at IGI at University of California, Berkeley is using a DGX Spark and NVIDIA Evo 2 model to predict bacterial traits directly from genome sequences by comparing embeddings from genomic and protein language models against the classical baselines. With no 11-hour cluster queue times, results arrived 15x sooner on DGX Spark. The Hartwig Group at UC Berkeley is using a DGX Spark to perform LoRA fine-tuning on the Nemotron 3 Super 120B-A12B model for chemistry machine learning, training a prediction head on experimental values. By running locally on the Spark using NVFP4 quantization, the lab successfully fit a 120B-class model on a single device and bypassed multi-day cluster queue times, allowing them to run continuous eight- to 24-hour training fits back-to-back. Where to Find the Kit The developer kit is on display at SC26 and available for sale. DGX Spark products and cables can be purchased from top OEM partners and are also available through NVIDIA Marketplace . Partners include Acer, ASUS, Dell Technologies, GIGABYTE, H3C, HP, Lenovo, MSI and xFusion. An NVIDIA playbook for building and running the NVIDIA HPC SDK, a software development kit for scientific computing, is coming soon. Once available, it will give scientists and researchers a local platform to develop multi-node GPU applications, explore FP32 and mixed-precision algorithms and run molecular dynamics and materials simulations using LAMMPS with Kokkos before scaling to data center systems. Learn more about NVIDIA DGX Spark . Subscribe to the NVIDIA Local AI newsletter . Follow NVIDIA RTX Spark on X , Instagram , TikTok and Facebook . See notice regarding software product information. Try Deepgram for voice agents that truly understand your context! #contextiseverything Not many people know that Stable Diffusion is why I went fulltime into AI (I aptly titled Multiverse, not Metaverse to call out Zuck’s mistaken investment). It turns out that Dustin Podell also had the same aha moment - quitting his day job when the model came out. But we took very different paths… I stuck to what I knew in human content creation, and Dustin immersed deep into AI content creation with Andreas Blattmann , co-inventor of Latent Diffusion and the rest of the world-leading imagegen crew at Stability AI. Stability fell apart, but Anj Midha helped the core group spin out to BFL, which immediately built an incredible new imagegen model in the Flux series. But why are they now going into video and world models? Andreas gives an example you can try with one hand. If somebody tosses you a ball, your hand starts moving before the ball reaches you. You can do that without being able to write down the trajectory. When he talks about building visual intelligence , that’s the kind of knowledge he means. A still can show you where the ball is. A video shows you how it got there. The sound of impact can tell you when it hit something, even if the camera missed the contact. That’s BFL’s argument for training FLUX 3 on the three signals together. BFL’s FLUX 3 release The horse in motion is one of the FLUX 3 examples we show in the intro. The audio examples are worth playing with the sound on. FLUX 3 Video What a moving camera teaches you Suppose the camera starts in front of a person and pans around them. At some point the model owes you the back of their head. Andreas thinks ordinary two-dimensional video contains a great deal of evidence about what objects look like from other angles. That doesn’t settle whether a model “understands physics,” a point we go back and forth on. It does give you a much better test than asking whether one frame looks convincing. There’s a good engineering example late in the episode. Sharpen each frame of a clip independently and each frame might look terrific. Hit play and the extra detail can shimmer, because the upscaler made a slightly different decision every time. BFL derives its video upscaler from the same FLUX 3 backbone. Temporal consistency matters even when all the user asked for was a higher-resolution file. What’s worth spending training compute on? One of the questions I had for them was whether autoregression was taking over image generation. Andreas gives the other side its due. An autoregressive model can learn from all the tokens in a training example at once. On the diffusion side, the team can distill a long sampling process down to a handful of steps. Which advantage matters depends on whether you’re paying to train the model or waiting for an image to finish. Dustin’s early Kontext experiment is a nice example of how they decide where to invest. He suspected an image model that could draw a dog wearing a hat already knew something about where hats go. He and a colleague collected a small set of photos labeled with relationships. A training run of a few hours got the model to put a logo on a shirt. It was rough, but it was enough to take to the next offsite. The team then spent months on the data and the model. FLUX Kontext examples My favorite user story comes near the end. People were feeding FLUX old, degraded family photos, restoring them, then showing the pictures to their families. Dustin says he hadn’t predicted that use. After talking about preserving somebody’s identity across edits and across frames, it’s a lovely example of who actually notices if you get it right. articles.title: How the World’s Most Advanced AI Infrastructure Supply Chain Invents the Future
articles.snippet: Deb Shoquist leads operations at NVIDIA, overseeing the supply chain and manufacturing behind its AI platforms. That description sums up the job, but it doesn’t begin to encompass what Shoquist has made possible over decades. Shoquist, her team and their global network of manufacturing partners enable NVIDIA to introduce world-leading technologies year-round. Much of the team’s success comes down to her deep relationships with some of the world’s most accomplished manufacturers, including TSMC, Foxconn, Wistron, SPIL, King Yuan Electronics (KYEC), Unimicron, Lumentum, Coherent and Amkor. TSMC has partnered with NVIDIA since 1998. SPIL and KYEC were assembling and testing its chips more than two decades ago. For Shoquist, those relationships grow stronger through each challenge solved together on the factory floor, as every generation of technology demands more from the people and tools behind it. Ask her about the global network she relies on, and she starts with the people. There’s the supplier in Taiwan so eager to get production moving that he calls her at 3 a.m. with a fix to the latest problem. There are the factory workers in Vietnam whose only ask of her are more tools to get more work done. She remembers the partners that supported NVIDIA when it was small, and the work they’ve done to help each other grow. Shoquist meets with key suppliers quarterly and spends six weeks each year on the road visiting partners in Taiwan, China, Korea, Vietnam and the U.S., where conversations move from meeting rooms to factory floors. Recently, she paused her travels to accept the 2026 Dr. Lisa Su Woman of Innovation Award — and to share how she finds the right people and companies to imagine and produce at massive scale technology that has never been built before. Foxconn Q: How would you describe your job to someone outside NVIDIA? A: At the most basic level, our job is to convert designs into the physical world. Our design team creates a blueprint, and our job is to transition it into a reliable, high-performance supply chain. A matchmaker is probably the best analogy. You have to find the partner that matches your ramp style and has the technology that can meet the needs of very precise designs. The supplier has to be financially strong enough to invest in our ramps. They have to be highly technical. And they have to be willing to do something that has never been done before. If you don’t have all three, you can’t create products at the volume and speed that we need. You need those three legs, and in some cases, if you only have two, you have to invest in the company to make them a partner. Q: What’s an example of that in practice ? A: Amphenol’s cable cartridge is the most complex interconnect assembly they have ever built. When I recently visited the Vietnam factory, now in full production, I was struck by the level of precision required to build a product of this complexity. In this large cable cartridge, there are 1,500 small cable legs. Each one requires a very precise assembly to yield a quality level of less than 1 DPPM, or defect part per million. Amphenol built over a hundred automated lines to produce this product at the speed and scale we require. That takes know-how and technology, but it also takes heart, willingness and dedication. Creating anything of that complexity and precision with a supplier forges the partnership. The partners NVIDIA maintains are the ones who supported us when we were small, and yet are willing to scale with us today. Q: What changed as NVIDIA went from selling chips to building systems and platforms? A: When we were primarily a chip manufacturer, we were small, and the semiconductor industry was at scale. In that environment, it was about picking the best technology match for the products we envisioned. As we became a data center systems company, we needed more partners. But we’ve also now entered into new technology areas where the scale of the supply base is still developing. For example, our optical component partners have the technology and the willingness, but they don’t yet have the scale or capital to build fabs for the volume we need. To grow, we needed to support and invest, like we did with Coherent and Lumentum . Beyond that, with products like CPO (co-packaged optics), we’re creating entirely new supply chains with scale partners that are new to the optics world. Leading the integration of talent across the supply chain is the key to driving this incredible technology to high volume quickly. Wistron Q: You clearly enjoy spending time with supply partners, and in particular on the factory floor. What have you learned there over time that can’t be learned anywhere else? A: Over 20 years, you meet many individuals key to the success of your supply. You meet not only the CEOs, but also the people that are running the production floor. These are the people that really know the problems of manufacturing. If you don’t have a tight working relationship with the people deeper in the organization, then it’s hard to have an open dialogue about any challenges. But when you have tight relationships, they want to help you, and they feel comfortable enough telling you, “I need better technical support on the floor. I need more quality engineers. We need a better design. We need to automate this. We need more buffers of material.” That’s what 20 years of working with our suppliers has taught us. It’s year after year of learning from people, getting to know people deeper in the organization and creating the trust where they can tell us what we need to do to be successful with them. Q: Demand for NVIDIA technology is already massive and growing. Your job is to make sure NVIDIA’s volume can keep up. How do you make it happen? A: It goes back to relationships. articles.title: Agile Robots raises $500M to increase production capacity
articles.snippet: Agile Robots’ Agile ONE humanoid moving between workstations. | Source: Agile Robots Agile Robots has raised $500 million in Series F funding. This brings the company’s valuation to $8.5 billion and total funding raised to $2 billion. Agile Robots builds and deploys a range of robots, including humanoids , mobile robots , robotic arms , and robotic hands . It also builds the software and AI models behind these robots. The company’s customers include leaders in the automotive , consumer electronics, healthcare , and service industries. “Physical AI will fundamentally change how the world builds, moves and makes things,” CEO and Founder of Agile Robots Dr. Zhaopeng Chen said. “Our vision is intelligent robots working alongside people in factories and warehouses everywhere, and Agile Robots is determined to lead that shift. We bring physical AI out of the lab and into industrial production, across logistics, automotive, electronics and manufacturing. This funding allows us to accelerate our global expansion, strengthen our presence in key markets and build out production capacity.” SoftBank Group led the Series F round, which also included NVIDIA , Hitachi Group (Hitachi and Hitachi Ventures) and T.Capital. Other investors spanned the automotive, artificial intelligence, digital and industrial technology sectors. “We believe physical AI will transform industries. Agile Robots combines deep robotics expertise with the ability to execute at industrial scale, enabling it to bring physical AI into everyday operations,” said Dennis Chang, managing partner at SoftBank Investment Advisers. “We are pleased to continue partnering with Dr. Chen and the Agile Robots team as they advance breakthroughs in industrial-scale automation.” Inside Agile Robots’ plans to grow The company said it will use the latest funding to support increased production capacity and expansion into key markets. Agile Robots plans to strengthen its presence in the United States and accelerate the development of innovative robotics applications. Agile Robots is one of more than 200 companies tracked in The Robot Report ‘s humanoid robot database , which provides a snapshot of the market. The database tracks each developer’s robots, locomotion systems (wheeled or legged), commercial availability and headquarters location. Agile Robots will also continue to build out production capacity, including in Germany. The company opened earlier in 2026 a production site at Fürstenfeldbruck, near Munich, Germany, to meet rising demand. The site has the capacity to produce up to 10,000 legged and wheeled humanoid robots annually. Agile Robots was founded in 2018 as a spin-off from the German Aerospace Center (DLR), with the goal of applying world-class robotics research to real world industry. Since then, the company has deployed 20,000 industrial robots for customers in the automotive, consumer electronics, logistics and other industries. Now, the company has a growing portfolio of subsidiaries. These include including the global AI robotics research platform, Franka Robotics , and industrial deployment specialist Krause Automation, recently acquired from thyssenkrupp AG. Agile Robots manufactures in-house, including in Germany. Humanoid robots rake in the funding in 2026 Some of the biggest humanoid robot funding rounds in 2026. | Source: The Robot Report 2026 has been a good year for humanoid robot funding. NEURA Robotics brought in the biggest round of the year so far. In June, it announced $1.4 billion in Series C funding. The company said its financing from global technology leaders will help it accelerate its development of “cognitive robots.” Outside of traditional funding rounds, two humanoid robot companies, Unitree Robotics and Agility Robotics, have gone public this year. Unitree Robotics went public on the Shanghai Stock Exchange in August. The company said it raised $905 million from the debut. More recently, Agility Robotics went public on the Nasdaq via a SPAC merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI. Agility previously projected more than $620 million in proceeds from the deal if no shareholders redeemed. Submit your innovation now! articles.title: Paul Christiano – We could be 12 months away from AIs that can overthrow the government
articles.snippet: Paul Christiano is head of the Alignment Research Center. Previously, he was head of AI safety at the US AI Safety Institute. Before that, he led alignment at OpenAI, where he invented RLHF. He’s recently joined OpenAI’s board (though here he is speaking as a private citizen). Paul thinks that on the current trajectory (absent any slowing down), there is a 1 in 3 chance that we could have superintelligence powerful enough to overthrow the government within a year. (He articulates a concrete scenario). He argues that the labs should pause further algorithmic progress until they can secure their weights and research secrets. Otherwise China could simply steal the superintelligence in the middle of the intelligence explosion, and the labs would no longer be able to slow down even if they saw their models going off the rails. He also explains how AIs will be trained during the intelligence explosion, and why even a system trained entirely inside a data center could still have the capabilities profile such that humans would have very little chance of competing with it or controlling it. And he discusses the plan for alignment - basically, making a superintelligence that actually does what we ask the way we mean it. Fixing reward hacks and building better graders will help up till the next few model generations, but he thinks that no single current approach has better than even odds of letting us control superintelligence. The hope is that the AIs figure out the solution to this problem during the intelligence explosion. Watch on YouTube ; listen on Apple Podcasts or Spotify . Sponsors Jane Street has finally come around on formal methods. Ron Minsky, who co-heads Jane Street’s technology group, told me that up until recently, formal methods just weren’t worth the cost. But coding agents have made them easier to apply AND increased the importance of code verification. So now Jane Street is hiring Formal Methods Engineers in both their London and New York offices. If you’re interested, or if you want to watch my full conversation with Ron, go to janestreet.com/dwarkesh Antithesis is NOT another LLM-based code-review tool. It doesn’t try to reason abstractly about how a PR might break your system. Instead, it just runs your code. You start by defining the rules that your system must never break. Then, whenever an agent proposes a change, Antithesis runs your code through thousands of adversarial worlds, testing whether or not it still adheres to your rules. If you want to try it, go to antithesis.com/dwarkesh and use code DWARKESH for 50% off your first month. WorkOS lets you give agents their own sign-up flow. This matters because agents tend to pick tools they can use right away, rather than ones that require humans to register. Fortunately, providing this kind of dedicated path is easy: if you already use WorkOS for login, you just toggle on “Agent Registration” in the WorkOS dashboard. Once it’s enabled, you can decide what agents are allowed to do on their own, and what needs to wait until the person they’re working for gets involved, all with the permissions you’ve already set up. Learn more at workos.com/authkit Timestamps (00:00:00) – We could be <12 months away from AIs that can overthrow the government (00:11:44) – Why an AI might want to takeover (00:20:49) – How an AI takeover could happen (00:35:35) – If labs keep racing without security, China will just steal the weights of superintelligence (00:53:15) – The case for pausing now instead of later (00:59:31) – Superintelligence will be good at learning from real-world experience (01:11:32) – Crossing the sim-to-real gap (01:22:23) – METR says AI progress doubled, so why is revenue growth slowing? (01:27:57) – The best plan we have is to build the plane as we fly it Transcript 0:00:00 – We could be <12 months away from AIs that can overthrow the government Dwarkesh Patel My guest today is Paul Christiano . He is the head of the Alignment Research Center . He recently joined OpenAI’s board . Before that, he was the head of the US Government AI Safety Institute , and before that, he led alignment at OpenAI, where he helped invent RLHF. Paul, what is your assessment of our situation today? Paul Christiano A couple things are on my mind, especially over the last few weeks. Probably the most salient possibility is that we seem to be on this trajectory to build very, very powerful AI, potentially very, very soon. If you asked me, I’d say there’s a reasonable chance that in a year we will produce AI systems much better than humans at almost everything, where humans would have very little chance of competing with them or controlling them. That’s the first big thing on my mind. I think that puts us in a potentially really dangerous situation, even in the short term. It’s quite likely that if we have a rapid intelligence explosion leading to superintelligence , at some point during that process we’ll be unable to control the AI systems we’re producing. Then I am worried that it will be very costly and painful for us to slow down during that process. In part because the security of frontier labs is not strong enough . I think if we produced very powerful AI and then tried to delay deployment for safety reasons, there is a good chance those systems would leak or be stolen, or the techniques to build them would leak or be stolen. I think our risk assessment and governance are also probably not mature enough to notice when things are starting to go off the rails and to respond in an appropriate way. At a high level, that is mostly what is on my mind right now. We have moved from there being some hypothetical risk at some point in the future to there being a pretty severe risk even over the next 6-12 months. Dwarkesh Patel A risk of takeover, of AIs taking over or disempowering humanity within the next 6-12 months? Paul Christiano That’s right. Dwarkesh Patel Where would you place that risk? Paul Christiano I would say we are looking more like a 10%

articles.title: Lambda Boosts AI Factory Resiliency and Efficiency With NVIDIA Photonics
articles.snippet: To train an AI model, thousands of GPUs have to work together, requiring a network that’s fast, efficient and resilient. Lambda is tackling the network piece of the puzzle with NVIDIA Photonics co-packaged optics (CPO) switches. The cloud provider is using the switches to connect NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 racks with more than 10,000 GPUs, delivering lower power, higher resiliency and longer mean time between interruptions (MTBI) to an AI factory at scale. “Networking has to keep pace with the demands of increasingly large AI clusters,” said Dave Ward, president of cloud services at Lambda. “Bringing co-packaged optics into a deployment of this scale is an important step toward building the infrastructure needed to support the next generation of AI.” Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26 In the company’s tests using the switches, network latency — the time needed for moving data — dropped by about 4% at rack scale and by up to about 10% at pod scale. Across rack, scalable unit and pod configurations, the network maintains the same throughput as conventional pluggable optics. Delivering Power Efficiency and Resiliency at Scale Improving power efficiency and resiliency matters because the network sits at the center of AI factory productivity. In a large training job, one interrupted link can stall thousands of GPUs. With agentic inference, one network disruption can introduce cascading latency effects on many agents. Every interruption costs time, and every watt spent on networking is a watt not available for compute. NVIDIA Photonics addresses both power efficiency and resiliency. By replacing pluggable transceivers with co-packaged optical engines on the switch package, it delivers up to 5x better power efficiency and up to 15x higher reliability than conventional pluggable optics. It also uses 4x fewer lasers, which means fewer components that can fail. Cooler Optics, Replaceable Light Sources Increase Resiliency Lambda’s deployment uses NVIDIA Photonics switches, each with 144 ports running at 800Gb/s. Liquid cooling carries heat away from the switch chip and optical engines. The company reports a median optics temperature of 36°C, compared with 51°C for conventional pluggable optics, and its tests find more stable signal integrity. NVIDIA Photonics also brings the electrical-to-optical conversion closer to the switch chip. Each switch has 18 removable external light sources, which supply light to the optical engines. Optical engines sit alongside the chip on the same package and convert electrical signals into light that carries data over fiber between parts of the cluster. Technicians can replace the light-source modules in the field, unlike traditional pluggable optics, which require replacing the entire module if a laser fails. Co-packaging shortens the electrical path from inches to millimeters, which reduces signal loss. It also removes the need for retimer chips, cutting both power draw and the number of parts in the signal path. Explore NVIDIA Photonics and read Lambda’s deployment announcement .
