Loving vs. Being in Love: Jane Welsh Carlyle on Navigating the Heart’s Contradictions
articles.snippet: “A passion, like the torrent in the violence of its course, might perhaps too, like the torrent, leave ruin and desolation behind… My love for you… is deep and calm, more like the quiet river, which refreshes and beautifies where it flows.” Like Alice James — the brilliant diarist who lived and wrote in the shadow of her brothers, Henry and William James — Jane Welsh Carlyle (January 14, 1801–April 21, 1866), unpublished and shadowed by her famous husband, was a literary genius whose private letters stand as masterpieces of prose in their own right. Virginia Woolf admired her as “so brilliant, so deeply versed in life and scornful of its humbugs… the most caustic, the most concrete, the most clear-sighted of women.” Charles Dickens considered her a greater storyteller, with a superior talent for observation and character development, than any of the published women novelists of her day. For a time, she was rumored to have authored the pseudonymously published Jane Eyre . What lent her letters their shimmering intensity of insight was Jane’s uncommon openness to and insight into the complex, often confusing inner workings of the human heart and is maddening contradictions. Jane Welsh Carlyle (Portrait by Samuel Laurence, 1952) Shortly after her twentieth birthday, Jane Welsh met Thomas Carlyle — the essayist, mathematician, historian, and philosopher, who was then a struggling young writer of lower social stature, with no stable income and no intellectual achievement to his name, but would later become Scotland’s most esteemed polymath. At first, she spurned his courtship with the adamant insistence — perhaps out of self-knowledge, perhaps out of self-protection and fear — that she is constitutionally incapable of romantic love, uninterested in marriage at the expense of her intellectual ambitions, and would only hurt him if she consented to a relationship. In a letter from early 1823, found in the devastatingly titled I Too Am Here: Selections from the Letters of Jane Welsh Carlyle ( public library ), she pushes him away with equal parts magnanimity toward his needs and uncompromising clarity about hers: To cause unhappiness to others, above all to those I esteem, and would do anything within my duties and abilities to serve, is the cruelest pain I know — but positively I can not fall in love — and to sacrifice myself out of pity is a degree of generosity of which I am not capable — besides matrimony under any circumstances would interfere shockingly with my plans. Carlyle, conflicted in his own right at the prospect of getting hurt but besotted nonetheless, plays into this game of push and pull, charging that it is “useless and dangerous” for him to love her and that she has made his “happiness wrecked” by letting him fall in love with her and then rejecting him. Jane responds by insisting that her love for him is true, but not the kind he yearns for. In the last week of summer, she grows even more resolute in her dual pledge that she will never leave him as a friend but will never be with him as a romantic partner: My Friend I love you — I repeat it tho’ the expression a rash one — all the best feelings of my nature are concerned in loving you — But were you my Brother I would love you the same, were I married to another I would love you the same — and is this sentiment so calm, so delightful — but so unimpassioned enough to recompense the freedom of my heart, enough to reconcile me to the existence of a married woman the hopes and wishes and ambitions of which are all different from mine, the cares and occupations of which are my disgust — Oh no! Your Friend I will be, your truest most devoted friend, while I breathe the breath of life; but your wife! never never! But then, having issued this most vehement of self-protective disclaimers, she adds: Write to me and reassure me — for God’s sake reassure me if you can! Your Friendship at this time is almost necessary to my existence. Yet I will resign it cost what it may — will, will resign it if it can only be enjoyed at the risk of your future peace — … They continued this conflicted dance for more than a year, until it became clear they had to make a choice. In a letter penned in the first days of 1825, a week before Jane’s twenty-fourth birthday, she confronts the abiding question of how you know whether you are in love, as opposed to merely infatuated: I love you — I have told you so a hundred times; and I should be the most ungrateful, and injudicious of mortals if I did not — but I am not in love with you — that is to say — my love for you is not a passion which overclouds my judgement; and absorbs all my regards for myself and others — it is a simple, honest, serene affection, made up of admiration and sympathy, and better perhaps, to found domestic enjoyment on than any other — In short it is a love which influences , does not make the destiny of a life. Jane Welsh Carlyle (from the miniature by Kenneth Macleay, painted July 1826) Jane had two primary reservations about marrying Carlyle: that their differences — of class, of means, of ambitions — were too vast, and that a life of domesticity would keep her from actualizing herself as a writer. Asserting that “the idea of a sacrifice should have no place in a voluntary union,” she suggests that marrying him would be a self-sacrifice — a form of settling for a life smaller than the life she wants. And yet she also acknowledges that her choice is not between marrying him and marrying someone else, but between marrying him and not marrying at all. She writes: I should have goodsense enough to abate something of my romantic ideal, and to content myself with stopping short on this side idolatry — At all events I will marry no one else — This is all the promise I can or will make. A positive engagement to marry a certain person at a certain time, at all haps and hazards, I have always considered the most ridiculous thing on earth: it is either altogether useless or altogether mise

articles.title: Six AGIBOT G2 Robots Complete 1,730 Tasks in 24-Hour Shanghai Convenience Store Trial
articles.snippet: Four of the six robots pass a performance assessment as the trial puts customer service, retail operations and embodied AI capabilities to the test in a working store. Six AGIBOT G2 wheeled humanoid robots completed a 24-hour trial at an operating convenience store in Shanghai’s Xuhui District, performing a combined 1,730 tasks ranging from customer assistance and coffee preparation to shelf restocking and cleaning. The trial ran from 10 a.m. on November 2 to 10 a.m. on November 3 and was livestreamed to an audience of more than two million viewers across online platforms. Four of the six robots passed the final performance assessment. The event marked the conclusion of AGIBOT’s AI WAVE technology showcase, launched on October 22. Following a series of releases spanning robotics data, simulation, AI models, hardware and operational software, the convenience store trial brought these technologies together in a real-world setting to examine how robots perform everyday tasks over an extended operating period. More broadly, the trial showed how embodied AI could move beyond controlled demonstrations and operate in the changing conditions of a live, customer-facing environment. Six Robots Take on Everyday Store Operations The six G2 robots were assigned different responsibilities: customer assistance, shelf inspections, restocking, coffee preparation, checkout and hot food service, and store cleaning. Over the 24-hour period, they completed 683 customer-service interactions, 369 product pickups and deliveries, 147 coffee orders, 126 breakfast servings, 277 shelf inspections and restocking tasks, and 128 table-cleaning tasks. The trial covered four operating periods: the lunchtime rush, evening peak hours, overnight operations and the following morning’s breakfast rush. Each period brought different demands, from handling customer requests during busy hours to maintaining store operations overnight. The robots were assessed on their time on duty, task completion, customer feedback, response times and ability to handle unexpected situations. Four passed the final assessment, while two did not meet all the criteria. Two evaluators also conducted rounds of practical tests based on situations robots might encounter while serving customers. In one test, they ordered regular and sugar-free Coca-Cola to check whether the robots could distinguish between similar-looking products. In another, they rearranged packs of chewing gum on a shelf and asked the robots to return them to their correct positions. The evaluators also blocked an aisle with a person and a box to test whether the robots could identify obstacles and navigate around them. Real-World Retail Tasks Test Precision and Adaptability A convenience store may appear to be a relatively straightforward environment for robots. Its layout is compact and many tasks follow standard procedures. Yet everyday activities such as picking up products, restocking shelves and preparing food require robots to adapt to small but frequent changes. A bag of candy hanging at a slightly different angle can be difficult to grasp without disturbing nearby products. Handling a delicate item, such as a slice of cake, requires careful control of gripping force to avoid dropping or damaging it. Unlike a controlled laboratory, an operating store presents constantly changing conditions. Customers move through the aisles, products are picked up and returned, and items vary in position, orientation and packaging. Even when a robot repeats the same task, the conditions may differ from one attempt to the next. During the trial, the G2 robots demonstrated several capabilities designed to address these challenges. They used real-time visual information to identify misplaced merchandise and return it to designated shelf positions rather than relying solely on preset coordinates. A robot assigned to restocking detected gaps on shelves and replenished products without a specific prompt. In the cleaning area, another robot distinguished spills from countertop patterns and selected appropriate tools for cleaning. These tasks tested more than individual movements. They required the robots to perceive their surroundings, make task-specific decisions and adjust their actions as conditions changed. Genie Master Connects Robot Actions with Continuous Improvement The trial also tested how AGIBOT’s Genie Master embodied AI agent framework could support task coordination, error correction and learning from operational experience. Even routine store tasks do not always go as planned. A robot may fail to grasp an item correctly, encounter an unexpected obstacle or need to adjust its movements. Beyond completing individual tasks, the trial examined how robots could respond to these situations and use the resulting feedback to improve future performance. Genie Master provides a shared framework for coordinating the six robots and connecting their actions with subsequent analysis and learning. Through the Embodied Execution Protocol (EEP), Genie Master links task planning, execution and feedback. The system organizes work according to each robot’s capabilities and the conditions in the store. Robots then perform their assigned tasks using action policies and real-time observations, with execution results returned to Genie Master for analysis and troubleshooting. The framework also supports learning from previous attempts. By reviewing successful and unsuccessful task executions, it can retain relevant experience in long-term memory for use in similar situations. Effective adjustments can also be converted into training data to help refine the robots’ action policies. This approach is intended to help robots build on previous experience rather than treating each task as an isolated operation. AGIBOT has been using operational feedback to improve G2 performance on tasks requiring precise manipulation, including additional practice during quieter overnight periods. You can also use Runway in ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, Cursor, Replit and more via the Runway MCP . Create any idea with Runway now (1) Google DeepMind Releases AlphaGenome 2 So, uhhh, pretty good time to be Google, huh? On Wednesday, as Nvidia was in turmoil, the maker of GPU competitor TPUs, and our favorite chef of models outside of your plain vanilla LLM, released AlphaGenome 2. Last year’s AlphaGenome 1 took a million letters of DNA and predicted what they do, but averaged across whole tissues. It was very cool! But averages can hide things, like variants that might cause disease in only one rare cell type or only after a cell gets activated. AG2 takes the same million letters plus a condition, which can be a tissue, a cell type, a cell state, or data from a few dozen of your own cells that it has never seen before, and it predicts what the DNA does there specifically. It trained on more than 107 million individual cell profiles from 68 human and mouse tissues. On a benchmark of 28 immune cell types, it found 30% of the variants scientists believe are causal, versus 16% for the old model. As longtime readers know, my process for figuring out whether something in bio is legit is to text Elliot, but this time, he tweeted before I had to: Genome-wide association studies have handed us an enormous pile of DNA variants linked to diseases, and for most of them, scientists are still trying to figure out which gene they touch or which cell they act in, which often takes a lot of real world experimentation. That's a big part of why genetics - we mapped the whole human genome! you can now get yours done for like $100! - hasn’t turned into drugs as fast as everyone hoped. But AG2 can pick up signals from all of that data computationally, which means we’ll be able to rev through them to (hopefully) find cures much more quickly. AG2 still misses most of them (30% is 30%), but going from 16% to 30% in one generation is great progress, and there’s a lot scientists can do with that 30%. Bad time to be a disease. (1a) Argenx Acquires Unnatural Products for Up to $1.15B Real bad time to be a disease, because even if you can use things like AG2 to find targets, you still have to drug them. Which is what macrocycles do. Macrocycles are ring-shaped peptides that sit somewhere between the small molecules that come in pills and antibodies that need to be injected. The promise is the precision of a biologic in a pill that can slip inside cells to hit targets antibodies can't reach. Think something like an oral GLP-1 or cancer therapeutic. Macrocycles are what not boring capital portfolio company Unnatural Products does, and now, it will be doing them inside of argenx. On Monday, argenx announced that it's acquiring UNP for $550 million in cash upfront and up to $595 million more if it hits development and regulatory milestones. Big win for Cam, Josh, and the UNP team! argenx and UNP have been partners since last year, and argenx was already an investor, so it knows what it’s buying. They’ve been working on a pill that goes after FcRn, the same target as Vyvgart, the argenx drug that did $1.72 billion in sales last quarter. The team will keep working out of Santa Cruz, where they have huge lush trees right outside the window, and will become argenx's home for peptide discovery. Naturally, I’m very excited about the win, and we should all be excited to get more of the potential miracle cures we talk about here delivered in effective pill form in the years ahead. (2) Path Robotics Raises $300M for Robot Welders Good welders are insanely valuable. I remember touring SpaceX a few years back and hearing them talk about the one guy who could weld everything in hushed tones. Just this week, I was talking to someone about a golden gloves welder somewhere else who pulls $1 million a year. Welding is the same story we often hear: not enough welders, let alone great welders, to make all of the things we need to make. Back in Dose #214 , we covered Anduril’s $3.7 billion Arsenal-2 shipyard, its answer to the US’ shipbuilding problem. But even with big shipyards, we’re going to need a lot of welders. They just might not all be human welders. Path Robotics , which brothers Andy and Alex Lonsberry started in Columbus, Ohio in 2018

articles.title: How Rhoda AI is using video data to create generalized AI models for robots
articles.snippet: Rhoda pretrains its models on internet-scale video to build a strong prior on motion, physics, and physical interaction. | Source: Rhoda AI Earlier this year, Rhoda AI emerged from 18 months of stealth with $450 million in Series A funding. The company is working with customers in automotive, manufacturing, logistics, and e-commerce to deploy its direct video action, or DVA, model for robotics. “We’re focused on deploying in the real world, and that means you have to deal with the messiness of the real world. Every run can be different,” Jagdeep Singh, the co-founder and CEO of Rhoda AI, told The Robot Report . “Every configuration can be different, and you need a really robust model. To build a robust model, you need a massive training dataset.” A large training dataset is exactly what allowed large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT to rapidly progress in recent years. Physical AI has trailed behind those models because the same dataset doesn’t exist for the physical world, noted Singh. “Every word ever put on the internet, from Shakespeare to Reddit, was used to train these AI models. In the physical AI world, you didn’t have an internet-scale dataset,” he said. “People tried to collect their own data by tele-operating robots, and that approach made for interesting lab demonstrations in robots that could fold T-shirts or make coffees and so on, but none of those demonstrations were robust enough to cross over into the real world. The number of autonomous manipulation capable robots that are solving real world problems today is effectively zero.” Rhoda AI is betting on using video to data to close this gap and to create truly generalized robotics. How does a DVA model work? Many physical AI developers are creating vision-language-action (VLA) models, which allow robots to learn from data from images or videos of its surroundings and text instructions. These models, however, still struggle to cope with the variability of the real world, according to Rhoda AI. The company claimed that its DVA model, which it recently extended with mobile DVA, combines manipulation and mobility into one policy. “The way it works is the model will look at a history of video frames and action tokens and language tokens. From that history, or from that context, it will make a prediction in video for the next few 100 milliseconds, the next half second or so,” explained Singh. “It’ll predict the scene and what it thinks will happen in that scene. Once you have that prediction, you pass it to a second part of the model, which is an action converter. It takes the video scene and spits out robot actions.” “Once you have that action space output, you can execute those actions on a real robot. The robot then moves for that half second, and then you make a new observation, because the state of the world has changed, and you make a new prediction for the next half second,” he continued. “It’s basically making an observation, a prediction of what should happen next, a conversion to action, an execution of the action, and then you close the loop and make a new observation and a new prediction based on that new observation.” For Rhoda AI, quantity of data is key According to Singh, any AI model that’s trained on a small dataset is going to be very brittle. These models could work if the inference time distribution of data is very similar to the training time distribution, but as those distributions diverge, then the model starts to fail. “Hundreds of years of videos were used to train the model, so the model has seen just an incredible diversity of everything: baseball videos, people throwing darts, waves crashing on a beach, or trees blowing in the wind,” Singh said. “Not just videos that have humans in them. Every video has something to teach the model about how the world works. Essentially, the entire internet becomes like a physics classroom.” Rhoda AI uses video data for pretraining. “Once you’ve gotten that pretraining, you then apply a small amount of task-specific training, maybe 10 to 20 hours’ worth, similar to the way you would train a new worker on an assembly line,” said Singh. “They already come in with a certain set of skills, and you need to teach them the workflow of your particular company. With that little bit of post training, the model is able to do things that traditional robots cannot do.” The Palo Alto, Calif.-based company aims to make a model that can understand the world generally. For this, it doesn’t limit the data it uses to just human-centric videos. “We looked at more heavily curated videos that only had human, egocentric manipulation in them,” Singh said. “There was a question of maybe those videos were better to train on. We found that the models that perform the best were the ones actually trained on the broadest data sets, including things that were not obviously relevant to manipulation.” This generalization also enables Rhoda AI’s models to generalize across different robot embodiments. In fact, the specific robot embodiment only comes into play in the post-training phase. How does Rhoda AI offer its models? Singh said Rhoda AI is a full-stack company, and it offers its technology in a range of methods. “We always own the AI layer, that’s the core,” Singh said. “In terms of the body or hardware layer, we can run with our body or a third-party body. In terms of the skills, we can be the ones training the skills, or we can let third parties train the skills. That provides the largest set of solutions to our customers, and that’s really our mission.” Internally, Rhoda AI is focusing on developing skills in manufacturing and logistics . “We’re going after those areas because there’s an immediate problem there,” added Singh. “Many manufacturing and logistics companies have a shortage of labor. Many industries have been offshored for decades because its too expensive to build in those economies. So this technology offers a path to repatriate some of those industries.” Looking ahead, Rhod

articles.title: Narwal builds robot vacuums to serve regional needs
articles.snippet: Narwal has designed robots that can both vacuum and mop. Source: Narwal Robots have entered homes, but the path to consumer adoption has been long and winding. iRobot Corp. was the pioneer but entered bankruptcy proceedings late in 2025. Narwal Robotics Corp. has spent a decade on research and development, testing 30 technical routes to self-cleaning robotic mops, and building a supply chain to retain cost control. While iRobot has emerged from bankruptcy with a new owner, Narwal is working toward an initial public offering (IPO). The company , which has offices in Shenzhen, China, and Covina, Calif., is looking to embodied intelligence to take home robots from the “iPod stage” to the “iPhone moment,” according to founder and CEO Junbin Zhang. Zhang and Icey Bin, head of global brand at Narwal, replied to the following questions from The Robot Report : Narwal took time to understand the household space Why has the household robotics market been so difficult to break into? The household robotics market has exceptionally high barriers to entry in R&D, supply chain, and algorithm development. In the early days, there were no mature industry solutions to reference. For instance, Narwal spent three years with zero revenue solely focused on R&D, iterating the self-cleaning mop structure over 10 times from scratch. Additionally, contract manufacturers were initially reluctant to cooperate due to the complex product structures and low initial volumes. On the software side, features like automatic mop washing require extremely precise positioning algorithms for the robot to frequently return to its base station, which the industry lacked at the time. Most importantly, to achieve a high market penetration, a company must refine the product’s experience, quality, and cost to the reliable standards of mature home appliances, which is an incredibly difficult ceiling to break through. iRobot struggled for a number of reasons . Haven’t other vacuum providers such as Dyson picked up market share? Over the past decade, the core dimension of industry competition has fundamentally shifted from stacking hardware parameters to delivering a low-intervention, automated cleaning experience. While traditional handheld vacuums still have a place, overseas households face complex pain points that require automated solutions—such as deep cleaning for carpets and managing pet hair. To address this, Narwal innovated a dedicated carpet deep-cleaning module that automatically lifts the mop and increases suction, boosting carpet cleaning performance by 40% to 50% compared to traditional models. Furthermore, we pioneered the DualFlow tangle-free system to fundamentally solve the pet hair tangling issue. This paradigm shift toward comprehensive automation and solving highly specific pain points is why Chinese challengers have reshaped the global market landscape. Submit your innovation now! Technology and supply chain were built from scratch How is Narwal’s technology and business model different from those of existing cleaning robot players? Narwal stands out from incumbent players by rejecting the industry playbook of parameter stacking and scale-first growth, instead building original, user value-centered innovations across four core dimensions: Technology route: category-defining innovation from scratch: Instead of incremental upgrades to basic sweeping functions, Narwal created the entire self-cleaning robot mop category from its first product. Its proprietary technology portfolio — including self-developed SLAM algorithms, NarMind autonomous system, FlowWash hot water cleaning, and DualFlow tangle-free system — all target universal industry pain points rather than meaningless parameter competition. A model with full end-to-end control of the supply chain: Unlike the prevalent asset-light, OEM-heavy model, Narwal leverages the mature Greater Bay Area, a leading comprehensive manufacturing hub in southern China. Its full “Shenzhen R&D + Dongguan manufacturing” setup covers the full product lifecycle from development and design to manufacturing and delivery, enabling faster product iteration and consistent quality control. Operating logic: refined long-term management: Narwal rejects short-term tactics such as exchanging losses for market share and eroding brand value through price wars. It operates under a business-unit structure where R&D and frontline teams function as mutual profit centers, balancing innovation investment and market demand to avoid blind feature stacking or ineffective marketing spending. Strategic path: experience-first penetration: Contrary to the “chasing scale first, fixing experience later” industry norm, Narwal follows a long-term experience-first strategy: it polishes floor cleaning performance to mature home appliance standards first, then gradually reduces costs and drives market penetration through supply chain optimization, with the goal of turning robot vacuums from tech novelties into household essentials. In what geographic regions have you found the most traction and why? To date, Narwal’s products have entered more than 30 countries and regions globally, reaching over 6 million users. We have seen significant traction across North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific, and the Middle East. Between January and April 2026, our overseas revenue grew by nearly 50% year-on-year. This success is primarily because we practice a “one country, one policy” approach, heavily customizing product features based on local lifestyle needs. In North America, the U.S. is one of our most important markets. Our Flow 2 claimed the No. 1 spot in the robot vacuum new release category on Amazon U.S. within 24 hours of launch, with sales up 305% year over year versus the previous generation. Key local optimizations include battery capacity and path planning upgrades for large single-family homes, plus a dedicated carpet deep-clean mode and DualFlow tangle-free system roller brush tailored to the high pet ownership

articles.title: AI Is Helping Care Teams Get Patients the Right Care, Sooner
articles.snippet: From pediatric research to smart hospitals, AI is helping care teams spend less time on routine tasks and more time with patients. Health systems and startups are putting it to work across healthcare, from matching patients to clinical trials to supporting radiologists, hospital teams and patients at home. Clinicians stay at the center, reviewing AI outputs and guiding decisions, while NVIDIA technologies provide the compute behind the applications. Read on to learn how healthcare teams are using AI to improve and speed patient care. Tuesday, Nov. 17, 8:00 a.m. PT Proximie Helps Surgical Teams Spend Less Time on Logistics and More Time With Patients As AI advances healthcare, surgery is a high-stakes, highly regulated setting for its use — and one with significant opportunity for efficiency gains. Only about 10% of time spent in the operating room is clinical. The rest is devoted to scheduling, turnover and documentation. With the help of NVIDIA technology, Proximie is introducing AI into operating room (OR) logistics so that clinicians can focus on taking care of patients. A New Vantage Point Proximie is using NVIDIA Cosmos 3 , the frontier open world foundation model family for physical AI, to power a platform used in more than 700 ORs today. Trained on a decade of data, it captures real-time audio, video and device signals from a close-up view of the surgery as well as a wide view of the whole room. The comprehensive view offers context held by no single person in the room, whether the surgeon, scrub nurse or coordinator. Agentic notifications and voice AI tools can call the next patient when a room is ready, document alerts and capture practitioner notes. To protect privacy, Proximie’s models blur identifying details, such as faces, tattoos and onscreen text before footage leaves the OR. Surgeons control the blurring to ensure that recordings used for training still show what trainees need to see. Across health systems where Proximie’s technology has been applied, the platform has enabled clinical teams to handle 8% more cases, turn over the OR 45% faster and start procedures on time 26% more often. Next, the company hopes to turn its technology into an OR copilot that assists with staging equipment ahead of time, estimating time remaining and running implant safety checks. Proximie will also use NVIDIA Cosmos 3 to generate realistic synthetic scenes grounded in real ORs, so models can learn from the rarest, most critical scenarios. The goal is to create a room that runs itself, so practitioners can spend more time with patients and dedicate less time to documentation and preparation. Proximie is working with UC San Diego Health to build an AI model that learns from many kinds of surgical data at once using NVIDIA open models. Before being trained on Proximie’s data, Cosmos 3 could already identify 80% of key equipment in the OR with high accuracy. Training it further on Proximie’s footage made the model more accurate and smaller, so several models can run at once on a single computer in the OR alongside tools to protect patient privacy. Proximie is also among the first participants in Open-H-Hospital , an NVIDIA-led, community-driven open initiative that brings real hospital operation data together with simulation data to train the next generation of hospital AI and robotics. Learn more about Proximie. Tuesday, Nov. 17, 8:00 a.m. PT ConcertAI Matches Cancer Patients to Clinical Trials Faster Interest in clinical trials is high among people with cancer. More than half of those offered a trial say yes, but only about 7% of U.S. patients with cancer take part in one. The issue isn’t the availability of trials, but the time it takes to match patients to them. Care teams have to manually review months or years of medical records and pull together information like physician notes, pathology reports and genomic results from different systems. Built on NVIDIA AI, ConcertAI’s Cara AI engine and TriaLinQ module are speeding up that process, identifying eligible patients roughly 3x faster than manual methods. They assess trial eligibility across the CancerLinQ oncology network, ConcertAI’s data network that works across nearly 1,000 sites of care and over 13 million patient records. From Scattered Records to One View Cara pulls all relevant patient data into a single view for each person and updates it weekly with disease stage, biomarker status, treatment response and line of therapy. TriaLinQ, a module of the CancerLinQ suite, uses that information to assess a patient’s eligibility for a trial. “We use a chain of AI models and agents to parse all the information, understand really challenging concepts like progression or timelines within a diagnosis journey, and summarize it into a structured data model that can be queried from our software stack,” said Eron Kelly, CEO of ConcertAI. ConcertAI uses healthcare-specific NVIDIA microservices, software libraries and AI agent tools to accelerate its work. Clinicians Stay in Charge ConcertAI brings new technology to care teams, but treatment decisions stay with clinicians. “The promise of technology in oncology isn’t measured by how sophisticated the platform is, but instead by whether it meaningfully supports the clinicians delivering care and positively impacts patient outcomes,” said Dr. Shaalan Beg, chief medical officer of oncology at ConcertAI. “That’s the standard we hold ourselves to: AI that earns its place at the bedside.” Every eligibility finding links back to its source in the patient’s record, so oncologists and care teams can make fully informed treatment decisions. By integrating into the way care teams and clinicians already work, ConcertAI’s systems support up to 50% higher trial enrollment, helping more patients find treatment options when they need them. Learn more about ConcertAI. Monday, Nov. 16, 8:00 a.m. PT Artisight Helps Nurses Prevent Patient Falls With In-Room AI Device Roughly 700,000 to 1 million patients fall in U.S.

articles.title: 10 Friday AM Reads
articles.snippet: My end-of-week morning reads: ​• Venture Is Dead (Again) : Benchmark raised $425 million in 2024, plus $170 million from its partners, and told LPs it was holding fund size flat to force discipline. This June it raised $2 billion, including its first-ever $1.25 billion growth fund. Ballooning fund sizes are forcing venture partners to make bad deals or take on less uncertainty. History suggests it won’t end well. ( Colossus ) • Spies Like Trump : The president is a national security risk. Always has been. How could this have happened? How could the president of the United States find himself at the center of a massive security breach? ( The Bulwark ) see also Lutnick stalled Trump’s Nvidia–China chip curbs after Oval talks : President Trump on Thursday authorized a crack down on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia’s advanced AI chips to China for the third time this year — even consulting Elon Musk before giving the go-ahead. One administration official has repeatedly stood in the way: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. ( Axios ) ​• This Shipping Lane Is Now the World’s Deadliest. It Isn’t Hormuz. : A series of attacks in the Black Sea has killed more people than strikes on shipping so far in the U.S.-Iran war, disrupting trade routes. Fatal attacks in the Black Sea have jumped, disrupting trade routes and posing a new test for NATO ( Wall Street Journal ) ​• The Wisdom of Prediction Markets : Michael Mauboussin of Morgan Stanley’s Counterpoint Global starts with Baruch’s foreword to Mackay and Surowiecki’s wisdom of crowds, then asks what a theory of markets must explain: why prices are usually sensible and periodically go bonkers. ( Financial Times ) • Key voices rushed to defend Jensen Huang online. But many commenters were fake . Some of the world’s richest men (Elon Musk, Shaun Maguire and Bill Ackman) supported Nvidia CEO online after revelations of an affair with an alleged spy. But research suggests many online posts were fake. ( Washington Post ) ​• ‘Screwed Twice’: The CFPB Says It’s Looking Out for Consumers. Its Own Data Tells a Different Story : Complaints about banks and other financial players keep rising as Trump officials squelch enforcement actions at the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau Sophie Sullivan and Byard Duncan, Co-published with the Economic Hardship Reporting Project. ( The Guardian ) ​• The Rise of the Overprepared Concertgoer : Cassidy Sollazzo on fans who study setlists like exams, with a TikTok post that drew 400-plus agreeing comments as the hook. More and more pop fans are arriving at concerts with setlists memorized. What’s driving this intense, need-to-know energy? ( Paste ) ​• Why Pollsters Think Surveys Undershot Democrats’ Midterm Strength : Diagnosing the causes of polling misses often takes many months. But The Pollwatcher asked pollsters from a range of backgrounds for their initial thoughts on why most surveys underestimated Democrats as well as the overall performance of election polls this year. Scott Clement: polls underestimated Democrats by about four points in key contests, a break from the fairly accurate 2018 and 2022 midterms and from the last three presidential elections, which erred the other way. ( Washington Post ) See also : Why Polls Fail: Attitude, Intention, Behavior 1. What do people really believe? 2. How well do they know their own actual intentions? 3. How likely are they to act on those? ( The Big Picture ) • Wonderful Weather: Floods and Foreboding in 17th-Century Britain : When the Bristol Channel flooded in 1607, it was not just one of the worst natural disasters in British history, it was also a sign, for many, that they had strayed from the path of God. Erik Crnkovich examines the overlap of miraculous weather and the early modern printing industry, which cultivated a thirst for all things occult, exotic, and odd. ( Public Domain Review ) ​• Phil Collins Knew He Was ‘Lucky,’ if Not Cool : Jon Pareles on the 75-year-old Collins, who goes into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame as a solo act on Nov. 14, sixteen years after Genesis got in. Three divorces, alcoholism and years of being mocked as uncool, and he still calls himself lucky. ( New York Times ) Video of the day : Psychology of IQ Levels: How Each Mind Gets Fooled (IQ 85 vs IQ 160) (Turn Wiser) Be sure to check out our Masters in Business interview this weekend with Salim Ramji, CEO of Vanguard Group, the world’s largest asset manager. He became the firm’s first CEO recruited from outside Vanguard, arriving after a decade at BlackRock, where he led its enormous iShares and index-investing business. CEO exits from history (lol Ballmer) Source: Financiual Times Sign up for our reads-only mailing list here . The post 10 Friday AM Reads appeared first on The Big Picture .

articles.title: Ten minutes a day
articles.snippet: You can’t become fluent in a foreign language in ten minutes a day, even if you try for months. On the other hand, here are a dozen things many of us can do (or do better) if we stick with it: Three-ball juggling Touch typing Rubik’s Cube Drawing Mental math Memorizing a deck of cards or people’s names Meditating History or geography Finding joy in small things Typography Ukulele Italic handwriting Morse code Excel and HTML There are two hard parts: The seven minutes after minute three Doing it again tomorrow “I can’t do that,” might often be more honestly reported as, “I haven’t chosen to be able to do that.”

articles.title: [AINews] Jensen Huang resigns after 33 years leading NVIDIA
articles.snippet: Congrats to Gemini 4 Hydrogen on their launch and it seems Anthropic’s IPO is well under way, but today’s headline was only ever going to be about one thing, the most earthshaking leadership change in AI (after Demis/Jeff/et al at Google DeepMind). Yesterday we covered reports that NVIDIA’s board was preparing to replace Jensen Huang following an NYT report of an affair with an accused Chinese spy . Following news of a second affair , today NVIDIA announced his resignation (correlation/causation is debatable here), presumably forced by the board: View post on X ↗ There is also some discussion of the extent that Chinese models can demonstrably be shown to be trained on Blackwell GPUs that they should not have access to… though the scale is debated . After 33 years, Jensen Huang has stepped down as CEO, president and boardmember. Colette Kress, NVIDIA’s CFO since 2013, will keep that job while serving as interim CEO… leading into what will presumably the best attended earnings call in the history of $NVDA next week. AI News for 11/11/2026-11/12/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! AI Twitter Recap Gemini 4 Hydrogen: Google's Fast Gemini 4 Tier Ships Broadly Launch : Google DeepMind released Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a speed-first model positioned alongside Carbon and Argon. Google says it completes tasks 2.5x faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash and edges Argon on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, 51 vs 50 at default thinking and 54 at the new xhigh level ( DeepMind , Koray Kavukcuoglu ). Specs and pricing : The model offers four thinking levels (low, medium, high and xhigh) and a 1M context window. It costs $1.50/$7.50 per million input/output tokens, with a 95% discount on cached input ( Phil Schmid , Artificial Analysis ). Official claims : Google reports 57% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and more than 3x Gemini 3.8 Flash on Terminal-Bench 4.1. It also claims more than 5x fewer fabricated claims, #1 on Vals Tax Agent Bench and leading results on AutomationBench-AA and Agents' Last Exam ( Google ). Availability : Hydrogen is available on all Gemini API tiers, including a free tier in AI Studio. It is the default model in Search AI Mode, and free Gemini app users get it through auto-selection. Paid Pro and Ultra subscribers can use it in Antigravity ( Sundar Pichai , GeminiApp , Search ). Orchestrator multi-model mode : In Antigravity, Carbon plans while Hydrogen writes and tests code. Google says this reaches near-Carbon success on Terminal-Bench 4.0 with 24% less quota and 19% faster completion. It is rolling out to Ultra subscribers ( Google , Mohan ). Artificial Analysis measurements : The independent results show a mixed profile. Intelligence and cost : At xhigh, Hydrogen scores 54, one point behind Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max) and GPT-6.1 Sol (max). Its cost is about 32% of Sonnet's but about 2.5x Sol's. Cost per task is $3.16 at xhigh and $1.87 at high. Output speed is about 200 tok/s ( AA ). Strengths : Hydrogen has an 8% hallucination rate on AA-Omniscience, versus 43% for Sonnet and 52% for Sol. It also shares the #1 score on GDP.pdf visual reasoning. Weaknesses : It scores 54% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 at both high and xhigh, below Sonnet at 64% and Sol at 56%. Third-party leaderboards : Agent Arena : Hydrogen debuts at #5 with +14.8% net improvement across 6.5k sessions. It is the fastest model in the top 10 at 5.3 minutes per task median, with a median cost of $1.6 per task ( Arena ). Code Arena WebDev : It ranks #10 with 1703 points ( Arena ). Vals Index : It is #6 at 68.5%, 2 points behind Carbon at 38% of Carbon's price ( Vals ). Coding agents : CursorBench rises to 54.3% from 39.6% for 3.8 Flash ( Cursor ). Cognition's FrontierCode 2.0 shows 38.2%, just behind Sol ( Cognition ). SWE-sweep shows 13.5%, versus 9.5% for Astra ( KLieret ). Caveats from users : Runaway reasoning : One tester saw xhigh spend 131K thinking tokens and about $1.08 without answering a jersey-number image question. The same tester reports budget exhaustion on 1.8% of a text benchmark ( skalskip92 ). Weak spots : Hydrogen scored 1% on MazeBench ( patience_cave ). Pricing structure : Simon Willison says Hydrogen is only a 25% discount on the Carbon/Argon token price, though those models reportedly double in price on Dec 1 ( simonw ). Speed : Theo disputes the "built for speed" framing based on his own timings ( theo ). Open-Weight Releases: Inkling 2 Small Leads Inkling 2 Small : Thinking Machines released the weights under Apache 2.0 ( thinkymachines , Mira Murati ). Size : It is a 594B-total / 17B-active MoE with text and image input and up to 1M context ( HF ). Architecture : New components include attention residuals with a q/k/v split, gated attention, a dynamic attention sink, dynamic shortconv and value norm ( Songlin Yang ). Experts use NVFP4 in layers 0–39 and MXFP8 in the last eight, with SWA widened to 1k and softcaps on the LM head and SwiGLU ( eliebakouch ). Day-0 serving : On vLLM, it fits on one GB200/GB300 node and reaches up to 630 tok/s per user at TP4. Its native DSpark speculator has an acceptance length of about 3.5 at T=1.0 ( vLLM , details ). SGLang reports 576 tok/s per user at batch 1 on Vera Rubin and text-plus-vision RL on 8 Blackwells ( SGLang ). SkyRL validates MXFP8, BF16 and LoRA RL ( erictang ). Evals : It is the #1 US open model on Code Arena WebDev at 1647 points ( Arena ). On Agent Arena it is #2 among open models, with a median cost of $0.26 per task ( Arena ). It also holds the top open-model spot on MathArena's BrokenArXiv ( MathArena ). Edge0-145B/120B : These are device-native open-weight models. The developer claims 86.5% on Terminal-Bench 2.1, versus 78.2% for Claude Opus 4.6, in about 29GB of memory at 75+ tok/s decode ( Samuel Zeng ). These figures are vendor claims. articles.title: AI Ambition: ArtCraft Cloned Photoshop and Now Wants to "Rebuild Everything"
articles.snippet: The theme of day two of the AI Engineer Code Summit in San Francisco was increasing ambition using AI . And there have been few projects as ambitious as ArtCraft in the AI era. So far the fledgling company has released 17 open source versions of popular software tools , starting with a Photoshop alternative built from scratch in Rust called PhotoCraft . You could feel the excitement in the room this morning when ArtCraft founder and CEO Brandon Thomas presented a kind of manifesto for AI-based open source at AIE Code. When he mentioned that ArtCraft had cloned Adobe’s Acrobat, with a product called PdfCraft, it got a round of applause from the audience. In wrapping up, his rallying cries of “let's take back the entire internet” and “let's rebuild everything” were greeted with whoops and cheers. Thomas began his presentation by reliving the internet’s early history. In his view, the web started out with the right intentions, but things got screwed up once Web 2.0 hit the mainstream. “We had a bunch of chat applications that were completely open,” he said, regarding the 1990s internet. “So, IRC is like Discord, but you can spin up your own servers that you actually own. You can use whatever programs to automate them and interrogate them without rules.” His point wasn’t necessarily that everything was open source, but that web users could freely build things. With Flash, for example — a commercial animation tool eventually acquired by Adobe — “kids were making all kinds of animations.” When Web 2.0 came along, with its superior broadband and smartphones, “it brought everybody into the fold.” Thomas acknowledged that this widened the scope of internet software, but at the cost of that freedom to build with leading apps. “The diffuse, experimental, early web started to disappear,” he said. “The APIs got taken away from us, and then we started seeing distribution being gatekept by the big providers.” It seems Adobe in particular annoyed Thomas. He described getting billed with an unexpected fee when he cancelled a monthly plan. “It's really frustrating that the web — that was once really, really promising and open and free — has turned into this extractive, owned, rent-seeking world.” This inspired him to start ArtCraft, “with the ethos of ‘let's build everything open source.’” A message even anti-AI people have gotten behind, according to Thomas. In addition to PhotoCraft, they’ve copied other apps in the Adobe suite, cloned Figma, and created a Microsoft-like word processor called WordCraft. There are also independent apps such as SolidCraft, a community-led CAD project distributed through ArtCraft’s launcher. Thomas reiterated that these AI-built applications are 100% open — “not only the desktop apps, but the actual infrastructure as well.” PhotoCraft: The development process ArtCraft is starting with rewriting familiar tools. Thomas’s longer-term vision is for users (such as artists who were previously using Photoshop) to tailor the software to their own workflows. As he framed it, they want to “undo what had happened during Web 2.0 , when everything became owned and consolidated and gatekept, and just give people back their applications.” AI is the means to achieve that, he said. But aren’t there already open source alternatives to Photoshop, like GIMP? “GIMP isn't really used by artists,” said Thomas during his presentation. “We actually observed artists vibe coding their own workflows on top of the software that we gave them.” To begin creating PhotoCraft, the team gave an AI model a detailed prompt outlining Photoshop’s tools, data structures and file importers. After that, they “laid out a large, large prompt to say, let's build out the application.” As part of that process, they made everything MCP and CLI compatible . Within 24 hours, said Thomas, “we were looking at a pretty good approximation of what Photoshop was — and it kind of blew our minds away.” PhotoCraft interface; via ArtCraft website Thomas noted that PhotoCraft is “still not at 100% parity” — he said they’ve just passed 60% — but the team has set an internal goal to reach as close to 100% as possible. ( The project’s GitHub claims about 76% parity for feature breadth and about 46% for professional readiness.) “Right now, we want to fill the muscle memory of all the artists that use Adobe. So we are going for Adobe , their interface and ‘look and feel’ directly.” But after ArtCraft has achieved that, they plan to “build new apps that have new interfaces that are more agentic. ” A big reaction Thomas said he was surprised by the amount of attention PhotoCraft, in particular, has gotten — ranging from the New York Times requesting an interview, to a swelling of its open source community to about 4,000 developers . “I'm still struggling to bear with what has happened. It struck a nerve with people. They felt sort of maligned by Adobe and other tech companies . And what we built has really resonated with them.” After his presentation, Thomas was mobbed by AIE Code attendees. ArtCraft’s apps are being downloaded at the rate of about 1.7 million per day, which Thomas said is still accelerating. In addition to the 17 official apps, there are around 300 being developed by the community, he added. Rust is key, but there have been technical challenges Other than the AI technology, Thomas said that Rust was a crucial part of making the apps performant — he claimed that PhotoCraft opens ten times faster than Photoshop, for example. “Rust was probably essential in this product's success,” he said. “We've seen people do it in Electron before, but for high-quality creative apps, you really need something that's native. ” For those engineers who are not experts in Rust, Thomas has good news for you. “Do you need to know Rust to start using Rust today as an engineer? Definitely not. [...] Your agents will drive it just fine.” However, Thomas admitted that not everything has gone swimmingly. “We've run into a lot of gotchas — like permi

How to Hear the Song of Life
articles.snippet: “When we have learned how to listen to trees,” Hermann Hesse wrote in one of his least known, most beautiful essays , “then the brevity and the quickness and the childlike hastiness of our thoughts achieve an incomparable joy. Whoever has learned how to listen to trees no longer wants to be a tree. He wants to be nothing except what he is. That is home. That is happiness.” To be ourselves is rooted in the recognition that, rather than a tree, a self is a forest ; to be at home in the world is rooted in the recognition that a forest is a self. While indigenous cultures have known this since the dawn of knowledge, we are only just beginning to unlearn everything we have been taught by the erasure of our creaturely belonging that we call civilization in order to remember what we were born knowing: Life and its rights are not something we can claim for ourselves unless we accord them to everything else that exists, bound to us by the mesh of mutuality that makes this drifting rock a living world. In 2021, Ecuador led the way in this great unlearning by granting the Los Cedros Cloud Forest legal rights of personhood: the right to exist and flourish in the future. The Los Cedros Cloud Forest Five years later, four pioneers of the rippling rights-of-nature movement have joined forces with the forest itself to celebrate the landmark decision, as Copernican in the history of our civilization as the Cambridge Declaration of Consciousness: Robert Macfarlane (who has asked the urgent, self-answering question “Is a river alive?” and who remains the closest thing to a Rachel Carson of our time), Giuliana Furci (who has changed not only how we think about nature with her Fungi Foundation work but the very container of our thoughts, language, coining the word funga , now inducted into the Cambridge Dictionary , to stand alongside flora and fauna in our classification of the living world), César Rodríguez-Garavito (whose legal scholarship and activism have anchored the rights-of-nature movement), and Cosmo Sheldrake (who has devoted his life to turning the soundscapes of the living world into music). That they have named the Los Cedros Cloud Forest itself as co-author is both a radical gesture — a first in the history of literature — and a kind of homecoming to an elemental reality our sciences are only just beginning to confirm: that we think not with the brain but with the world , that place and personhood are indelibly entwined , that life is a song singing us back to ourselves so that when we die we may be sung across the threshold into the rhizomatic everythingness of everything . Illustrated by Ecuadorian artist Paula Terán Ospina, Song of the Cedars is a painted serenade to what the cloud forest can teach us about the song of life: about the time of stones , about the wisdom of rivers , about the creative tenacity of fungi . It is a project breathtakingly beautiful in spirit and in matter, the song sung along the river that carries the ecosystem and unfolds like a paper harmonica to carry the words that break the civilizational spell of indifference with enchantment. Trees speak in your leaves please And streams tell me your dreams Birds sing me your rhymes please And stones teach me your times Earth cover my limbs now And mold thrive on my skin Clouds deepen my sight please And storms lend me your light The back matter, following five short essays by the different contributors, is a painted encounter with the cloud forest’s wonderland of flora, fauna, and funga — 81 creatures each identified by their common and Linnaean names, occupying every niche and scale of existence, from the fierce ocelot ( Leopardus pardalis ) to the tender rosy flannel moth ( Trosia neigropunetigera ), from the air plant hovering ethereal midway between the canopy and the ground to the lichen clinging to the rocks more tenaciously than gravity itself — a vibrant reminder that, as Giuliana writes in her essay, “wherever we look, life is there.” Beholding this loving song of life, I am struck by what a rare achievement it is in this culture to teach without preaching, to protest not with militancy but with tenacious tenderness, to remember that care is a stronger and longer lever of change than complaint, that how we show up for the summons of conscience, as individuals and as a civilization, is the deepest measure of who and what we are. donating = loving For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If this labor makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider lending a helping hand with a donation .
