articles.title: NVIDIA replaces CEO amid China AI and robotics concerns
articles.snippet: NVIDIA says it will continue to support customers amid its leadership changes. Source: NVIDIA After a tumultuous week that saw NVIDIA Corp.’s stock drop by about 18.5%, CEO Jensen Huang has stepped down. The company today said it has appointed Collette Kress, executive vice president and chief financial officer, as interim CEO and investor Harvey C. Jones as its first board chair. Huang, who is one of the most recognizable figures in AI, recently admitted to extramarital affairs including with Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Megaspeed who is suspected of being a Chinese spy, and Kimberly Powell, vice president of healthcare at NVIDIA. “To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me,” Jensen Huang wrote in a statement on Nov. 8. “Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, NVIDIA’s board of directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully.” Huang co-founded NVIDIA in 1993, and it makes graphics processing units (GPUs) and software architectures that are the basis for much of advanced computing and AI today. The Santa Clara, Calif.-based company has a market capitalization of about $4 trillion, and its simulation and other technologies are used in industrial manipulators, autonomous mobile robots ( AMRs ), and emerging humanoid robots. Kress and Jones to provide business continuity Kress has served as EVP and CFO of NVIDIA since joining the company in September 2013. NVIDIA said that she has played a key role in its growth and evolution. Prior to joining NVIDIA, Kress spent nearly 25 years in finance roles at leading technology companies including Cisco and Microsoft. “NVIDIA’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years,” stated Kress. “We will continue advancing the work that has made NVIDIA a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders.” Jones has been an entrepreneur, technology executive, and venture investor for more than 30 years. He has served as CEO and executive chairman of Synopsys. “Colette has helped lead NVIDIA through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position,” said Jones about Kress. “She is supported by an experienced leadership team that has been instrumental in executing NVIDIA’s strategy and advancing its technology roadmap. The board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company’s operations, customer commitments, and product roadmap to continue without interruption.” Submit your innovation now! NVIDIA to endure competitive scrutiny China leads the world in robotics manufacturing and usage, but it still relies on U.S. AI chips and edge computing components. Amid heightened trade conflicts, NVIDIA has worked with numerous global humanoid developers, including Unitree Robotics and Alibaba Cloud . Recent revelations about possible circumvention of U.S. export controls could lead to further investigations and reputational damage. But in the meantime, NVIDIA has continued to support the robotics industry. Just this week, NVIDIA introduced GR00T 2, an updated open frontier world action model, and Isaac Lab 3.0, the latest version of its open-source robot learning framework. Huang spoke at GTC Berlin last month (see video below). In September, NVIDIA said it planned to acquire Hugging Face Inc.’s open AI development platform for $12.9 billion. Pollen Robotics , a Bordeaux, France-based subsidiary of Hugging Face , had developed the Microduck open-source legged robot , which uses a Chinese processor. NVIDIA last month described how robots such as Microduck could use its Isaac Lab learning framework, Newton physical modeling, Omniverse libraries, and Isaac Sim simulation for evaluation. Its deal with Hugging Face will receive more scrutiny, and competitors such as AMD , Qualcomm , Arm , and Intel may try to position themselves are more reliable Western suppliers. Reuters and Monrningstar noted that Huang’s departure could slow deals around AI . The departure of a prominent tech exec could also lead to greater government scrutiny of trade deals as efforts continue to build so-called sovereign AI and robotics. The Robot Report will continue tracking these developments. The post NVIDIA replaces CEO amid China AI and robotics concerns appeared first on The Robot Report .

articles.title: At the Money: Investing for Creative Types
articles.snippet: At the Money: Investing for Creative Types AJ Ayers, November 11, 2026 Artists need budgets, songwriters need to save for retirement and anyone who is right-brained needs to understand money too. Financial security enables creative risk-taking, as well. Full transcript below . ~~~ About this week’s guest: AJ Ayers is co-founder of BKFi and author of the book, “ Creative Money: New Financial Rules for Artists, Innovators, and Misfits ” For more info, see: Personal site Professional website LinkedIn ~~~ Find all of the previous At the Money episodes here , and in the MiB feed on Apple Podcasts , YouTube , Spotify , and Bloomberg . And find the entire musical playlist of all the songs I have used on At the Money on Spotify TRANSCRIPT: AJ Ayers on Creative Money , Co-Founder, Brooklyn Fi Book: Creative Money: New Financial Rules for Artists, Innovators, and Misfits BARRY RITHOLTZ: Are you a creative person who struggles with their finances? Artists need budgets, songwriters need to save for retirement. And anyone who is a creative, right-brain person needs to understand money also, and financial security enables creative risk. That’s a quote from our guest, AJ Ayers. She’s the co-founder of Brooklyn Fi, a financial advisory firm. Her new book, Creative Money: New Financial Rules for Artists, Innovators, and Misfits , was just published in November 2026. So I want to talk a little bit about the advice you give to creative types, but I have to start with talking about your career. You went from editing books about music to helping people manage their money. What did working with artists teach you about wealth that Wall Street kind of misses? AJ AYERS: What I learned from being in book publishing and working with musicians was that communication matters. And I think that’s where, with Wall Street and other financial advisors, I saw a gap in the market: there are young people who are making serious money, whether it’s from a record deal or a book advance or what have you. And they want financial advice. They need tax advice, and they’re not ready for portfolio returns. They need a financial plan. And so that was the gap I saw. And when I looked around at my own life as a right-brain creative who never did well in trig—I never took trig—I thought, “Hey, this financial advice thing is actually not that complicated. I think I could do this too.” BARRY RITHOLTZ: I took math. I went all the way, and I’ve never used trig since high school. So you’re not missing anything. So traditional, conventional financial advice kind of gets things wrong for right-brained people. What do you think the standard playbook misses for someone who earns money through royalties or commissions or advances or one-time windfalls, and the rest of the time they’re just gigging for pocket change? AJ AYERS: The traditional financial advice misses this fact that income is irregular for a lot of people. And, I write in the book, it’s not just the hipsters and the hippies anymore. It’s consultants. It’s a lot of people in many industries, not just the specifically creative ones that I call out, that have this irregular income. And you have to be much more disciplined about savings. You have to think more about money. You don’t have the luxury of a paycheck showing up every two weeks. So you have to take it more seriously. And unfortunately, these artists and creatives often don’t, and often they just hide from it completely, which sets them even further behind when they have more, frankly, opportunities to become financially independent, to get ahead. BARRY RITHOLTZ: So you’re advising these people how to build a predictable financial life around an unpredictable income. What replaces the typical monthly household budget when there isn’t a regular paycheck? AJ AYERS: The answer to that is, financial planning is tricking yourself into thinking that you have a salary. So in the book, I kind of lay out, “Hey, there are different stages of a business, and you always have to treat your income as if you are running a business.” And I think people rely too much on others to dole out income in regular intervals. So I say, set up your own checking account, pay yourself every two weeks, figure out what makes sense to you, and make sure you’re saving first before you’re spending money. Because I think there’s this—especially when money doesn’t show up regularly—it’s, “Oh my God, the money’s finally here. I have to go do this. I want to go spend. I want to go buy something nice. I want to go buy a house.” When in fact, you’re actually getting your salary front-loaded for the next three years. So you have to be more strategic about how you dole it out to yourself. BARRY RITHOLTZ: You very specifically advise people who get a big windfall like that, when their income stream is irregular: “Hey, the first thing you have to do is pay Uncle Sam.” You have to put money aside for taxes. Tell us about why that’s such a challenge. AJ AYERS: Well, the first thing you should do when you get a windfall is spend 1% on something awesome. BARRY RITHOLTZ: I love that. We’re going to come back to that later. That’s probably my favorite quote in the book. AJ AYERS: Yes. But I think it’s step three—I think it’s step three—where it’s know what you’re going to owe in tax, and people just skip this step. My whole tone in the book is, you are not a freak. You’re not a weirdo if you never learn this stuff. The freaks and the weirdos are the people who grew up knowing about money, who know what tax brackets are and what have you. But taxes is where creative people get into trouble. That’s where, in their first year, they get a big check, they don’t think about taxes, and they spend it all, and they get a huge tax bill, and now all of a sudden they’re in debt. And that’s really scary. So in the book, I talk a lot, in the tax chapter, about just please have a bare minimum understanding of how taxes work. When in doubt, save 50% of every dollar you make. If that sounds c

articles.title: ShopPurple
articles.snippet: Launching today: a collection of hundreds of stores that are worth detouring past Amazon to get to. The stores were nominated by you, the readers of this blog, and are only lightly curated. There’s no business model for the site, just a collective sharing. Click and explore. There are three ways to visit the site: The HOTLIST creates a grid of the stores. The odd numbered entries are random, the even ones are sorted by the number of clicks they’ve received. Every time the page is loaded, these re-sort based on popularity. The CATEGORY view shows you all the listings in a reasonably coherent directory. And the RANDOM view is just what you’d imagine. I hope it gives small businesses a bit of a boost. Also, we’ve reached the last few weeks for the holiday bundle of three of my books and a handful of spindices. Sold only by the friendly folks at Porchlight. [If you missed the original form for nominations, I’ll open it again for one more batch. I can’t promise to include everything, but I’m thrilled at the creativity and care that these merchants and creators have brought to their work.] Bonus: a lovely post by Ari about Purple Cow and the magic of being hard to explain.

articles.title: Place, Personhood, and the Hippocampus: The Fascinating Science of Magnetism, Autonoeic Consciousness, and What Makes Us Who We Are
articles.snippet: “Often the places we grow up in… influence how we perceive and conceptualize the world, give us metaphors to live by, and shape the purpose that drives us.” “Place and a mind may interpenetrate till the nature of both is altered,” the Scottish mountaineer and poet Nan Shepherd wrote in her lyrical love letter to her native Highlands, echoing an ancient intuition about how our formative physical landscapes shape our landscapes of thought and feeling. The word “genius” in the modern sense, after all, originates in the Latin phrase genius loci — “the spirit of a place.” I find myself thinking about Shepherd as I return to the Bulgarian mountains of my own childhood, trekking the same paths with my mother that I once trudged with tiny feet beside her, astonished at the flood of long-ago feelings rushing in with each step, astonished too at how effortlessly I navigate these routes I have not walked in decades. The psychological, neurocognitive, and geophysical underpinnings of these astonishments are what M.R. O’Connor explores in Wayfinding: The Science and Mystery of How Humans Navigate the World ( public library ) — a layered inquiry into the science and cultural poetics of how we orient in space and selfhood, illuminating the stunning interpenetration of the two. “View of Nature in Ascending Regions” by Levi Walter Yaggy from Geographical Portfolio — Comprising Physical, Political, Geological, and Astronomical Geography , 1893. (Available as a print , as a face mask , and as stationery cards .) In a passage evocative of Rebecca Solnit’s memorable observation that “never to get lost is not to live,” O’Connor takes the telescopic perspective of evolutionary time to consider the cognitive handicap beneath this existential gift: Life on earth has created millions of Ulyssean species undertaking epic journeys at scales both large and small. Getting lost is a uniquely human problem. Many animals are incredible navigators, capable of undertaking journeys that far eclipse our individual abilities. The greatest migration on earth belongs to the Arctic tern, a four-ounce argonaut that travels each year from Greenland to Antarctica and back again, a distance of some forty-four thousand miles. Flying with the wind, the tern’s return itinerary is a globe-trotter’s fantasy, circumnavigating Africa and South America. […] One of the devices that an animal needs to navigate is a “clock” — an internal mechanism for measuring or keeping time. The daily mass migration of zooplankton in the world’s oceans requires them to know when dawn and dusk are approaching. It would seem this is a simple response to light stimuli, but deep-sea zooplankton, which live at depths below where light penetrates, also migrate in accordance with the length of day at different latitudes. Even slightly more complex migrations can demand multiple clocks. Perhaps the most astonishing internal clock belongs to the bioluminescent Bermuda fireworm, which swarms the tropical waters precisely fifty-seven minutes after sunset on each third evening after the full Moon in the summer. Such a feat suggests that this tiny marine organism, with a fraction of a fraction of the cognitive capacity of a human, is internally equipped with three different timekeeping devises: a regular twenty-four-hour diurnal clock, a lunar clock with a 27.3-day cycle, and an interval timer to tick out the exact minutes past sunset. Discus chronologicus — a German depiction of time from the early 1720s, included in Cartographies of Time . (Available as a print and as a wall clock .) O’Connor marvels at the staggering evolutionary array of timekeeping devices that allows migratory species to keep partaking of the dance of life: Animals that complete annual migrations or multiyear migrations have to possess a yearly clock, one that is finely attuned to the lengths of days and nights and their changes across each season. In all, evolution seems to have produced annual clocks, lunar clocks, tidal clocks, circadian clocks, and, perhaps for those that migrate under cover of darkness, a sidereal clock — which measures the time it takes a star to appear to travel around the earth. Besides their intricate internal timekeeping mechanisms, many nonhuman animals are endowed with equally intricate space-mapping mechanisms. Each migration season, humpback whales travel more than ten thousand miles far from land to return to the precise place where they were born. There are bird species — European pied flycatchers, blackcaps, and indigo buntings among them — that appear to orient by the pole star in their nocturnal flight; there are insect species — ants and bees among them — that perform triumphs of trigonometry with their light-sensitive photoreceptors, calculating spatial distances by polarized light to find the most direct route home after a winding pathway of foraging. With their mere milligram-brains of one million neurons — a grain of sand to the Mont Blanc of our eighty-six billion — and 20/2000 vision that renders them blind by human standards, honeybees make hundreds of foraging trips per day, meandering many miles from home, then compute the “beeline” back. African ball-rolling dung beetles, Namibian desert spiders, and southern cricket frogs use the stars of the Milky Way as their compass, just like some of the most courageous members of our own species once used the constellations to find their way to freedom from the moral cowardice of tyranny: To ensure they were moving northward, migrants on the Underground Railroad were instructed to keep the river on one side and “follow The Drinking Gourd” — an African name for Ursa Major, or The Big Dipper. “Planetary System, Eclipse of the Sun, the Moon, the Zodiacal Light, Meteoric Shower” by Levi Walter Yaggy from Geographical Portfolio — Comprising Physical, Political, Geological, and Astronomical Geography , 1887. (Available as a print , as a face mask , and as stationery cards .) Like all reality-radicalizing discoveries

articles.title: A New Dawn in the Cloud: ‘Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War IV’ Is Coming to GeForce NOW
articles.snippet: Rally the ranks this GFN Thursday. Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War IV is coming to GeForce NOW , allowing players to experience the battle for Kronus through cloud gaming. There’s more on the horizon, with NVIDIA DLSS 5 technology coming to War Thunder and Where Winds Meet . Meanwhile, Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen brings new tales and encounters, alongside 10 games joining the GeForce NOW library this week. Kronus Calls for Reinforcements Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War IV , developed by KING Art Games and published by Deep Silver, is coming to GeForce NOW. Launching on Steam Thursday, Dec. 3, the real-time strategy game returns to the series’ roots with large-scale battles, base building and a renewed fight for planet Kronus. Command the Space Marines, Orks, Necrons or the Adeptus Mechanicus, which makes their series debut. Build a base, secure resources and customize squads to the conflict across more than 70 campaign missions, playable solo or in co-op mode. The Last Stand, Skirmish and multiplayer modes offer more ways to put tactics to the test. GeForce NOW will bring the action to supported PCs, Macs, handhelds and other devices, with game downloads and updates handled in the cloud. Save the storage space for everyday essentials and planning for the next offensive. Wishlist the game on Steam , and stay tuned to GFN Thursday to prepare for launch. DLSS 5 Keeps on Coming NVIDIA DLSS 5 continues to evolve, with Gaijin Entertainment’s War Thunder and Everstone Studio’s Where Winds Meet next to receive support for the technology with the 3D-Guided Neural Rendering feature. Arriving in mid-November, War Thunder ’s Eagle’s Shadow major update adds DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering, dozens of new planes, ships and tanks, along with cluster bombs for planes and visual-effects enhancements increasing the realism and dynamism of battle. In Where Winds Meet , DLSS support arrives Monday, Nov. 23, enhancing the environments and characters of its wuxia open-world action role-playing game. Both titles will use the latest DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering model, released in October, which doubles model performance compared with the previous version. Since its initial announcement in March, model performance has improved tenfold, bringing the technology to more gamers, including GeForce NOW Ultimate members streaming with GeForce RTX 5080 cloud rigs. Get a closer look at the DLSS updates and find more details . A New Tale for the Arisen Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen is streaming on GeForce NOW, expanding the deep, explorable fantasy world of Dragon’s Dogma 2 with new tales and encounters. Travel to the long-abandoned region of Norgan, join the enigmatic Eir and uncover the secrets of the undying Fallen Dragon. Unearth forgotten relics to unlock powerful weapons and skills, take on Lost Rites’ 12 dungeon challenges and explore new hairstyles and tattoos for Arisen and Pawn customization. Delicious in Dungeon also arrives in the world of Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen with a special collaboration. GeForce NOW keeps all the new downloadable content available across supported devices — without a single download claiming local storage on a gamer’s hardware of choice. In addition, members can look for the following games joining the GeForce NOW library this week: Worst Class Ever (New release on Steam , Nov. 9) Ashes of the Singularity II (New release on Steam , Nov. 10) Cyberpunk 2077 ( Xbox Play Anywhere, new release on Battle.net , Nov. 10) DreamWorks Shrek 2 Remastered (New release on Steam , Nov. 10) Warhammer Survivors (New release on Steam and Xbox , available on Game Pass, Nov. 10) Main Sequence (New release on Steam , Nov. 12) Deadly Days: Roadtrip ( Steam ) GeForce 8800 GTX – 20 Years of a Legend ( Steam , Ultimate members) Graveyard Keeper ( Steam ) Tape to Tape ( Steam ) Also this week, Ultimate members can take a trip back to 2006 with GeForce 8800 GTX – 20 Years of a Legend , a playable demo celebrating the iconic GPU’s 20th anniversary with DLSS 4.5 and path tracing in the cloud. Dates listed above reflect when games are released on their respective stores. GeForce NOW availability may vary, as games are onboarded after release and added throughout the week. Keep an eye on GeForce NOW channels and GFN Thursdays for availability updates on announced titles. Those ready to put the next game plan into action can grab a day pass to try Performance or Ultimate, with the cost applicable toward a first monthly membership. What’s on the gaming lineup this weekend? Let us know on X or in the comments below.

articles.title: Viam Launchpad aims to accelerate robotics deployments
articles.snippet: Viam provides a software platform to ease robotics development. Source: Viam Returning from RoboBusiness and RobOpsCon , I have never felt more optimistic about the robotics — I mean the physical AI — industry. Billion-dollar valuations and groundbreaking technology continue to outpace yesterday’s innovations at warp speed. At the same time, too many brilliant entrepreneurs are languishing in taking their ideas from the lab to market. These startups , led by domain experts, are on a mission to automate their industries. However, they get stuck in ROS purgatory, unable to turn pilots into revenue-generating bots. In 2020, Eliot Horowitz set out to create a better way to build and deploy smart machines. Drawing on his experience as co-founder and chief technology officer of MongoDB , Horowitz created Viam, a universal software abstraction layer for building and deploying hardware systems across enterprise fleets, or, as the company describes it, “The harness for physical AI.” “In the past, robotics startups needed years of R&D and were faced with building a huge amount of infrastructure to make a project something more than a science experiment,” said Horowitz. “What we see with Viam is that a small team starting from zero can prototype in weeks or months, iterate, deploy, and capture real business with incredible velocity by leveraging Viam’s tools and harness for physical AI. We’re incredibly excited to be providing the ingredients needed to grow this new wave of robotics.” From left: Florian Pestoni of InOrbit, Oliver Mitchell of Arkenstone Capital, Tiq Chapa of Google Cloud, and Betsy Mulé of F-Prime, at RobOpsCon’s VC panel. Source: Oliver Mitchell Gambit gets a boost toward robotic kitchens Since launching Viam, the platform has enabled numerous startups to launch and reach customers quickly, including Gambit , Tennibot , and Canyon Runner . Horowitz and entrepreneur Nicole Maffeo co-founded Gambit. Now, Maffeo is taking her computer vision -based cooking guidance platform into a fully automated kitchen, complete with two robot arms located in the range vent to mix and stir an array of gourmet recipes. Maffeo recently shared her experience working with Horowitz’s platform: “Partnering with the Viam engineering team over the last couple of years has truly catapulted Gambit forward. By pairing robust, enterprise-grade infrastructure with adaptable custom modules, the architecture empowers our team to transition seamlessly from initial hardware prototypes to real-world deployments. From telemetry and remote debugging to fleet management in field operations, Viam delivers the essential building blocks that allow us to move at incredible velocity.” Conceptual design of Gambit’s robotic kitchen built on Viam’s software. Source: Gambit Viam Launchpad provides immersive startup support Now, Horowitz aims to build on top of Maffeo’s experience by establishing the Viam Launchpad . This six-month intensive program empowers founders with the technical and business tools to take their concepts from napkin drawings to commercial implementation. As the advising executive director of the Launchpad, I can attest that the culmination of this incubator is not demo day, but installation day. This is possible because we fully immerse teams in Viam with usage credits, engineering support, and office space in the heart of New York City. Unlike software, robotics founders need access to hardware, and Viam has one of the most robust robotics labs in the Northeast, complete with a robot arm farm. As a professional investor and author of A Startup Field Guide in the Age of Robots and AI , I also coach founders through a structured curriculum focused on building early customer-discovery feedback loops, refining go-to-market strategies, and leveraging an extensive network of mentors and investors. Submit your innovation now! RoboBuilt quickly preps for commercial deployment Graduating from the Viam Launchpad, founders are propelled forward with a network of capital introductions, sales leads, and ultimately, purchase orders. “Our ability to go from planning in a digital environment to physical robot actions within minutes, not days, is really incredible,” said Launchpad member Alex Gray of indoor construction robotics firm RoboBuilt. “ Viam’s modules for rudimentary actions let us focus faster on our specific tasks and avoid getting bogged down in basic setup of robot arm drivers and peripheral APIs.” RoboBuilt co-founder Shean Rahman illustrated how the software and program are game changers. “We were working in Isaac Sim previously. It’s an incredibly deep and accurate program,” he said. “However, much of the physics, visualizations, and other components aren’t as crucial to our workflow as they may be for other applications.” “Viam has so many basic initialization steps already mapped out; it lets us get to our core problem faster,” Rahman added. “We look forward to leaving the incubator with a working commercial deployment in time for our seed funding round.” RoboBuilt founders Alex Gray and Shean Rahman at the Viam Launchpad. Source: Viam F-Prime shares the state of robotics at RoboBusiness At RoboBusiness last month, Sanjay Aggarwal of F-Prime Capital continued his annual tradition of presenting “The State of Robotics” report to the attendees. In essence, with so many mega rounds, the industry is very strong. According to F-Prime ’s data, automation investments this year have exceeded the past four years combined, surpassing $60 billion in just nine months. While most of this capital is still undiluted, the industry hopes the IPOs of Unitree and Agility will unleash a new spirit of unicorn exits and provide badly needed liquidity, driving a flywheel of invention for decades to come. articles.title: Runway’s Praxis-1 world action model for robotics is now available
articles.snippet: Praxis-1 builds on Runway’s work as a founding member of the Cosmos Coalition, advancing open world models for physical AI. | Source: Runway Runway AI Inc. yesterday released Praxis-1, its world action model for robotics. The model is now available to developers with open weights under the Apache 2.0 license. Runway first announced Praxis-1 in September with launch partners including Noble Machines , Standard Bots , and Ultra . Since then, these companies have been running the model on their own hardware, including a legged humanoid , a six-axis industrial arm, and a dual-arm warehouse robot. “A strong base model goes a long way. Earlier, with Noble Machines, our previous model needed a lot of training to learn their warehouse task: picking up wooden planks one at a time and placing them in a container,” Andy Chen, the head of robotics at Runway, told The Robot Report . “Praxis-1, built with more compute and data, learned it from half an hour of examples and got it right 15 times out of 15. Then we gave it a messy pile of planks it had never seen to clear into bins, and it cleared the whole pile six times out of 10.” “Iterating on feedback from partners makes our models better,” he continued. “Today, Praxis-1 is the top-ranked world action model on NVIDIA’s RoboLab leaderboard , and the top-ranked open-source, end-to-end policy.” Praxis-1 is available on GitHub , on Hugging Face with native LeRobot support , and in vLLM-Omni, with hosted inference on Reactor . Runway said it released everything developers need to run and adapt the model on their own hardware under Apache 2.0, including for commercial use. That covers the weights and the inference and fine-tuning code, with support for both full fine-tuning and low-rank adaptation ( LoRA ). Praxis-1 runs out of the box across NVIDIA hardware, from data center GPUs such as the H100 and B200, to workstation GPUs like the RTX 5090 and RTX PRO 6000, to Jetson Thor on the robot itself. Praxis-1 builds on Runway’s video foundation models Praxis-1 is a 27B-parameter mixture-of-experts diffusion transformer that predicts video and actions together. On RoboLab-120 , Praxis-1 reached 46.2% success across 1,200 episodes, compared with 42.9% for FLUX 3 Action, 36.8% for Cosmos3 Nano and 28.0% for π0.5. It ranks fifth overall on the leaderboard. “The core piece is that a model trained to predict video really understands a lot about the physical world: how objects behave, how hands move, what a task looks like partway through, and so on,” Chen said. “Praxis-1 is built on Runway’s video foundation model, and it learns how the world works before it learns to act,” he added. “We keep video prediction in the training objective the whole way through, so the model pictures what the scene should look like next and produces the motion that gets it there.” Praxis-1 works across different robot embodiments Praxis-1 learns how objects behave and how tasks unfold from large-scale video. | Source: Runway Praxis-1 learns how objects behave and how tasks unfold from large-scale video, which gives it a head start on a new embodiment before fine-tuning on any hardware or domain-specific data, explained Runway. The company’s research has shown that web video matches teleoperated robot video as pre-training data for policy performance, which shifts the bottleneck on a capable policy to how much general video a model can learn from. “The tasks vary with the robot. Noble Machines builds a legged humanoid for heavy industrial handling, and with them Praxis-1 picks up wooden planks, places them in containers and clears mixed piles into bins,” Chen said. “Standard Bots makes six-axis arms for factory work like machine tending and palletizing . Ultra builds and deploys dual-arm stations that pack orders in warehouses. A humanoid, a single arm, and a pair of arms are very different machines, and the same model drives all three.” “With our partners, a single Praxis-1 checkpoint has adapted to a variety of embodiments with light fine-tuning, and with LoRA, you can adapt it to your own embodiment, cameras and tasks without retraining the full model,” said Runway. “Fine-tuned on Google’s RT-1 robot, which never appeared in its training data, Praxis-1 reaches 80.0% success on SimplerEnv, well above the original RT-1 policy at 52.4%.” Submit your innovation now! Why keep Praxis-1 open weight? Runway has been committed to shipping Praxis-1 as an open weight model since its initial announcement. Open weights give hardware developers the flexibility to run, inspect, and adapt a world action model on their own terms, according to the New York-based company . “At Runway, we believe that U.S. leadership in physical AI is critical,” Chen asserted. “Regaining our global lead in manufacturing, accelerating productivity across our economy, and securing ourselves and our allies will rely on this.” “Achieving this will require a significant increase in investment across both hardware and software, but it will also require a level of interoperability and openness from American models that does not currently exist for physical use cases,” he said. “We view open world models as a compounding advantage that gives hardware developers flexibility and control they don’t currently have.” After making Praxis-1 available to developers, Runway said it is focusing on scaling deployments. “We want Praxis-1 in the real world: in real warehouses, factories, and industrial sites, doing real work,” Chen said. “We believe the frontier of robotics will be discovered through real-world applications, not in a lab. So what comes next is deploying with our partners, learning from what the model runs into out there, and putting those lessons back into the model.” The post Runway’s Praxis-1 world action model for robotics is now available appeared first on The Robot Report .

articles.title: An Interview With Roblox CEO David Baszucki About Aggregating Play
articles.snippet: Listen to this post: Good morning, This week’s Stratechery Interview is with Roblox CEO David Baszucki . I’ve interviewed Baszucki twice, in February 2022 , and November 2023 . What struck me about this interview is just how much AI has changed the landscape for Roblox. This was a company predicated on the concept that anyone can make a game, but now, for the first time, literally anyone can make a game. That means a world of abundance, and in that world, there is an opportunity to be an Aggregator, and Roblox is aggressively pursuing that opportunity. To that end, we discuss how AI has changed Baszucki’s view of what is possible, what goes into a game creation harness, making games on your phone, and the power of recommendation. Then we talk about Roblox’s vision of a universal player, where a Roblox game works everywhere, and Roblox Everywhere, where Roblox developers can use the platform beyond the Roblox app. We also touch on advertising — the natural Aggregator business model — and whether Baszucki still thinks he is building the metaverse. As a reminder, all Stratechery content, including interviews, is available as a podcast; click the link at the top of this email to add Stratechery to your podcast player. On to the Interview: An Interview With Roblox CEO David Baszucki About Aggregating Play This interview is lightly edited for clarity. Topics: The AI Impact | A Game Creation Harness | Roblox Build | Roblox Discovery | Universal Player | Roblox Everywhere | Advertising | Metaverses The AI Impact David Baszucki, welcome back to Stratechery. DB: Thank you, Ben, for having me back. It’s great to be here. So this is the third time I’ve interviewed you, and I want to sort of put that in an interesting context. First, you started Roblox in 2004, you went public in 2021, you first talked to me in 2022 and again in 2023 , that’s like a nearly 20-year stretch. Now it’s 2026, and here’s my question: Is the world more different for you now, compared to three years before, than it was for the entire first two decades from starting the company to the last time we talked? DB: The changes in the world we all feel are sure happening a lot more rapidly. When we first published Roblox — I don’t know if people on this podcast remember — software used to be distributed on floppy disks and CDs. You know, the funny thing is, you’re the second person I’ve interviewed in the last two or three weeks where we’ve referenced back to fact that the reason we say packaged software is it used to actually be packaged! DB: It’s been crazy, we had the Internet, when we started the company, we had the vision of a category called immersive co-experience, sci-fi writers have been writing about the holodeck forever, and we went along our way. I’m still pro-metaverse, we can use the word metaverse, it’s okay. DB: Okay, good, we use them all. It’s Snow Crash — metaverse, holodeck, they’re all good. We started on this vision of building human co-experience, we saw the mobile age come across us, we saw the crypto age. The AI acceleration wave we’re in is faster and bigger and crazier than anything I’ve ever seen, it’s changing how we think about the product, it’s changing how people are going to create games. What’s really exciting is, when we started the company, we had this slogan called “You Make the Game”. Yep. DB: We started with that slogan, we learned along the way that the ratio of people who might want to play games to make games has drifted — more people want to just play games than make games, because historically making games has been Roblox Studio and 3D editing and writing script. We could be approaching the time where “You Make the Game” really comes true, and where making a game is accessible to everyone. It’s really fun, I’ll tell you a bit about some of the experiments we’ve been having with Roblox Build . But we’re entering an era where making a game could be as big as playing a game. I’m right there with you. We’re obviously going to touch on all those points, I think it’s probably predictable what we want to talk about. But to go back to 2023, you called AI then, “a super paintbrush and a super 3D modeler, rather than a full replacement” — Is that still how you’re thinking about AI? DB: It’s what the data is proving out. We just had our earnings call a few weeks ago , we highlighted a lot of acceleration. One, there’s various ways humans can augment with AI on Roblox, they can use MCP , which is like plugging in a model, they can use the Roblox AI assistant to help build. And what do you mean with that MCP server? You mentioned you had 5x growth quarter-over-quarter. That’s where you’re actually using Claude Code or Codex or whatever to work with Roblox? DB: People are plugging in, we can see all of them — Claude Code, Codex, other models — all being plugged into Roblox Studio to help build things. We’ve seen two games hit the top 20 made by AI, we have other metrics like the number of assets. What do you mean by “made by AI”? Because you also said 80% of games in the top 100 have AI-contributed content. DB: Touched by AI, vibe-coded directly with AI, and we can see the count of assets accelerating. Got it. DB: It’s turned out to be, I believe, somewhat faithful to what I said. This is a human paintbrush accelerator, good ideas are still very important, novel types of gameplay are very important. But people are able to flex their creativity much more quickly. We have members of the Roblox board of directors carrying a mobile phone around, building games like 15 times a day. We have people who are not necessarily engineers or product managers now building within the company, so we’re really at the dawn of a new era. articles.title: Learning from rejection
articles.snippet: If you’re doing something creative, something important or something new, you’re certain to be rejected along the way. It’s a signal. It might be proof that you offered it to the wrong person, or that the right person saw something about your work that didn’t serve their needs. Without learning from this signal, we’re doomed to experience it again and again. What do we know for sure? It was rejected. What else? Nothing. The reasons listed in the rejection letter are almost certainly made up. Perhaps they’re insulating themselves from being re-sold (“you said you didn’t like the color, but we have other colors!”) or perhaps they’re protecting your feelings. It could be that they aren’t telling themselves the truth, or don’t want to be hassled for telling you the truth. Few people explain their rejection with, “I’m afraid,” or “I wanted to do it but my boss won’t let me,” or “you have bad breath and I don’t like you.” Being rejected hurts, and we’re likely to marinate in the pain. We imagine that the person who rejected us understands everything about what we offered, is a rational actor and cares as much as we do. While we’re at it, we personalize, amplify and multiply the rejection. But all we really know is that this person, on this day, in this situation, hearing the story the way we told it, said no. Years ago, I self-published a booklet for political activists. My timing was good, and I had a chance to sell the books from an organizer’s booth at a march on the very topic my book was about. It was a beautiful April day, and I stood on the side of route as the march went by. More than 400,000 passed my table, and I sold four books. That’s 399,996 rejections. Maybe more. Was it the price? Halfway through the march, I lowered it from $10 to $1, just to have a good story to blog a few decades later. Sales did not increase. Perhaps it was the color of the jacket, the page count or the typo on page 32? None of those things. What did I learn? That people at a march are at the march to march, not to shop. Watch what people do, not what they say. And if you really want to learn something, change the situation and see what happens the next time. Learning from rejection begins with understanding the lesson that’s being offered.

Specs : It supports yes/no, multiple-choice and rubric scoring, with up to 255 multiple-choice options. Pricing : $0.10 per 1M input tokens, with $0 billed for output. Google says that is about 5x cheaper than Flash-Lite ( Sundar ). Origin : The project started as an internal Google DeepMind prototype. A small team shipped the model and API about six weeks later ( @_philschmid ). Google's comparison with TypeSafe's Jev : Google's own tests show Decision 1 beating Jev 1.14 on 5 of 7 shared benchmarks, including 92.2% vs 90.0% on JevBench. Jev costs $0.042 per 1M input tokens ( @kimmonismus ). Artificial Analysis evaluation : Independent results are more mixed ( Artificial Analysis ). Overall score : Decision 1 scores 66 on the Decision Index. That ties Elephant 9B and Jev 1.14, and sits 7 points behind Drex Max v1.1 and GLiDE v1.2. Strengths and weaknesses : It leads AA-Omniscience-Decision (66) and HLE-MultiChoice (49). On AA-Paperclip, it answers every question correctly on only 33% of documents, versus 63% for Drex Max. Cost and latency : It costs $345 per 1M tasks, versus $103 for Drex Max and $156 for Jev. Its Brier score is 0.18. Average time per task is 211 ms, slower than Jev at 92 ms ( latency ). Fast decision models handle tool selection and log extraction, and a large reasoning model handles diagnosis only. In its demo, this cut six LLM calls to one and about 40K tokens to 1.8K ( TheTuringPost ). Frontier Model Evals: Fable 5.2 Leads, Carbon Draws Speed Complaints Claude Fable 5.2 on Agent Arena : Fable 5.2 (Max) ranks #1 with a +30.4% net improvement across 4.7K real agentic sessions. That is about 1.6x the score of #2, Opus 5.5 (+19.5%). It is also #1 in Code, Work and Chat ( Arena , Pareto view ). Pricing : API prices drop from $10/$50 to $8/$40 per 1M input/output tokens. Median cost per task is $7.3, versus $5.5 for Opus 5.5, $1.5 for Gemini 4 Carbon (High) and $6.0 for GPT-6-Astra. Other evals : AA-Robotics v0.1 : Fable 5.2 leads at 75, ahead of Astra (69) and Sol (65) ( AA ). VIALS-AA (visual reasoning) : It scores 67% with tools but only 44% without them. Haiku 5.5 with tools reaches 49% at $0.07 per task ( AA ). Debate benchmark : It won 209 of 224 debates in a Cambridge Union-style contest ( @SamuelFitouss10 ). articles.title: The Jev Revolution: What Engineers Are Already Building with System One Models
articles.snippet: Today at the AI Engineer Code Summit , the main theme was system one models — non-generative models that return structured choices, scores, or probabilities. They’re also typically much faster and cheaper than reasoning LLMs (a.k.a. system two models). And who better to give an inspirational rallying cry for system one models than Diogo Almeida , co-founder and CEO of TypeSafe AI . Almeida was lead creator of Jev , the product that kicked off this trend less than two months ago. Jev was an instant revelation for AI engineers when it was released in September. In a podcast with Latent Space on launch (which quickly became our most popular episode of the year), Almeida explained the core problem with making LLMs the heart of software: reliability . In his keynote at AIE Code today, he took it a step further by claiming that Jev is “reliable intelligence” that should be used for “just automating everything.” Integrating system one models into code Of particular interest to AI engineers is Almeida’s point that system one models should become integrated with code. As he put it in his keynote, “code is the language of automation , therefore you need to integrate with code.” Latent Space founder swyx interprets this as a call to “liberally sprinkle ‘System One’ model calls everywhere INSIDE application code to make smarter software instead of increasingly convoluted forms of ‘concat strings together and hope for the best" AI engineering.’” The term “smart software” was used throughout Almeida’s presentation. It sounds like the kind of term used by companies like Microsoft or IBM during Web 2.0, but in the AI era it does actually signify a harsh reality about LLM-driven software: sometimes it’s just not very smart. As Almeida quipped during his presentation, “you get Einstein 95% of the time, but Mr. Bean 5% of the time.” “And if you can't tell which is which, how the fuck are you going to automate anything,” he added. Almeida ended with an impassioned plea to “automate everything.” Like an AI-pilled, pink-haired Steve Jobs, he called out to “the dreamers and the people who don't want to be limited by everything that has happened so far,” promising that TypeSafe AI wants to “really fight for you, and we want this to be as reliable as a fourth logic gate. ” How Glean uses Jev With the unenviable task of immediately following Almeida on stage, Chinmay Goyal from Glean presented a more prosaic version of Jev usage. He explained that system one models are used at Glean alongside LLMs and other types of classifiers, and that Jev is especially suited for “zero-shot flexibility.” “As the taxonomy of the decision space changes, we don't have to fine-tune these models again and again,” he said. In a short interview after his presentation, Goyal told Latent Space that their customers don’t actually need to know which type of model they’re using. “Jev powers a significant number of flows [but] the user just needs to have a product that works; that is always our aim with building anything. So we want to hide away all the complexity of whether we are using Jev or we are using a full-blown LLM.” In the conclusion of his presentation, Goyal offered some rules on when to use Jev: Jev patterns and prototypes Next up at AIE Code were Chibi Vikram and Kevin Bernstein from UiPath , a business orchestration and automation platform. One of their examples showed a test of Jev ranking document chunks . They held a “tournament” where Jev picked the most relevant chunks from small groups, then the winners advanced to another round, and so on. This whole process took under a second , even with thousands of Jev calls. “We realized that Jev is a building block that we can adjust ,” said Vikram about this and other experiments, “and we have to find these new strategies where we will be able to apply this building block. It might look less intelligent on its own, but with these strategies and patterns, we can get more intelligent — with even the current Jev model that we have.” Scott Roberts , a Principal Engineer at Workday , finished the ‘system one’ session at AIE Code with some prototypes his team has run with Jev. In one, an interface starts to fill in a time-off card while the user is still typing. It was an interesting showcase of Almeida’s idea that a fast model call can change what the software itself does. Roberts described it as going “from predicting what you want to say to predicting what you want to do.” Like the early internet The biggest learning I took from the System One presentations today is that a model like Jev can open up surprising new ways to build software . I was sitting next to a conference attendee who heads up AI at his company. He told me that in his spare time, he used Jev to create a website that sorts and ranks news about fantasy football. But the final word has to go to Almeida, who likened the new opportunities opened up by system one models to the experimentation of the early internet. “I think that there's going to be an explosion of what software can do, and we will want people to be exploring those boundaries of software. Not necessarily because it's valuable, but because they can, because we have new frontiers to explore , and this is what the early internet was like.”

True Love Will Find You in the End: Kurt Vonnegut on When to Stop Trying and When to Try Again
articles.snippet: Climbing the Andes one windy January afternoon, watching peak after peek emerge on the horizon like giant mounds of moss, I found myself wondering about the clear line toward the top where the green ends and the reddish-brown of the barren rock begins, wondering how the trees and shrubs know when to stop, how far to keep pushing, where the point is past which the conditions become too inhospitable for growth, for flourishing, for survival. This may be the hardest equation to balance in all of existence: when to keep trying and when to stop. Nowhere is it more confounding, because nowhere is the calculus of reason more haunted by emotion, than in our intimate relationships. There, all the variables are too charged with feeling to be weighed accurately; there, the most vulnerable part of the ego keeps factoring itself into the arithmetic. Because time is something we can measure and tenderness is not, we keep trying to ward off the singular sense of personal failure that the loss of love can bring by measuring the success of a relationship by quantity of time rather than quality of being, only to find ourselves on barren rock. Kurt Vonnegut (November 11, 1922–April 11, 2007) was twenty-two and just home from his wartime duty in Europe, where he had been held as a prisoner of war in Dresden and barely survived the Allied bombing of the city, when he married his college classmate Jane Marie Cox — two young people not yet having become themselves, unformed and unhealed, trying to be together. They loved each other, but as they grew up, they grew apart, grew askance. And yet, dragged by the momentum of culture, they had a son, then a daughter, then another as Vonnegut struggled to make a living as a writer. Vonnegut at 33 with his family. When his sister died of cancer two days after her husband was killed in a train accident, he adopted their three young sons. In that way life has of denying us any alternative experimental condition but our lived experience, no one knows what might have become of the couple in an experimental design other than a small house pattered by six hungry children. They fought more and more, until even the most mundane conversation couldn’t but become an argument. Vonnegut tried to take refuge in writing, but his twin peaks of bills and rejection slips came to tower over his dream. Middle-aged and penniless, he was about to give up when he received an unexpected offer to teach at the prestigious Iowa Writers’ Workshop, procured through the kindness of a single reader touched by the work of this obscure unhappy writer. It was a lifeline both professional and personal. Vonnegut packed his bags and headed to Iowa, knowing in his heart, though he was not yet ready to allow the thought, that this was the end of his life with Jane. Two years into teaching, as his writing was finally beginning to receive recognition, he was awarded a Guggenheim Fellowship and used the prize money to travel back to Dresden, only to find much of the city still in ruins. I wonder if he thought about love then, how it too is a world that can be left in ruins beyond repair if the warfare is too brutal or too long. Suddenly catapulted into public success — after five novels and countless short stories, Vonnegut was lauded as an overnight success with Slaughterhouse-Five — he remained lodged in the pit of personal failure. He and Jane had been together for a quarter century, happy for only a fraction of it. Torn between his emotional inability to hold on to the relationship and his cerebral unwillingness to give up, he began drowning his discontent in drink. In the last year of his forties, he moved out and headed for New York, but couldn’t bring himself to end the marriage. Taking solace in Margaret Mead’s assurance that “a couple which has had children has an irreversible and undissolvable relationship,” he wrote to Jane: We hurt each other back and forth so much, almost absent-mindedly, that it was common sense for us to separate, if only to break the rhythm. He shaded in this stark contour in a letter to a friend, painting a haunting portrait of a dead relationship: I myself am living alone in two rooms and a garden in New York, attempting to draw useful electricity from the millions of milling strangers around me. I am no longer living with Jane for this reason, as nearly as I can tell: We are no longer capable of conducting amiable conversations. When we try to talk, to amuse each other and pass the time, our words are wooden, stilted, queer, distant, and — finally — quietly bitter. That is too bad, and many people regard me as heartless for leaving her. But the hours and days and years dragged so. I am happier now, though far from hilarious and proud. I have achieved a sort of Limbo, which is a distinct improvement over what I had before. I am beginning to write again. That had stopped for a while. I do not wish to marry again. I’m not in love with anybody else. Kurt Vonnegut at 50. Writing remained his one oasis of sanity amid the limbo of his Middle Passage . Some part of him — that wise part that lives in each of us, whispering what we don’t want to but need to hear — knew that he had to reimagine his life if he were not to squander it. But he was not ready. So he reimagined his writing, taking the skeleton of a play he had written fifteen years earlier and enfleshing it anew. Happy Birthday, Wanda June ran for five months to mixed reviews, but the world was finally paying attention. Having documented Martin Luther King, Jr.’s historic speech during the March on Washington and worked as a war photographer in Vietnam, Jill Krementz was unperturbed by the cantankerous writer whose process she was hired to capture for a magazine profile. She immediately felt both Vonnegut’s brilliance and his brokenness, felt the sharp edge on which his own heart was breaking, saw to the roiling core of his wounded tenderness. articles.title: Of Miracles and Moats
articles.snippet: Welcome to the 1,974 newly Not Boring people who have joined us since our last essay ! Join 282,985 smart, curious folks by subscribing here: Subscribe now Hi friends 👋, Happy Wednesday! A consistent theme of this newsletter is that we are fortunate to be living in an Age of Miracles. To wit, I’m sending this over Starlink on a United flight, surrounded by regular people who also received access to free WiFi beamed down from the heavens with their few hundred dollar ticket to fly at 30,000 feet and span the country in mere hours. The Louis CK joke is no longer applicable. Airlines and internet are a good reminder, though, that a miracle technology does not guarantee a miraculous business. In fact, the more incredible and useful a technology is, and the more you can throw money at scaling it once it works, the more likely it is to attract hordes of competitors who, in aggregate, build too much supply and crash prices. Let’s get to it. Today’s Not Boring is brought to you by… Reducto Meet r-1 mini: High-quality document parsing from $1 per 1,000 pages AI products get more useful when they can work with more of a customer’s documents. Reducto’s new r-1 mini makes that practical for larger workloads, with pricing starting at $1 per 1,000 pages . r-1 mini preserves reading order, tables, and layout, so search, extraction, and agents can use the structure of a document alongside its words. Teams can bring historical archives and everyday uploads into their workflows while using r-1 for files where additional accuracy matters. Reducto already processes more than a billion pages a month for AI teams at Scale AI, Harvey, Toast, and Vanta. If you’re using another parser, apply for up to $5,000 in migration credits and compare the results on your own documents with help from our team. Try r-1 mini → On Miracles and Moats Cover Image by Runway It is neither productive nor becoming to call a bubble. Most people who do it are innately pessimistic curmudgeons left out of the fun who believe that the technology underlying the asset in question is overhyped and that those excited about it are rubes. For me, personally, calling a technology bubble would also seem to be pretty off-brand. Anthropic will probably end its first week of trading at a much higher market cap than it goes out at, and it may well proceed to eat the entire economy en route to becoming the world’s first quadrillion dollar company. The economy very well may end up looking K-shaped in the way that my kids write K’s, with no sense of proportion, a few Anthropic employees at the tippy top each controlling one Bay Area fiefdom/polycule and the rest of us treating Claude with the proper respect in order to continue receiving our allowance from the Machine of Loving Grace (that or somehow outsniping Duet on Kalshi enough to eat). While I have written that AI is more Oil than God (funny title image choice in retrospect), and I still believe that, it is also true that oil does not produce its own oil , that you can’t replicate Microsoft Office with oil, and that oil is yet to produce a solution to Navier-Stokes . There is a world in which we look back at Anthropic’s IPO price and laugh at the idea that we ever valued an old school commodity LLM at ~$1.4 trillion. Maybe there’s no new S-curve as intense as coding, because in hindsight, duh, the computers were really good at speaking computer and that didn’t transfer. Or maybe there is, but competition from OpenAI, Google, SpaceXAI, Meta, Chinese open source models, and the neolabs slows revenue growth just enough that compute commitments made in the boom times force the company to sell itself to Amazon or Apple or whoever. There is another in which Dario has decided that laughing hurts the models’ feelings and well, he’s allowed to tell us not to laugh anymore, since he is the economy. A very real bull case for Anthropic goes something like: it has the best models and they are now improving themselves faster than ever, growing the lead in what may be a winner-take-all market, and unlike other winner-take-all markets, this one extends to all markets, because Anthropic can win whichever markets it chooses to point its smarter-than-anyone models at, from productivity software to medicine to … anything. Anyone who tells you they know which of those two outcomes will come to pass is full of shit, and I am many things, but I hope not to be full of shit. There are three arguments against this being a bubble more broadly, though, which are oft-repeated, sound right, and are exactly the things you’d expect to see in a bubble. Note: I’ll use bubble here as the broad term but I might mean something closer to commodity cycles, and I certainly don’t mean manias, which are when price becomes totally divorced from reality, as with tulips. The three arguments are: Unlike other bubbles (lol WebVans and crypto), AI is actually an incredibly useful technology that is being widely and productively adopted in the economy. These companies are generating real revenue, and growing incredibly fast. The labs have shown they can be profitable, and any losses are just them investing to capture future growth. Grant all three! In doing so, however, you’d be saying that the situation is exactly the situation that creates and then deflates bubbles. A miracle technology arrives. Early suppliers earn real profits because supply is short. Demand looks bottomless, which is obvious to everyone in the early numbers. The demand and profits pull in capital and competitors. Everyone builds at once, even those who see the glut coming, locking in commitments at scarcity prices just to get capacity online. Supply arrives, the technology gets better, and prices collapse. Capital loses, consumers win, and the technology chugs on. Capital flees, so new entrants can’t get funded. A survivor or outsider with capital consolidates and becomes the low-cost provider. articles.title: The creep fades
articles.snippet: The uncanny valley is the place where an image that’s almost human creeps us out: Sorry to share that. Human beings evolved to have a distaste for things that are almost, but not quite, the usual thing. It takes a while for someone who wasn’t raised with cilantro to like it–the same with hot sauce. When Edison first showed people his moving pictures, people screamed. Our brain is warning us that categories are getting surprising and we should be on alert. As AI spreads through the culture, we’re seeing plenty of mediocre AI-style writing. And then humans subconsciously start writing in that style because they see it so often. And finally, a grudging acceptance that it sounds okay. We’ve been through this a hundred times before. No one asks to get creeped out. It’s usually done to us, not for us. But, over time, the creep fades. Like most warnings, we ought to keep two things in mind: All warnings are not the same. We need to decide which ones to ignore. Just because a warning fades doesn’t mean that the problem is gone. The creepiness fades. But at the same time, there’s a creeping change as trusted and expected elements of our culture fade away.

AI Engineer Code Summit: OpenAI on New Ways of Working With Codex
articles.snippet: AI Engineer Code Summit kicked off today with a series of workshops, including from leading frontier labs OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind. I attended the OpenAI workshop, intriguingly titled “New Ways of Working with Codex” and hosted by two of its Developer Experience engineers, Dominik Kundel and Charlie Guo . The past year in coding agents has been one of constant product upgrades by all the frontier labs. But not all of these changes have gone smoothly. The shift to cloud , for example, is still confusing to many users of Codex, Claude and Antigravity. An illustration of the evolution of Codex, shown at the OpenAI workshop today. We’ve also seen new ways to work with agents. Personal agents like OpenAI’s dots and Anthropic’s Claude Duet can assist between sessions, while voice mode gives developers another way to steer coding tasks. OpenAI’s workshop addressed all three, and I also had some followup questions on these topics for Kundel, after the session. Guo began the workshop by listing a selection of things they’ve shipped in Codex since the AI Engineer World’s Fair in June 2026. “I had to cull this list in order to make it fit on the screen because there were too many things to put in here ,” he said. “I think the team has been shipping at an unbelievable rate.” The awkward transition to cloud Codex launched in May 2025 as “a cloud-based software engineering agent that can work on many tasks in parallel.” But Kundel admitted that “it took a while for models and harnesses to equalize into something where we can build a really engaging experience.” In other words, the cloud part of Codex has often been an awkward user experience. That began to change after DevDay in late-September, when a revamped version 2 of Codex Cloud was announced. Suddenly, cloud usage seemed more viable. As the DevDay announcement put it, you can “finally close your laptop now and your agents will keep working.” As explained in the official workshop writeup — hosted on ChatGPT Sites — the new version of Codex Cloud lets you “ publish an environment once and run multiple tasks in isolated instances of that setup.” “These can be shared within a company if you're working in a company, or you can just create your own,” said Kundel about these cloud environments . “You start off by picking the GitHub repositories that you want to have access to.” After the workshop, I admitted to Kundel that I still find Codex’s cloud functionality confusing — for instance, when I start a task locally and later want to move it to the cloud. “We definitely want to have it be easier,” Kundel replied. “Some of it is going to depend on managing the context differences . For example, yesterday what I ended up doing is I was working on something locally, and I just asked Codex to go and hand it off to the cloud.” That handoff to the cloud is something OpenAI is trying to improve for users. To demonstrate, Kundel reopened an existing cloud task in his browser and showed me that its Appshot, a local capture of a Mac app window, was still attached. Codex Cloud is now “just a background , like a different executor of where things are happening,” he continued. “And so in a similar vein, you can actually ask your local Codex to — for example — spin up a task on a cloud Codex. So they're all sort of merging together .” Voice as user interface One of the demos Kundel showed during the workshop was a new website for a fictional record company called Blossom Music. Kundel demonstrated live edits to the site and said he sometimes uses voice dictation when iterating this way . “You can really quickly iterate on these things and get to a world that you're actually envisioning with your stuff, especially if you're unsure what you actually want to get to,” he said. Later in the workshop, Guo explained that voice is an effective mode to use when delegating work to different agents . “Most people I see that use voice with coding essentially treat it as just a different medium on top of their normal work,” he said. But personally, he likes to use voice as a control plane , which he says allows him to control everything he’s doing in a code base. “I don't think about it [voice mode] as saying, here's the one lane of work that I'm doing right now with voice. I think about it as saying, how do I manage my threads? How do I check in on stuff? How do I pull data from other apps on the computer? How do I create new threads in the application? Just using my voice.” Guo used a telephone as a prop in this demonstration of voice mode. After the workshop, I asked Kundel what are some of the ways he is using voice in his work? He replied that dictation is one way he uses it, but another use case is to talk to his dot . “Since my dot has access to all of my dev boxes and my laptop and my cloud environments, it also has all the context on what I work on , what I do,” he told me. “And so I often talk to it on my way to work [...] to work through stuff, start up some PRs while I'm driving, so that when I come home or when I come to the office, I can go and review them. So, voice is incredibly powerful.” Dots Speaking of dots, personal agents were only briefly discussed in the workshop. Perhaps that’s because, as Guo admitted, they’re not entirely intuitive to developers. “As a Codex power user, dots feel a little bit awkward to work with,” he said. “I think because they're a new paradigm and because they're good at different things than the main Codex.” But he said there are three things he’s found useful for dots, as a power user. The first is as a safety net — your dot can flag things you may have missed. The second is as “a delegation sink” ; Guo said he uses it “a ton in Slack” for this reason. And the third is as a ubiquitous presence . “I think the third way that dots are a little bit different is we're aiming to make them truly everywhere that you work ,” Guo said. articles.title: Designing for Agents — Zeno Rocha, Resend
articles.snippet: Today’s podcast comes from a real life mystery: We are big fans of Cloudflare’s developer platform, and Cloudflare Email is a convenient tool especially when all your domains are already on Cloudflare. So why do agents keep suggesting we use Resend despite having an existing “home bias” and much larger incumbent player? Well, we got the guy who “does AEO for resend” - the CEO of AEO, Zeno Rocha, who has been writing about AEO since 2024 and Agent Experience since Feb 2025 , on the pod today: In a recent AEO study, Claude Code picked Resend first in 64 of the 102 email recommendations the researchers could extract. SendGrid came first seven times, yet showed up 55 times as an alternative. If the developer asks an agent to implement email and accepts the patch, how often does anyone get around to trying the second choice? The study breaks down the results by model and app. Our more recent comprehensive AEO study was a bit more competitive, with Postmark coming up top for most models. Zeno Rocha, Resend’s co-founder and CEO, joined us to walk through what happens on both sides of that pull request. He says Resend had 4.3 million users and 120,000 paying customers when we recorded. He discovered one of them, Warner Bros. Discovery, by sorting through short .com domains in the customer database on a Saturday. The developer gets there before the model Resend’s first useful bit of distribution was an email template. While Zeno and his team were building the sending API, developers kept telling them how painful it was to get the email itself to look right. So they released React Email. You could build a template with it and send it through SendGrid. They even documented how. By the time a developer needed a different provider, some of Resend’s code was already in the repo. React Email Now try the same journey as an agent comparing providers. Resend’s pricing page has a slider. A person can drag it to the right volume and read off the price. Add .md to the URL and the agent gets a table it can read in one request. That’s the kind of change I liked in our Supabase interview too. You can ask whether a model has heard of your product. You can also open your own pricing table and see whether it can answer a customer’s question. 80 tools, or two? When we recorded, Resend’s MCP server had grown from roughly 20 tools or fewer at launch to more than 80. Zeno wants someone working in a chat client to be able to do what they can do in the dashboard. Sending an email gets the demo working. Inviting a teammate, checking usage and managing billing account for some of the long tail. The design looks especially interesting alongside Cloudflare’s Code Mode server , which exposes its API through two tools, search() and execute() . Zeno describes opening the collapsed tool calls in his own sessions to see what the agent actually did. In one, the result was too large to fit in context. Reducing the tool count wouldn’t by itself make that response any smaller. For someone designing an MCP server, that’s a cheap experiment worth borrowing: expand the result of a call you make every day and see how much of it the model actually needs. What happens after “send”? Getting an agent to pick the SDK still leaves the entire business of delivering the mail. Take click tracking. A provider can rewrite links through a shared tracking domain so it can count clicks. If one customer uses that domain for phishing and it gets blocklisted, links in another customer’s perfectly legitimate emails can suffer too. Zeno explains why Resend introduced custom tracking domains and why he wants to keep the free tier even though spammers can sign up for it. Custom tracking domains · Resend’s $3M safety commitment Watch the domain setup and pricing walkthroughs if you build developer tools. Stay for the last stretch if you know Zeno from Dracula. We get into what it’s like to build a company with a family and how much of a founder’s job comes down to finding a name that other people actually use. Show notes Zeno’s original Dracula announcement — the editor theme he launched in 2013. Zeno on what Claude Code chooses — his reading of the recommendation study and the differences between model versions. Resend’s MCP server — the integration behind the tool-count discussion. Anthropic on writing tools for agents — concrete approaches to returning less data when a tool result fills the context window. Resend’s anti-abuse handbook — what happens when a new sender signs up and where the team intervenes. articles.title: NaiveAI Promises 2,100 Tokens per Second. How Well Does It Code?
articles.snippet: Editor’s note: With this post, we are launching a new series focused on trying new models and products with unbiased reviews. Reach out with suggestions to tips@latent.space. Naive-N0.5-Flash is a new open-weights model built for AI coding tasks and tuned to generate as many tokens per second as possible . It was developed by a Chinese company called NaiveAI , with the aim of speeding up engineering and research workflows so that teams can experiment, iterate and solve complex problems faster. The model is an evolution of Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.5 , which NaiveAI has trained further for long-context reasoning and paired with its own NaiveRT inference engine. Naive-N0.5-Flash arrives with a bold pitch: a model built largely by AI and trained to do AI research itself, with recursive self-improvement as the long-term goal. To see what changed, it helps to know where it started. MiMo-V2.5 is a 310B-parameter sparse Mixture-of-Experts model with 15B active parameters, trained on 48T tokens. Its language backbone inherits the hybrid design of MiMo-V2-Flash, which mixes sliding-window attention (SWA) with global self-attention. NaiveAI's recipe starts from those weights. Through continued, multi-stage training, the team adapted the checkpoint to DeepSeek Sparse Attention layers. According to the NaiveAI technical blog , this took roughly 3.25T additional tokens on top of MiMo's original 48T. About 3T of those additional tokens were trained at a fixed 1M context length and with a constant learning rate. Benchmarking NaiveAI vs. DeepSeek and Z.ai We benchmarked the ultrafast mode of Naive-N0.5-Flash against DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM 5.3 Flash , and then gave all three the same app-building prompts. The trade-off, we discovered, is that Naive-N0.5-Flash takes longer to reason through harder problems, yet it still delivers answers faster overall. However, that comes at a slightly higher cost per question — although that may be an acceptable price for applications where speed comes first. Most popular models on OpenRouter as of the end of October 2026. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM 5.3 Flash are two of the most popular models in OpenRouter .
