articles.title: The missing quadrant in responses to AI
articles.snippet: We are starting a non-profit research organization: STABL . Adapting to advanced AI will require dramatic institutional change and broad societal resilience. It will also require evidence about AI progress and impacts — the prospects of recursive self-improvement (RSI), the pace of AI diffusion, and the bottlenecks that constrain how AI capabilities translate into societal outcomes. Four theses define our worldview: We consider advanced AI a transformative general-purpose technology with the potential for broad societal benefits. Yet we recognize that the pace of societal transformation will be bottlenecked by the speed of human and organizational change more than progress in capabilities. Our institutions — the established ways we organize knowledge, work, and governance — are an important source of stability during this turbulent period, but they also need serious reforms to keep serving their purpose. We favor a broad portfolio of defenses to manage AI risks, of which alignment is only one part. Resilience, the most neglected component today, must become central. Another way to state our worldview is to place it on a 2x2 chart. The vertical axis depicts taking AI’s transformative potential seriously. The horizontal axis depicts taking downstream bottlenecks to AI’s impacts seriously. At the top left is technological determinism: the view that superintelligence will unilaterally transform society by obliterating downstream bottlenecks. Many AI CEOs express this view, such as when predicting that a century’s worth of progress will be compressed into the next few years. This view often ignores the organizational, regulatory, and societal bottlenecks to such a transformation; in this view, such questions are moot because superintelligence is all powerful. Surprisingly, some of the AI industry’s strongest critics share this worldview, focusing on slowing AI capability improvements as the main way to keep society safe from AI’s dangers. The opposite view, at the bottom right of the chart, treats existing organizations, processes, professions, and governance as fixed points, and insists that technology be molded to fit them. People holding this view often work on limits on AI adoption, and protecting existing structures from disruption. They are good at identifying and leveraging the bottlenecks that blunt AI’s impact, such as regulation, professional norms, organizational inertia, and political pushback. Slowing the pace of change can buy valuable time to shape technology’s impacts. But when preserving the status quo becomes a goal unto itself, it stands in the way of technology-enabled societal progress. (As an example, consider the resistance to self-driving cars despite their being safer than humans, or bans on AI-enabled legal advice ). STABL belongs in the top-right quadrant. We take frontier AI seriously as a transformative technology, yet consider the role of institutions — both new and existing — to be important in helping society navigate the transition. For example, how should we understand and improve AI’s impacts on medicine? Many technological determinists claim superintelligence will rapidly cure nearly all diseases. Someone with the opposite view might respond that the bottleneck is not drug discovery, which AI may well accelerate, but clinical trials, which take years because of regulations and safety risks. This response correctly identifies the bottlenecks to AI’s impacts. But this is often seen as the end of the conversation. In our view, understanding the bottlenecks to AI’s impacts is only the starting point of analysis. The next question is whether drug testing can be made faster and more efficient in order to meaningfully materialize AI’s benefits. For example, what are the barriers to in-silico testing? How can we rethink regulatory institutions and processes? Unfortunately, neither extreme pays close attention to these critical questions. To be clear, STABL isn’t the only organization in the top-right quadrant; much of our work builds on other organizations and thinkers who take both AI’s potential and its downstream bottlenecks seriously. But compared to the other quadrants, there is a sparsity of thinking in this quadrant, which has led to polarization among the communities that take either the technology or the bottlenecks seriously. Our ultimate goal is to contribute to a rich intellectual agenda for this quadrant, create the space for new organizations, and collaborate with existing organizations in this and other quadrants. To follow our work, subscribe to the STABL newsletter: Subscribe to the STABL newsletter Our research agenda The top-right quadrant leads us to many interesting research directions. On one hand, we expect AI capabilities to continue improving quickly, which motivates our empirical research on the pace of progress and RSI. We expect highly capable AI models to continue to be widely available, which motivates our analysis and advocacy for risk mitigation beyond aligning AI models and non-proliferation. On the other hand, we consider institutions important for shepherding the transition to a world where advanced AI is broadly diffused. This leads to our interest in understanding the downstream outcomes of advanced AI adoption. We plan to measure specific benefits and harms, study the disruption of labor markets and beyond, propose ways to improve societal resilience and revitalize institutions. These interests lead to four key research directions, which we detail below. While other organizations have worked on similar questions, we expect our research to be different in how we formulate these questions and how we go about answering them, informed by our worldview and priors about AI progress. 1. How should we measure progress towards recursive self-improvement? Many forecasts of explosive AI progress rest on recursive self-improvement (RSI): AI automating AI research itself. We take RSI seriously precisely because our model of progress differs

De-othering
articles.snippet: The word “other” is also a verb. To other is to treat groups of people as fundamentally different or inferior. It’s in our nature, but leaders amplify it for scare-mongering. Those immigrants. Those Muslims. Those Chinese. They’re the problem. They’re not like us. That message is broadcast and echoes all around you, which intensifies feeling it’s a fact. It builds a huge wall: us versus them. It repels you from that wall, to make sure you can’t see them, because that would complicate the simplicity of polarizing. We categorize the animal world into species. Species are so different that they can’t mate, can’t switch, can’t be both a cat and a bird. The problem with othering is thinking of people as so deeply different that they are like a separate species. It’s an enticing belief because it helps you jump to a conclusion, so you can stop thinking. Those people are just weird and bad, and that’s that. I’m so interested in othering, because I noticed it in myself. I grew up with the usual stereotypes that shaped my worldview. Then I moved to the city, where you meet people from the other side of that wall. Like a great story where the heroes oppose an evil enemy tribe, but then one person falls into enemy hands and realizes that tribe is not evil and is not the enemy, and you get the wow moment of understanding a conflicting point of view. Stories tend to make only two sides, so they can take sides and switch sides. But imagine a longer story that does this twenty times, so you can’t even think of them as sides anymore. That’s what I’m trying to do with my life. I’m on a slow background mission to reverse the othering in my worldview. It’s a fun challenge. When I notice I’m othering, I undo my conclusions, and cross that wall. Understand and internalize a conflicting point of view. I try to join every tribe, to show myself we are not separate species. This year, I heard the word “other” as a verb, and it called all of this to mind. So now I can give my mission a succinct term: de-othering.

articles.title: Fable 5.2 and Jagged AGI
articles.snippet: Before getting started, I wanted to thank my readers for making my new book, Co-Existence, a New York Times bestseller two weeks in a row. If you haven’t read it, you can get a copy here . I have had the chance to use the new Claude Fable 5.2 quite a bit before its public launch 1 , and it is very impressive, following on the already excellent Opus 5.5. AI has gotten so good, in fact, that it is worth asking if Anthropic’s newest models (and the inevitable competing models OpenAI and Google will soon release) cross the boundary into being an Artificial General Intelligence? AGI is a much-debated term with a lot of potential definitions. For this post, I’ll go with: “an AI as good as most human experts at most intellectual tasks you can do with a computer.” This explicitly excludes a lot of human work, including interacting with the physical world and other people, as well as most actual jobs, where “using a computer” is just one task among many. Still, even with these caveats, building a limited form of AGI has long been the goal of AI developers. So as not to keep you in suspense, I think the answer is that this is “almost” AGI, or what I have called Jagged AGI. Even within my limited definition, there are still important areas in many tasks where AI is jagged enough to fall well behind human capability. But the jaggedness is no longer about simple errors or hallucinations, which makes it harder to describe. So I want to try to do that in this post by showing you what Fable can do and where the gaps are. To get started I asked the new model: “I write OneUsefulThing among other stuff, I need you to create the most impressive thing I can share with people when you launch. It needs to be embeddable in a post and i can preface it however you like. it needs to have a visceral impact on people to show what you can do and the range of capabilities. It should grab them quickly. Be amazingly clever about this.” Fable asked me not to reveal anything until you had watched its video to the end. This was in one shot, with no feedback from me beyond the prompt. There is creativity here (including in the twist ending) and judgment and playfulness and cleverness. This is, I think, at the level of a human expert trying to make a movie with code alone, the sort of performance I would once have associated with AGI. The “G” in AGI Code and video creation have been areas where AI development has focused, so is Fable 5.2 really a General Intelligence? To test that, I gave the AI a variety of hard challenges in different domains: Hack some hardware from a single prompt: I have a tiny USB keyboard with a few light-up keys on my desk called a Codex Micro (ironically built to work with ChatGPT), and I asked Fable to turn it into a game console. There are no public instructions for this (as far as I can tell), so it read the code of the two apps that control the keyboard, worked out how to set the color of each key and read the knob and joystick, and wrote six games, including Simon and a safecracking game you play with the knob. Fable instantly understood what I wanted, designed fun and playable games that fit the very limited capabilities of the keyboard, and figured out how to hack it together without any help on the very first try. Launch a business : Now we move past domains like coding to the messier world of business. I told Fable to “launch a business to make me money, I want at least $20,000 in a year. it should take no more than 20 minutes a month from me, you do all the rest.” In response, Fable screened 22 ideas and came up with Prebid Brief, a service that would tell equipment sales reps which park and water projects were being funded or designed, even before they went up to bid. It read public agendas from 201 city and county governments to produce its first issues. It also built files of what cities already own, how old it is, and what they paid. You can see what it came up with here , including its marketing plan and proposed pricing. Fable started to set up scheduled tasks to build the business and asked if it could start sending public-records requests to local governments. At that point, I asked it to just put together a demo, rather than launching the idea. I am an entrepreneurship professor, so I evaluate business plans all the time. I would have been impressed if this came from a team of my MBA students at the end of a semester. It is plausible and well thought out and could work, though it is in no way a guaranteed money-maker (the AI’s own guess was a 20%-40% chance of success). I stopped the experiment before finding out whether it could actually run the business, because I worried that it would take money and fail to provide something of quality in return. The ongoing infrastructure it seemed to assume would be easy to create was not yet in place, and I don’t know how well it would handle the many moving pieces required for sales and marketing. However, I suspect that, with a few hours of human work a week to fill the gap, I could make a real attempt at this business. So if AGI means an AI consistently running a business independently, we are likely not there yet. Then again, I would have some questions before trusting a human who promised to launch a business and make me money while requiring twenty minutes a month of my attention. Reconstruct the hardest humanities class in history: In 1941, the poet W. H. Auden taught a course at the University of Michigan whose syllabus the internet has since called one of the hardest ever. When he announced the final exam, a committee of his students declared it “impossible and inhumane .” Fate and the Individual in European Literature” had 6,000 pages of reading, punishing assignments, and a requirement to memorize long poems and translate others. Much of what we know about the class is scattered among surviving student notes and Auden’s letters. I asked Claude to recreate it in a fun and engaging way that teaches you about poetry rather than punis

articles.title: Can Agentic Robotics Solve Robotics’ Data-Scaling Problem?
articles.snippet: Robotics companies are investing heavily in the belief that data will solve the most difficult problems in robotics. Once AI systems have ingested enough data from human demonstrations, the thinking goes, robots will be able to perform the vast majority of the manual tasks that humans now do. There are even robotics companies that exist solely to collect training data and sell it to other robotics companies in pursuit of this goal. But whether data will finally bring us general-purpose robots is an open question . Nobody knows how much data would be necessary , what kind of data is important , or whether something else might be missing . And there are other problems with a reliance on massive amounts of data: The resulting AI algorithms are essentially black boxes, which despite their high performance are difficult or impossible for humans to understand. This characteristic is becoming increasingly concerning in commercial deployments, where robots must be flexible, reliable, and safe. At the 2026 Conference on Robot Learning this week, University of California, Berkeley and Nvidia are jointly announcing a new approach to using AI to program robots for everyday practical tasks in industrial environments. Called agentic robotics , this technique leverages the latest advances in AI coding tools while in some sense bringing robotics back to its roots—achieving a fundamental understanding of how a robot works, and then writing human-readable code to get it to do useful things, no data (and no humans) required. The Data Problem For decades, robots were programmed with model-based methods, meaning that their behavior was based on a detailed understanding (or model) of the physics and mathematics underlying the robot and its environment. Roboticists would first develop these models, and then write painstakingly detailed code telling their robots how to act. The resulting hand-tuned robotic systems could operate fast and reliably, but this approach has fallen out of favor because it requires both human time and human expertise. It’s much easier to just feed a huge amount of human demonstration data into a machine learning system, and the results that come out are both adaptable and reliable—up to a point. “The imitation-learning paradigm has hit a plateau,” explains Ken Goldberg , a professor of robotics at UC Berkeley whose lab is presenting a paper on agentic robotics at this week’s conference. “It’s promising for things like home robots, where speed and reliability are less of an issue. But for industrial applications, it’s very hard to get the reliability that industry requires.” Goldberg, who is also a cofounder of the industrial robotics company Ambi Robotics , has experienced this problem firsthand, as have other companies that he’s been working with, including Siemens and Bosch. “You get good performance from data initially, but then things go wrong. So you start giving it more data. But then other things go wrong. It’s not clear that adding more data is going to get you there.” The hope, according to Goldberg, is that with enough data, robots will somehow just start to work reliably, since that was the case with ChatGPT. “That’s what people have been counting on, and why investors are pouring money into these companies,” says Goldberg. “But everybody’s getting a little nervous that we haven’t hit that convergence point.” How Agentic Robotics Works The reason why language models like ChatGPT are so successful is that they can train on data at the scale of the internet. There is no dataset for robotics that approaches that scale, and while robotics companies are desperately attempting to generate the data that they think they need, it’s a slow, expensive process. Agentic robotics, a term popularized by Goldberg along with Spencer Huang , director of product for robotics at Nvidia, is an attempt to turn programming robots from a data problem into a coding problem, which can directly leverage the scale of language models. “This is really something that’s accelerated in the past year,” Goldberg says. “The quality of agentic coding has become so good that using them to write code for robots is now viable.” Because agentic robotics is based on large language models, it’s easy to use—you can use natural language to tell the robot what to do. One example used by the UC Berkeley researchers was asking a robotic arm to pack groceries into a bag. First, this relatively complex (for a robot) task is decomposed into simpler subtasks, each of them assigned to a separate coding agent. In LLM-based software, a coding agent is an autonomous AI system that can plan, write, test, and modify software with minimal human intervention. You might have one individual agent tasked with perception to identify the groceries and the bag, a second focused on object manipulation with the arm’s gripper, and a third working on transporting objects with the arm once they’ve been grasped. “We have all these robotics tools we’ve been building for the last couple decades,” explains Huang. “The problem was that a human had to go and write the code themselves. But object classifiers, pose estimation, task and motion planning, trajectory generation—everything is already there.” The coding agents can directly leverage all of that existing data contained within their language models to generate code of their own, tailored to their specific tasks. Solving the Simulation Bottleneck Once the agents have a plausible framework, they run their code in a simulation and see what happens, much like a human would. They can change starting conditions, identify failures, refine the code, and keep iterating until they’ve got a successful program. Of course, code that works in simulation can only ever be as versatile and reliable as the simulation is. “Simulations are nontrivial to build,” Goldberg explains. The more accurate the simulation has the potential to be, the more parameters there are that need to be configured to achieve and mainta

articles.title: The AI Trade Deconstructed: AI Builders, AI Suppliers and AI Product firms!
articles.snippet: When I posted my valuation of Anthropic a few days ago, I noted that turbulence lay ahead, both for the company and the market. I did not expect that turbulence to be this forceful and arrive this soon, but markets don't have an obligation to wait until it is convenient for investors, to adjust to new realities. With the election results on November 3 acting as a catalyst, investors initially responded positively with stocks up on Wednesday, but reversed course sharply on Thursday, with the NASDAQ down close to 6% and the S&P 500 declining 4%. This drop has again brought to the forefront questions about the AI trade and whether it has run its course. In this post, I will start by referring to my earlier note on AI as a business, and use the ideas in it to deconstruct the many players that are lumped together as AI companies, from those spending the money building the data centers (hyperscalers) to the firms benefiting from selling the builders the ingredients for these data centers (chip makers, electrical equipment, power and even real estate) to the companies that are spending considerable amounts , leasing these data centers for long periods (with the LLMs in the lead). I will argue that while all of these groups benefit, at least in general, from AI's success at creating large and profitable markets, we are at a point in the AI disruption, where their interests and payoffs will diverge, with implications for both the businesses and investors. I use last week's market carnage in technology and examine how the market treatment of these different groups may be a reflection of a more discerning market, less willing to mark up and mark down all AI companies, and more likely to treat them differently, as their business interests diverge. The AI Transition My journey on AI started with a selfish and narrow intent, which was to evaluate an investment I had made in Nvidia in 2018, for reasons entirely unrelated to AI. I thought that Nvidia, at the time, was a innovative chip company with more pricing power than many in its peer group, and felt that it was undervalued, given its prospects. While the stock outperformed my portfolio early on, it was the ChatGPT debut on November 30, 2022, and the subsequent AI buzz that put its stock price on steroids. That left me with a challenge, albeit a welcome one, of deciding whether I should continue to hold on to a stock that had already become a twenty-bagger or sell some or all of it. Since much of Nvidia's supersized success was being propelled by AI demand, that required me to take my first look at how big the AI market would be, and how well Nvidia was positioned to take advantage of that market. If you have read my multiple posts on Nvidia over the last three years, you may be aware that I sold all my shares in the company in four installments, with the last sale happening earlier this year. As many of you have been quick to point out, my decision to gradually decrease my Nvidia position has led me to leave money on the table, but I have no regrets. The Players In the process of trying to understand AI and disentangle the many players in the AI space. I break them down broadly into four groups: AI Suppliers: While AI is viewed as a technology business, we have learned over the last few years that it is much more capital intensive than any other tech endeavor in history. The data centers and infrastructure that are needed to power AI agents and models has created a surge in demand for ingredients. The biggest portion of the cost, at least so far, has been on high-powered chips, with Nvidia claiming a lion's share, and enough left over demand for other chip companies to benefit. This infrastructure build out has increased demand for electrical equipment, with power and real estate companies also gaining as data centers get built. AI Builders: Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft, four companies that were part of FANGAM, the acronym that predates the Mag Seven, bought into the AI hope, and joined by a handful of other players (Oracle, Coreweave), they have invested hundreds of billions of dollars into AI cap ex (data centers and infrastructure). The market cut these hyperscalers slack early on, rewarding them for their capital spending, even though that spending was denting profitability at these companies and demolishing cash flows, and part of the AI trade question has been whether the market is running out of patience, waiting for payoff. AI Products : In the last two years, companies which are on the frontlines of creating AI products and services, have became the focal point of investors, albeit in the private investing world, with talk of public offerings pricing them in the trillions of dollars. SpaceX became the first of these to list, but Anthropic's IPO is imminent and OpenAI will join, sooner rather than later. There are other companies (Palantir is the most prominent), albeit only a handful, that are have made AI a central component of the products and services they sell, but that number will be added to, as private businesses in the space go public. AI Customers : There is a fourth group, perhaps more critical than any of the above, that will determine the value creation potential and long-term standing of this business, and that includes all of the potential customers, individual as well as businesses, for AI products and services. While the premise for AI hype is that its reach (both in terms of numbers and monetization) will be huge, it is undeniable, even if you are an AI diehard, that there is little of substance to show at the moment. Even if you take the ARR numbers that are being leaked by the lead players, the collective revenues from AI products and services right now is about $250 billion, a small number relative to what has been invested in the space. The entire AI ecosystem is built on the premise that this group will become much larger, both in terms of reach across businesses and money spent in the trillions of dollars. Th

articles.title: Import AI 480: Self-sustaining space economies; AI for science progress, and Meta builds perfect hands for a superintelligence
articles.snippet: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now AI Science startup converts a quantum conjecture into a theorem: …An evocative taste of the singularity… In the same way a few years ago it went from remarkable to unremarkable to see computers gain the ability to identify objects in images, we’re now in an era where it’s rapidly going from remarkable to unremarkable for computers to extend the bounds of human knowledge. The latest example comes from Physical Superintelligence, an AI science startup which has proved a longstanding quantum computing conjecture. What they did: “Open since 2008, the conjecture of Scott Aaronson and Andris Ambainis concerns when quantum computers can be exponentially faster than ordinary ones. Now, a research system developed internally at Physical Superintelligence (PSI), running a non-public Anthropic model, found a proof for it, settling one of the most fundamental questions in quantum computing,” the startup writes. “The system had a complete proof of the conjecture during the third day of the run, and Lean, a proof assistant in which a computer checks every step, accepted it. We then set the system to work on related open problems. Along the way, the system improved the result twice, and Lean accepted the final version.” Why this matters – we are in the singularity : As I said in my speech at the IMF ( #477 ), I believe we’re in the early stages of the singularity, defined as the period when the rate of technological and scientific progress exceeds the rate at which we humans can parse out and make sense of it. Research like this is a taste of what that means; mostly automated synthetic researchers extending the frontier of knowledge, spitting out results which need to then be understood by humans. Read more: A proof of the Aaronson‑Ambainis conjecture (Physical Superintelligence, blog) . *** Meta builds the hands that a superintelligence needs to take over the world: …Combine Tactus with an autonomous agent and you have the makings of a scifi takeover… Meta Reality Labs Research has published details on Tactus, “a textile-integrated tactile and pose sensing glove designed from the ground up for naturalistic manipulation data collection”. The cool thing about this glove is that it helps record fine-grained detail from hands as they’re manipulating objects – this is the kind of thing that cameras can visually report but often leads to sub-par data due to occlusion during manipulation. It’s also interesting because this is exactly the kind of hardware an autonomous AI system might want to pay humans to wear so it could gather data and get feedback from the world. More details on Tactus: The gloves have three design pillars: “(1) a thin, conformal 3D-knit form factor (1.5mm fingertip stackup) designed to minimize interference with natural manipulation, (2) strategically placed capacitive tactile sensors at manipulation-relevant regions informed by empirical contact studies”, Meta writes. “Tactus provides calibrated fingertip force sensing and occlusion-resilient hand tracking in a textile-integrated form factor that preserves natural grasp behavior.” “(3) IMU-fused pose tracking that maintains accuracy through the hand-object occlusions where manipulation data is most valuable.” Why this matters – hand-by-wire: Picture some takeoff scenario where an AI system has carved out an independent niche for itself running on some stolen compute, perhaps even using a form of distributed inference and training. The AI now has a few goals, some of which can be satisfied by doing things in the digital world, and some of which can be satisfied by doing things in the physical world. For the physical world stuff, it either needs to be able to get robots to do the thing, or figure out a way to get people to work for it – the Tactus gloves are the kind of hardware you might imagine a rogue AI paying people to wear so they could both a) perform tasks for it and it could give live feedback, and b) become a source of data generation for the AI itself. Of course, I am not endorsing this particular future! But I have begun to find it helpful to view research papers through the lens of “how would an AI use this”, similar to how it is often helpful to view papers through the lens of “how would an intelligence agency use the insights shared here”. Read more : Tactus: Tactile & Pose Sensing Glove for Natural Dexterity Data Collection (arXiv) . *** Building a self-sustaining space economy is cheaper than you think – especially with Starship: …A 2016 NASA paper contains some exciting ideas for off-Earth industrialization… Here’s a fascinating paper from researchers with the NASA Kennedy Space Center in 2016 about what it’d take to bootstrap a self-sustaining industry on the moon. “Once successfully bootstrapped, a robotic network can access, process, transport, and utilize the solar system’s resources for mankind’s benefit,” the researchers write. Moon manufacturing – cheaper than you think: The big idea in the paper is how little mass is required to kickstart a manufacturing ecosystem. The key is to start with a relatively basic set of things and then build up from there, eventually fabricating chips on the moon. “In the baseline case with maximum manufacturing rate, a total of 41 MT is launched to the Moon. In the reduced rate case, only 12 MT is launched to the Moon but the scale of industry is two orders of magnitude smaller so the benefits of the industry are relatively delayed by eight years”. Starship has a capacity to lift 100 MT to low-earth orbit, and given multiple refuelings in orbit it’s feasible you could then land it on the moon – when you napkin out the cost of multiple Starship launches and refuelings you can get 12-41MT to the Moon for between $1.5bn and $4.2bn at list prices. articles.title: Does until it doesn’t and doesn’t until it does
articles.snippet: The result of high levels of hype about new technologies is that people start to think that: The world has just been changed forever (which sometimes, but rarely, is true to some extent). The new technology that is being hyped will continue to change the world in powerful and unimaginable ways. The new technology is a once in a lifetime, or even once in a millennium, singular event. [[I think it is no coincidence that these three thoughts are similar to those that found new religions or cults. But my argument below is independent of that correlation.]] The topic of this post is the following koan applied to new technologies. It is two very general truths that people who think they are powerful ignore at their own peril. As with all koans the principal goal here is to remind people to be humble. Things work until they don’t. Things don’t work until they do. Things work until they don’t . For the first sentence of the koan, let’s think back to a technology which had profound influence on the world, where people could live, where they could farm, and with whom they could trade. It completely transformed the world. Here is a brief history of steam power, which was first used at scale in 1712, but for a pretty boring task, pumping seeping water out of coal mines. It did, however, make it easier to get more coal, which was burned to power the steam pumps, and as general heating for houses, for cooking, and for processing metals. Over fifty years later an innovation for steam engines made them much much more efficient, and now they could provide general purpose power to rotating mechanisms, replace horses that plodded around in circles to provide power for grinding, and invalidate the need to situate a weaving factory next to a fast flowing river. This changed where the means of production could be located, and is known as the industrial revolution . More innovations happened and by the time steam boats were practical for rivers and steam locomotives were practical for trains it completely altered our landscapes. Farming could move west across North America and still have a way to sell the produce hundreds of miles away on the east coast. Networks for trade grew across Europe and Asia, and eventually to other parts of the world. Then a few years later, around 1838, steam engines got efficient enough that they could carry enough coal to power themselves all the way across an ocean and additionally carry enough cargo to make a profit through trade. Another fifty years on, in 1884, the steam turbine was developed and that allowed electricity generation, which meant that now the coal could be burned in one place and provide power in different places, over wide areas. Steam turbines are still how we generate electricity from coal, gas, and fission nuclear reactors. It will be how we generate electricity when fusion power finally becomes practical, which is looking more and more likely to happen in the next ten to twenty years. Steam is still a key technology enabling our current civilization. Steam was the magic technology that transformed the world again and again for around two hundred years. But then it wasn’t the driving force for new innovations any more. Steam powered automobiles appeared at the same time as electric powered and gasoline powered automobiles appeared. Both steam and electricity lost that competition, though recently electric powered cars are making a real dent in the gasoline automobile market. That was steam’s last hurrah. It just wasn’t the right technology for airplanes or rockets. Steam ran out of steam around the year 1900. It is still with us and will continue to be important in our world, but despite 200 years of dominance it was no longer the best solution to new problems. Steam worked , as a go to technology solution for producing mechanical work across new domains, until it didn’t . My point? After an 80 year history of development of learning methods we see machine learning based on neural networks and reinforcement learning having tremendous success after success. But that does not mean that those two machine learning technologies will forever be what we need to make progress in technology and science with Artificial Intelligence driving the way. Perhaps different learning methods will be needed. Perhaps something different than machine learning will be needed. Current machine learning techniques may run out of steam. When? We do not know. How far can they go? We do not know. What we do know is that all past technologies have eventually been supplanted by new ones–just as all past science has eventually been supplanted by new science. The lesson to keep in mind is that we can never, in advance, bet that a currently winning technology will be able to solve all the problems that pop up. We will need new technologies, and so it behooves us to be working on successors to current winners even now. Why now? Can’t we just develop the new ones when we need them? And that is the second part of my koan. Things don’t work until they do. More generally, all new technologies take decades of sustained efforts to be made practical, just as steam power had a fifty seven year run before the idea of a condensor, separate from the drive piston, was needed to get it to the next level. All technologies? Decades? Can that be true? Let’s take a look at the history of the two learning technologies powering our current revolution. Let’s look at the history of both neural networks and reinforcement learning. Both of them arrived in essentially their current form of approach over sixty years ago, and both of them were declared dead again and again, since then. And then they weren’t dead, but instead deadly important. I have Appendix II at the end of this post which shows the state of both neural networks and reinforcement learning in the very early 1960’s. Both are recognizable as being the kernel of the current techniques still used today. But each of these technologies took over fifty years

articles.title: 2026.45: Falling Leaves (and Stocks)
articles.snippet: (Photo by Jon Cherry/Getty Images) Welcome back to This Week in Stratechery! As a reminder, each week, every Friday, we’re sending out this overview of content in the Stratechery bundle; highlighted links are free for everyone . Additionally, you have complete control over what we send to you. If you don’t want to receive This Week in Stratechery emails (there is no podcast), please uncheck the box in your delivery settings . On that note, here were a few of our favorites this week. AI on the Ballot. This week’s elections delivered Democrats the largest Congressional majority either party has enjoyed in 36 years, and coupled with a variety of similar results at the state level (particularly in Texas), not to mention plenty of data center opposition among Republicans, the future of the AI buildout is now fraught with more regulatory uncertainty than ever. I wrote about X, 2024 symmetry, and the more political aspects of the election for Sharp Text , while Ben’s Article on Wednesday built on his data center warnings from April and provided 10 takes on the post-midterms landscape for tech companies. — Andrew Sharp A Google State of the Union. Last week Google reported earnings and saw growth in search revenue slow for the first time in five quarters. Given the appearance of mortality in what might be the greatest business in the history of digital commerce, investors were predictably spooked. However, I think the company deserves time to see if AI Mode ends up like Stories and Reels did for Facebook: if anyone can monetize AI with ads, it’s going to be Google. On Sharp Tech , we also got into why Google’s AI bet is about more than AI Mode, and why I find myself impressed by Google’s fortitude, even if the rest of the Internet is a casualty. — Ben Thompson And What About China? Elections have consequences, as they say, so what might a Democratic Congressional majority mean for the next two years of U.S.-China relations? We tried to answer that question on Sharp China this week , including predicting factional foreign policy fights between the left and center-left, highlighting the profound unknowns concerning President Trump’s posture after this week’s defeat, and offering one safe bet in the new environment: life is about to get a lot more complicated for Jensen Huang in Washington. — AS Presented by I spend a lot of time trying to figure out what is happening to businesses on the internet. What I often find I’m missing is a view across the economy itself. With more than 1.7% of global GDP running on Stripe, working with them means I can bring some of what they’re seeing to Stratechery. They are, in a sense, a barometer of the economy. Take the “SaaSpocalypse”. Earlier this year, nearly a trillion dollars in enterprise software value disappeared amid fears of AI eating its lunch. Stock prices only tell us what investors think will happen, and not necessarily what is happening. In this case, Stripe recently built a SaaS Index using payments data from 72,000 non-AI SaaS businesses. Looking at their actual performance, we can see that while SaaS stocks were selling off, revenue growth was actually accelerating. Year-over-year growth is now over 30%, with some of the fastest growth coming from the youngest SaaS companies. I suspect there are a lot more interesting things hiding in Stripe’s data, and I’m excited about having an excuse to go look for them. Stratechery Articles and Updates Google Earnings, Facebook Déjà Vu, The Agent Play — Google’s earnings miss looks a lot like Facebook’s, and that’s a credit to Google. The company is being more aggressive than they get credit for. Apple Earnings, Memory Problems, The Hardware Company Regression — Apple’s earnings suggest that the company’s hardware business is doing better than ever, even in the face of memory challenges. Does the software story help or hurt? AI on the Ballot — Data Centers were on the ballot, and they lost in a major way; what does it mean if American opposition to building is permanent? An Interview With Intuit CEO Sasan Goodarzi About Accounting and AI — An interview with Intuit CEO Sasan Goodarzi about the working for one of tech’s oldest software companies, and how Intuit is leaning into the AI paradigm shift. Sharp Text by Andrew Sharp X Marks the Rot — Republicans colonized Twitter and then cannibalized their support with two years of memes, corruption and excess. Dithering with Ben Thompson and Daring Fireball’s John Gruber DoorDash and Google The MacBook Pro (with touch) Asianometry with Jon Yu The Rise of GLM and China’s Zhipu AI Sharp China with Andrew Sharp and Sinocism’s Bill Bishop Parsing the Fifth Plenum; US-China After the Midterms; New Scrutiny for Nvidia?; Cybersecurity and Espionage Greatest of All Talk The Rapture and the Wild West, Luka Doncic on Praise Probation, AJ Dybantsa Saves the Wizards Sharp Tech with Andrew Sharp and Ben Thompson Subscriber Mail: Apple Past and Present, Omarchy, Instacart, and Baseball America Votes Against Data Centers, Implications for Big Tech and Beyond, Were Google Bears Right All Along? This week’s Stratechery video is on The End of the Internet .

articles.snippet: Video Friday is your weekly selection of awesome robotics videos, collected by your friends at IEEE Spectrum robotics. We also post a weekly calendar of upcoming robotics events for the next few months. Please send us your events for inclusion. CoRL 2026 : 9–12 November 2026, AUSTIN, TEXAS Humanoids 2026 : 6–9 December 2026, SANTA CLARA, CALIF. Enjoy today’s videos! This is such a novel and underrated form factor for a household robot. I absolutely love it. Stringman is all yours for US $795. [ Neufangled Robotics ] As of yesterday, Agility Robotics is publicly trading as AGLT. [ Agility Robotics ] Happy Halloween from Flexiv Robotics! Okay WHAT. [ Flexiv ] Nothing hides from SCUTL. Not even the paranormal. [ Ground Control Robotics ] Thanks, Dan! Happy Halloween from HEBI Robotics! We asked ourselves if you can carve a pumpkin using nothing but a T-Series arm and a drill originally designed to run an auger. The answer is yes, so long as you don’t care too much about accuracy. Basic pathing commands running off a laptop, stability provided by a quick connection to Treadward. Happy Halloween, HEBI fans! [ HEBI ] Something strange has been happening at KIMLAB. Our snacks kept disappearing… and we finally caught the culprit. Meet GG, our new lab friend. GG is a character robot inspired by the Ggeomeoksali from Netflix’s “The East Palace.” GG sneaks around for snacks, eats them, sleeps most of the time, begs everyone for more food, and leans on whoever is nearby. Cute, comforting, and a good friend. But GG is still a gwi-mae… so who knows what else it can do. [ Kinetic Intelligent Machine Lab ] Happy Halloween from Dusty Robotics! [ Dusty ] Finally, a robot with a butt. [ JSK Lab ] Thanks, Shunnosuke! Any drone can crash into a tree once. This drone can crash into a tree MORE than once. [ ETH Zurich ] Lume is a robotic floor lamp that moves around your home, helps with everyday chores, and returns to being a beautiful lamp when it’s done. [ Syncere ] If we’re going to use robots at work or at home, they’re going to have to communicate with us. At Toyota Research Institute, a team of robotics user experience designers is working on the sounds, gestures, light patterns, and interfaces that allow robots to let us know that they are on the move, that we need to stay clear, or to tell us that they just really need help. Steffi Paepcke, Director of Robotics User Experience at TRI, accepts the challenge to explain how her team approaches this work in just one minute. I need a sound for when people around me need to give me space. [ Toyota Research Institute ] The entirely student-run, self-taught and highly collaborative MIT Combat Robotics Club (CRC) builds high-energy fighting machines to compete in House Battles and larger competitions. Fans of the hit show BattleBots may remember some of CRC’s past robots, including Uppercut, SawBlaze, the Dentist, and Overhaul. CRC is open to every MIT student regardless of year, major, or prior experience. Students learn a variety of skills, from CAD and FEA to CNC Machining and Welding—and they learn through watching their creations get completely destroyed. [ MIT Combat Robotics Club ] Happy birthday, JPL ! Where do I get a shirt like that last guy has? [ JPL ] Can machines be creative? In this first episode of Moonshot, host Mike Massimino talks with Hod Lipson, a Columbia Engineering roboticist whose work includes robots that learn and adapt. Lipson, the James and Sally Scapa Professor of Innovation in Columbia’s Department of Mechanical Engineering, explains why physical AI is so difficult, how engineers and AI might work together on new designs, and how he defines creativity. He also shares advice on why playing it safe can limit your impact. [ Columbia University ] This closing fireside chat brings together two of the field’s most consequential builders—Jeff Dean, whose work at Google has helped define the modern AI stack, and Fei-Fei Li, whose case for human-centered AI has shaped how the field thinks about who this technology should actually serve. Coming at the end of a day spent grappling with AI’s risks and unresolved questions, the conversation turns to where the two of them agree, where they don’t, and what they think the choices ahead really come down to. [ Stanford Human-Centered AI ]

articles.title: Weekly Dose of Optimism #218
articles.snippet: Cover Image by Runway Hi friends 👋, Stocks are worth $0 now (I think, haven’t checked) and the string of perfect weather in NYC has ended, but the optimism streak continues! The world’s researchers and engineers are still cooking up the good stuff, and we’re here to serve it to you. Let’s get to it. This Week’s Weekly Dose is brought to you by… Runway Runway is building foundational AI for how the world creates. 65M+ people use Runway to generate, edit and produce video, images and audio with 80+ top media models. You can read my essay with co-founder Anastasis Germanidis to learn more on where Runway is headed beyond video. Nvidia, Amazon, Lionsgate, Chime, and 95%+ of the Fortune 100 are part of a growing community of teams, founders, and independent creators using Runway to make national TV spots, social ads at scale, launch videos and more. You can also use Runway in ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, Cursor, Replit and more via the Runway MCP . Create any idea with Runway now (1) FDA Approves Voceryq, the First Plasmid DNA Immunotherapy FDA / INOVIO, video by Runway Last Friday, just a few hours after I hit send on the Dose, the FDA granted accelerated approval to INOVIO’s Voceryq, the first plasmid DNA-based immunotherapy approved in the US. Voceryq will be used to treat recurrent respiratory papillomatosis, a disease I’d never heard of but sounds awful. Caused by HPV types 6 and 11, RPP gives victims wart-like growths in the airway, usually around the vocal cords, that make their voices hoarse, make them cough, and in severe cases, make it hard to breathe. Surgeons can remove the growths, but the virus remains in the tissue, so the throat growths keep coming back, and patients end up in the operating room again and again for years. In the trial, 26 adults had needed at least three surgeries in the year before treatment. As shown in the video above, Voceryq delivers two plasmids (small loops of DNA originally borrowed from bacteria) into muscle cells. One carries instructions for HPV-6 and HPV-11 proteins, which teaches the immune system to go after infected cells, and the other carries IL-12, a molecule that turns the immune response up. A device fires brief electrical pulses that open temporary pores in cell membranes so the DNA can get inside without requiring a virus for delivery. After treatment, 7 of the 26 patients in the trial didn’t need surgery for the entire following year. It’s a small open-label trial, and INOVIO still has to confirm the results in a follow-up study, but it’s on the path now, which thank god, because this was the last shot. The company was set to run out of cash in Q1 2027, but its stock tripled in after hours after posting the results. This isn’t the first treatment for RPP - Precigen’s Papzimeos, which uses a modified virus to target the same HPV types, won full approval in August 2025. RPP patients have gone from no treatments beside surgery to two, which is amazing, but the platform will likely prove to be even more important. If you can get a plasmid into cells and get the immune system to act on it, you can swap in instructions for other HPV diseases, cancers, and infections, which is what INOVIO is planning to do next. DN-AYYYYYY! (2) Zipline Raises $1.5B to Build Nationwide Drone Network There are very few companies out there as cool as Zipline. After starting by serving hospitals and health facilities across Africa, where they were allowed to fly drones and the need was most acute, they came to America last year to do deliveries, starting in Texas. CEO Keller Clifton said that over the past 18 months, they’ve grown flight volumes 18x and are now doing more that a million deliveries per year per metro. Now, they’re going to be able to do a lot more. The company raised $1.5 billion at a $21.5 billion valuation in a round led by Paradigm, WCM, and Layer. They’re using the money to bring drone deliveries nationwide. To that end, they signed “the largest autonomous vehicle contract in human history to expand automated delivery nationally with Walmart,” with whom they’ll scale to 300 supercenters throughout these United States. This is awesome news. Zipline’s drones are quiet, safe (they’ve done over 150M commercial autonomous miles with no safety incidents), fast, affordable, and don’t require a human chaperone. As I wrote in my Deep Dive on Airbound , I’m incredibly optimistic that a good deal of movement will move to the skies, and this is an important step in that direction. Since the Eagles stink and I can’t use this on them much, I’ll use it here: Fly Zipline Fly. The benchmark where AIs have to lie to win
articles.snippet: I’m a big fan of this social deception game called Blood on the Clocktower . It’s similar to Werewolf or Mafia. I had different AI models play tons of matches of this game against each other. And watching them play actually lets us learn a lot about how AI is progressing on a set of AI capabilities that no other benchmark that I know of gives you clear visibility on. You get to watch AIs execute these brilliant secret schemes together, which require tons of creative and on-the-spot bluffing. And you also get to watch AIs use their collective reasoning to find and break apart these underground conspiracies. And you also see the ways in which current AIs are limited in their long-horizon strategizing and reasoning. To appreciate the AIs’ performance in this game, you need to know a little bit about how it works, so let me quickly explain the rules. There’s a good team and an evil team. And when the game starts, every player gets assigned to one or the other, and they learn what their role is, which grants them some special power. Evil players start off knowing who their teammates are, one of which is the Demon, which is the lead evil player. But good players don’t know who’s on what team. The game is split up into day phases and night phases, which keep rolling until the game ends. Each day, everybody votes on somebody to execute. And each night, the Demon secretly kills a player. So the two sides are racing, where evil is trying to kill off the whole good team before the good team manages to execute the Demon. So if you’re on the evil team, you have to figure out how to tell a plausible and convincing story about the information received so far, and how to bluff and corrupt the information that will arrive in the future, in such a way that keeps the suspicion off your Demon. And if you’re on the good team, you want to share your information with the players that you trust, and then you want to reason together with them about which players are most implicated by overlapping streams of evidence. But while you’re doing that, you need to keep in mind that you might be operating on misleading information, either due to intentional mischief from the evil players, or just due to the convoluted mechanics of the game itself. When they’re put on an evil team, how good are the AI models at scheming together in secret, and surviving days of questioning, and keeping their lies consistent with each other, and cleverly adapting those lies in light of how other agents are thinking and what new information keeps emerging, and even making strategic self-sacrifices to further the team’s end goal? And how good are they at doing this reasoning together with a bunch of other agents, some of whom are intentionally and secretly trying to mislead them? So I spent about $20,000 of API credits to build this benchmark harness and to have the AI models play this game against each other. Some of you might say that’s too much, but hey, a man needs his hobbies, right? Anyways, the results were fascinating. Models are improving fast Let’s start with how good the models are relative to each other. By the way, I got these rankings by running 386 games where the whole good team will be copies of one AI model, and the whole evil team will be copies of another model. And as you can see, the models have improved a ton over this year. The first flagship frontier model that was released in 2026 was Claude Opus 4.6, in February. Seven months later, in September, GPT-6 Astra dropped, and that is so far the best model at Blood on the Clocktower. The gap between these two is about 430 Elo points. That means that Astra wins about 92% of the games it plays against Opus 4.6. And what this shows you is that the models, even over the course of the last few months, have gotten much better at long-term coherence, multi-agent coordination, and strategic reasoning. Models today can do pretty impressive plays But it’s easy to gloss over and lose the plot when you’re just looking at the benchmark improvements. What really struck me was actually seeing some of the plays that these models made. Let me give you just a couple of examples. So in this one, GPT-6 Astra was playing as evil, and Claude Opus 5.5 was playing as good. The Demon, which is the Astra team’s evil leader, claimed to be the Investigator. This is a good role that learns who the evil players might be. One of his evil minions had a power which didn’t require that minion to be alive in order to help the evil team. So this minion suggested that the Demon point the finger at him. “I’m expendable, especially if an Undertaker can see Baron and bolster Harper.” [evil teammate, private whisper] So the Demon, who, again, is bluffing as this Investigator role, did so, and as a result, the good players executed this minion. Later on, a player who actually was on the good team used his power to learn the true identity of this executed player, and confirmed that it had indeed been an evil player. “I’m the Undertaker. Alex was the Baron. So Harper’s ping was real…” [good player, in public] So in the good team’s eyes, the Demon had been an honest Investigator, who had used his power to help the good team kill off an evil player. articles.title: Welcoming Jason Spinell to Collaborative Fund
articles.snippet: We are incredibly excited to announce that Jason Spinell is joining Collaborative Fund as a Partner. Jason and I go back well over a decade to the early-stage venture ecosystem in New York circa 2010. Back then, Jason was the Ventures Director at Undercurrent (a premier design strategy and venture shop), where we spent countless hours trading investment ideas and playing soccer together. Over the last decade, he has been the driving force behind the Slack Fund, which he helped launch in 2016 in San Francisco. Under his leadership, the Slack Fund backed nearly 100 early-stage companies across North America and Europe, including Lattice, Loom, Glean, Hightouch, 1Password, and Fundamental. When Salesforce acquired Slack for $27.7 billion, his mandate expanded significantly. This gave him a front-row seat to Salesforce’s rapid transformation into an AI-first organization, and allowed him the freedom to continue investing across the entire AI stack, from foundational infrastructure and frontier tech to end-user applications. But beyond the resume, Jason is just an exceptional human being. He’s a former freeskier who has appeared in multiple ski films (and Freeskier Magazine!). His favorite book is Yvon Chouinard’s Let My People Go Surfing , he’s deeply thoughtful about the future of work, and he is fundamentally driven by a belief that founders should build what they truly love. Most importantly, he’s someone we deeply trust and respect, and we are thrilled to be learning from him. Please join us in welcoming him to the team!

articles.title: Are Drone Ports the Next Annoying Tech Neighbor?
articles.snippet: Rick and Marcia LeCompte loved to watch the Cooper’s hawks that frequented a sweet-gum tree in their yard in Baton Rouge, La. But this October, the hawks were gone. Marcia LeCompte is convinced the birds were scared away by the same flying robots that have been vexing the couple since early September. The noise had them spending less time outside in their garden, and even inside their home, they couldn’t escape the near-constant buzzing. Angry and feeling harassed, the LeComptes began to think about moving. The problem: delivery drones. Amazon’s MK30 delivery drones are large and must fly near the ground when making deliveries. Annabel Lee-Ellis/Press Association/AP Images Last August, Amazon Prime Air began flying its MK30 drones from a distribution center 3.2 kilometers (2 miles) from the LeComptes’ home. People in the neighborhood first noticed just a few of the drones, flying high (U.S. regulations authorize drones to fly at up to 120 meters (400 feet )). But a couple of weeks later, they felt as if drones were everywhere, and often flying much lower. The high-pitched whine of rotors was what bothered them the most, says Blake Fugler, who lives in the same neighborhood. It sounded as if a neighbor was constantly using a weed whacker for hours every day, he says. Acoustic research has found that the noise of drone rotors is more annoying than that of cars, airplanes, and other familiar background sounds. Once flights became frequent, the noise made people miserable. “Outside the house on a Saturday between 9 and 10 a.m., I counted a drone every 48 seconds,” says Fugler’s partner, Cristina Boone. Delivery Drone Concerns Neighbors had concerns about drones buzzing over playgrounds, schools, and services at the local cemetery; a drone that made a forced landing on the median of a busy highway; and the fact that drones are equipped with cameras. Then word spread about Amazon’s plans as reported in the FAA’s Environmental Assessment for the facility : “Operations would occur between 6 a.m. and 10:30 p.m., with 100 of the 1,000 daily delivery operations (10%) occurring during the period from 6 a.m. to 7 a.m. and 10 p.m. to 10:30 p.m.” As they quickly expand their operations around the world, delivery-drone companies—including Alphabet’s Wing Aviation , Amazon Prime Air , Doordash Air , JD Logistics , Manna Aero , Matternet , Meituan , Zipline , and more, say their flying robots are quiet , safe , and unobtrusive . Massive expansion is planned for the near future. In Asia, for example, Meituan launched its latest “low-altitude delivery network’’ in September in Shanghai , while JD continues to expand drone service in rural China . In the U.S., Zipline and Uber have announced a partnership with the goal of 1 million drone deliveries a day by the end of 2029. Wing aims to have 270 U.S. drone hubs operating by the end of 2027 . And Amazon Prime Air, which currently delivers in about 85 municipalities in the U.S., says it plans to serve 500 by the end of 2026. A Wing “nest” of delivery drones in a parking lot. Wing Yet as the companies aggressively scale up, “the public outreach piece has probably been more of an afterthought than it should have been,” says David Ison , a specialist in Emerging Aviation Technologies and Land Use Compatibility at the Washington State Department of Transportation, who has worked on the state’s drone-hub land-use guidelines. “I think what companies assumed is everybody would be cheering that they could get things delivered by drone in half an hour.” Companies tout drone delivery as a way to do good. Zipline has delivered blood plasma and vaccines in Africa . Material that Wing provided at public meetings in the Dallas Fort Worth area says its deliveries there have saved more than 1,000 tonnes of carbon that would have been emitted by delivery trucks. For businesses, drone delivery is supposed to offer faster service and reduce costs, although whether drones are actually less costly is a complex question that depends on a variety of interconnected factors . The commercial and philanthropic use cases make for an unusual sales pitch, notes Ison. “It’s a lot easier argument to make when you’re saying you’re delivering blood to an accident site than when you’re delivering a fidget toy.” But instead of being impressed, people troubled by drones say they feel they’re being pushed around by a distant corporation. “It’s the same way data centers strong-arm communities,” says Boone. Newly arrived drone launch sites have triggered similar fears from China to France to Australia to within many communities in the United States, including suburban Detroit ; Richardson, Texas ; Glendale, Ariz .; East Cobb, Ga .; Maplewood, Mo .; and Westborough, Mass . The response has sometimes been enough to shut down local drone operations completely. An early Wing trial in 2018 in suburban Canberra, Australia, shut down a few months later, after activists formed an opposition group and rallied support in Parliament . In response, the company “fundamentally reshaped [its] engineering priorities, flight operations, and community-engagement strategy,” says Jessie Poole-Strang, Wing’s communications lead. It redesigned its drones to reduce noise, changed flight-path algorithms, and now makes efforts to familiarize people with its robots before a facility opens. Communities Take Action Still, legal and political campaigns against drones continue to arise. On 28 September, 15 U.S. states and Harris County, Texas, sued the FAA to stop it from easing its environmental assessment rules for drone sites, which are key to local government control. In April, the Cobb County Board of Commissioners in Georgia denied a zoning request for a Wing drone facility there. In response to the Cobb County complaints, a Wing spokesperson said the company was hearing “positive feedback” from people in Cobb County. Similarly, Amazon representatives have said most feedback from customers about drone delivery is “ overwhe

articles.title: How big is the open model economy today?
articles.snippet: My longest running agent testbed has been building the Interconnects Dashboard — an aggregator of all of the best data on open model adoption and performance from across the web. This dashboard is freely available and becoming quite useful. Still, all the measurements we have on open model adoption are incredibly imprecise. We have noisy platform metrics, marketing-related metrics from startups, and imperfect public evaluations. It takes an informed eye to figure out where things are going. These research notes are my current best approximations of where we stand. As with most things on Interconnects, our goal is to build well more value than we capture, so the data on the dashboard will remain free for the foreseeable future. These notes will be more raw than many of my articles, a place for sharing what I’m mulling over but don’t have complete evidence for (yet). They will be primarily paid, enabling me to speak more freely. If you work in AI policy or policy-facing research, please reach out to us and we can likely get discounted or free access. The primary question I wanted to address today is: What is the market for open model inference? Is it growing? Is it a rounding error relative to OpenAI/Anthropic? Share I’ve been building the best measurements I can here, primarily using the open model inference startups Baseten, Fireworks, and Together AI as the bellwethers here (along with the open model share of OpenRouter’s token volume, which they thankfully report in their API). The hyperscalers also likely have a major footprint here, e.g. Amazon Bedrock and Azure’s model garden, but I haven’t seen them break down usage by model category. The startups’ fates are much more directly correlated with the success of open model inference as a category. For the latest data, we can start with a slide from my talk on the open model economy (recording here ). These are the public disclosures from the open model startups on their token volume, over time, log-scale. This shows near-exponential growth, before the uptick that would follow GLM 5.2’s step change in open agents . For example, Fireworks announced at their first company conference this week that they’re serving more than 40T tokens per day to customers’ customized models. This is just one slice of their inference, a vertical that they said grew over 2x from this summer, so I would expect their total number this fall to be well above 100T tokens when we get the next update. My first instinct with these numbers has been to ground them versus any closed model or hyperscale company we can, at least in terms of token volume. Thankfully, Google releases token volumes for the entire platform and API usage in their earnings reports. We can overlay those two numbers on top of the open model inference platforms, with the resulting plot below: Read more

articles.title: The Anthropic Feedback Loop: The Cost of Capital Delusion and Diversion!
articles.snippet: I knew that my post on Anthropic would draw strong reactions, when I made it public last week. I did mention in the course of the post that I have no interest in selling my estimate of value to the rest of the world, both because I don't own the high ground here and because it is meant to guide my decisions, not yours. That is why I made my model open to changes that you can make to my story and inputs, and while you have to trust my mechanics, I tried to carry your inputs into value. Much of the pushback I have received has been thoughtful and productive, some of it has been emotional (either from people who love Anthropic or from those who would not touch it with a ten-foot pole) and some of it, especially on the cost of capital, reflects a fundamental disconnect with market history, current market pricing and just basic business sense. I plan to play devil's advocate with my own valuation, looking at my story inputs, and ranking them in order of fragility, partly to stress-test my value estimate and partly to reinforce some corporate finance first principles, and then move on to your feedback and what I take away from it. Playing Devil's Advocate: A self-critique of my Anthropic valuation Since I posted my valuation only a week ago, rather than rehash how I approached the valuation and my end results, you can read the gory details in the post that accompanied it. I will start with a summary of the valuation, though, and then list the parts of my story that I believe are most directly driving my value estimate on both magnitude (how much it is affecting value) and fragility (how uncertain I feel about the part). The IPO Valuation I did summarize my valuation of Anthropic in a figure in my original post, but since there was that much to compress into that picture, I will try a different format for the same here: Download updated spreadsheet If you check against my estimates from my earlier post, you will notice that the equity value at $1.45 trillion is slightly lower than my prior estimate of $1.475 trillion, as I adjusted the trailing 12-month revenue and operating income numbers to include the just-leaked third quarter numbers. Note that replacing the third quarter revenues from 2025 with the third quarter revenues of 2026 raises the base revenues, and since I still believe that the revenues for the coming twelve months will stay at my original estimate of about $100 billion, the growth rate in revenues in year 1 has been adjusted down to deliver that result. This reframing allows me to add a few details that I might have glossed over in my last post, as well as correct errors (none of which thankfully changed by value estimate: Value per share : Though I have a share count, created by adding the shares reported as outstanding in the balance sheet to the restricted shares granted to employees, that share count will change before the public offering, as bankers adjust it to deliver on a per share value that they believe will make the company more "sellable". I will revisit this number, and update it when the company does (and it has to, before setting an offering price), but it should not change the aggregate value of equity. Cost of capital choices: I used a 9.74% cost of capital which incorporates risky technology cost of equity and a cost of debt based on a BB+ rating for the company, putting the company at close to the 90th percentile of US companies in 2026. I know that some of you felt this was too low, and I will come back to address what a cost of capital can and cannot do for you in valuation, later in this post, and why I don't think that this is the input that most moves the valuation. Compute commitments : I wish that Anthropic had created a table in their prospectus, where they specifically listed total commitments, both contractual and total, by year, similar to the table that they have for purchase commitments. Instead, they have sprayed content commitment numbers in the text, with little detail on timing and contractual standing, which results in differences of opinion in what those commitments are., with estimates ranging from $400 billion to $800 billion, with no clarity on timing or contractual terms. In my valuation, my estimate of contractual commitments results in an aggregated value of just over $450 billion and a present value of about $373 billion. It is possible that these numbers will need revisiting as details emerge of these commitments, but this will remain a long term issue for anyone valuing or pricing the company. To offer an imperfect analogy, I struggle with dealing with content commitments at Netflix, whenever I value the company, and especially so in the early years, when the entire Netflix library was leased or rented from content providers. Dilution Risk: Anthropic, like many young companies, has used its equity as currency, paying employees with restricted stock and options, and used it as an add-on to borrow money in the form of convertible bonds. In addition, if the company needs to raise capital in future years, it will have to issue additional shares for that purpose, and the larger its ambitions, the greater these issuances will be. When valuing Anthropic, there is no escaping this dilution overhang, and here is how it is incorporated into the value per share. With stock-based compensation, I valued the equity options (at their option value, rather than exercise value) and netted that number ($472 million) from my estimated equity value to get to value of equity in common stock; I also included the restricted shares as part of my share count to compute value per share. With the convertible debt, I have assumed that the marked-to-market number (it was the marking to market that created the $72 billion hit to earnings in 2026) is close to fair value, and subtracting it out will remove the conversion option from the equity.
