articles.title: I Deliver Parcels in Beijing - by Hu Anyan
articles.snippet: summary: At first, it’s interesting autobiographical accounts by a man in China with low-status odd jobs. You learn what it's like to be a warehouse packer or delivery guy. Then near the end of the book he gets burnt-out, takes a two year break to stay at his parents house being a full-time writer, and you realize of course his stories are only shared here because he took the months to write them. But then he also shares a brilliant analysis of what makes rock music great, and says things like “as the German philosopher Gotthold Ephraim Lessing said”, so you find he’s actually a really thoughtful insightful guy that has his philosophical reasons for choosing simple manual jobs. Really surprisingly interesting book. recommend: 9/10 my notes: The customer is king? But there should only be one king. I have to serve hundreds every day. I watched my classmates change almost the moment they left. The gap between them and me only widened with time, our differences setting deeper in us. Meanwhile, this seemingly natural transformation continued to elude me. How they went from students to full-blown grown-ups just like that was a mystery. Had there been an adult version of them hidden inside their adolescent selves all along? They only needed to shed their student skins and the metamorphosis was complete. When disgruntled, the lowly among us only have each other to pick on, because going after the powerful will only cost us. Love is blind, people like to say. But if you ask me, love sees clearest of all. It is the least interested in personal gain, and the most true to itself. What’s blind is hatred. My earliest writings were just pale imitations of Salinger’s The Catcher in the Rye. The more literary works I read, the more distant I felt from my reality. This book required none of the effort of invention, I just put down things as they were. A distinctive characteristic of “rock as art form” is that its success depends heavily and directly on the artist having a unique spirit and personality. Rock’s charm comes from the synergy between artist and music: the artist’s soul (the content) and the music (the form). It is why true rock musicians are repelled by music that is elegant, refined, and skillful but lacks soul. The best rock isn’t necessarily the most moving song, most beautiful voice, or virtuoso performance; it’s about the opposite extreme: relishing the simple, the impulsive, and the rough around the edges, unique and insightful. Performance is the art form of presentation. The most standout personality, interrogating the soul, becoming ever more sensitive and radical, sustaining their artistic vitality and originality. They seek unique expressions for even the most insignificant parts of themselves. The artist crying out as they descend into the abyss. Consumerism is lifelong imprisonment, which only gives the appearance of freedom. They knew very little about my past, and I very little about theirs, and no one had any interest in prying. Selflessness might be a noble virtue, but it isn’t fundamental to being human. The landlord at my new place was an elderly Bai woman who couldn’t speak Mandarin but really enjoyed chatting. She wouldn’t let me go without a quick tongue wag whenever she saw me. Yet, in the year-plus that I knew her, I didn’t understand a single sentence she said. I just smiled at whatever came out of her mouth. She talked, I smiled, and it would eventually make her laugh. People’s mindsets are complex, even polyphonic. There can be multiple melodies all playing over the top of each other. Some remarkable individuals never let their considerable knowledge weigh them down. They navigate through it like seasoned sailors negotiating hidden reefs, mapping principles in their minds so as to never have one unexpectedly interfere with the simple joys of life. And as the German philosopher Gotthold Ephraim Lessing said, the pursuit of truth is more valuable than its possession. The same goes for freedom: The pursuit is more precious than the attainment. If we see no value in the work we do, beyond a means to make ends meet, then we are dooming ourselves to a bleak psychological landscape.

articles.title: Import AI 479: Spacewar; low-latency tasks versus LLMs; Genie 4
articles.snippet: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now LLMs are very bad at low-latency tasks: …Realtime-Bench says it’ll be a while till AI systems can play games or do online auctions for you… Researchers have built Realtime-Bench, “a suite of carefully curated dynamic tasks where delayed actions directly affect success”. The test helps evaluate how well modern, general-purpose AI systems can perform tasks where decisions need to be made in real-time. The benchmark consists of 50 interactive game and web tasks, split across 30 web tasks in four categories (travel, e-commerce, service, and security), and 20 game tasks (arcade, puzzle, strategy, and simulation). Who did the research: The benchmark was built by people at the University of Texas at Austin, Ohio State University, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, NVIDIA, Northwestern University, and Steadyworks. What it measures: The test is designed to probe for three qualities: temporal state awareness (”RT-Perceive”), where models can use observations to track changes in the world; adaptive deliberation (”RT-Deliberate”), where models alter their reasoning length and depth according to available time; and time-aware action selection (”RT-Act”) where models need to appropriately time their actions for the situation. “For example, an agent purchasing a ticket must track the sale status and assess whether observed availability is still current (RT-Perceive), limit further deliberation when the purchase window is closing (RT-Deliberate), and choose between waiting for sales to open and purchasing while tickets remain available (RT-Act).” They have three different conditions: Wall clock, which is designed to test out performance under real-world latency. Paused clock, which lets you arbitrarily pause things so you can get a sense of baseline capability, and Token clock, which “advances the environment at a fixed rate per generation token. An action is applied at the simulated time reached when it is committed, so consuming more tokens delays execution regardless of actual inference latency”. How well do models do? The authors tested out models from OpenAI (GPT-6-Astra, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-Realtime-2, OpenAI Decisions), Anthropic (Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Opus 5), Google (Gemini 3.8 Flash, Gemini 3.1 Flash Live, Gemini 3.8 Live), Jev 1.13, as well as Chinese models from Deepseek (V4.1) and Moonshot AI (Kimi-K3). GPT-6 Astra (high) got the highest pass rate on the ‘wall clock’ evaluation setting, with 36%. By comparison, with a paused clock, models with high reasoning get closer to 70% or even 80% success. Why this matters: This benchmark is an effective proxy for where AI agents will break – the low scores here point to tasks where AI agents cannot yet be expected to perform well. Check out the leaderboard : Realtime-Bench (official website) . Read the paper : Realtime-Bench: Can Frontier Models Solve Real-time Interactive Problems? (arXiv) . *** The future of spacewar, courtesy of the Defense Intelligence Agency: …Anti-satellite tech, space nukes, and more… Working in AI can be stressful so sometimes to relax myself I like to read about other topics to get a sense for what horrors lie elsewhere. I take the same approach with depression, where if I feel sad I will try and listen to music by people sadder than me in an attempt to cheer myself up (e.g., Radiohead, Neil Young, and in very dark moments Bill Callahan / Smog, etc). So with that in mind I recently read “Challenges to Security in Space”, by the Defense Intelligence Agency. What’s going on in space: As with conflict on Earth, space is defined by conflict between the US versus China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea, with China the most technologically sophisticated, and Russia the most seemingly gung ho. “China and Russia are developing a formidable spectrum of offensive capabilities to degrade or destroy space services of other countries, from kinetic destruction to sophisticated jamming and cyber operations,” the DIA writes. “China has more than tripled its space launches per year in the past decade, with 22 launches in 2016 and 93 launches in 2025… Beijing judges space is central to the United States and its allies’ operations. Beijing also considers space an offensive military domain, which has shaped integral components of PLA military planning and campaigns.” Spacewar: The general vibe you get from reading this 100+ page report is there is a huge amount of ugly, frightening stuff happening in space, or being done to things in space by things on the ground. Some example quotes: “By the late 2020s, China may field space-based directed energy systems and higher-powered ground-based directed energy systems capable of threatening satellites in higher orbits” “China is developing space-based technology, including on-orbit counterspace weapons, capable of holding space systems at risk” “Russia’s Peresvet, a ground-based laser system, is designed to dazzle enemy satellites’ optical systems to mask the movement of Russia’s strategic missile systems” “Russia has launched several satellites over the last few years which conducted test activities on orbit for technologies that could enable attacks on other countries’ satellites and result in temporary or permanent damage” China has a couple of spaceplanes, akin to the US’s hyper-secret X-37B vehicle, and they appear to be getting more sophisticated. In 2023, one of China’s aforementioned vehicles, “released and interacted with an object.” Satellite-on-satellite fights: It’s obvious throughout the report that we’re in a world where rival nations have satellites that try to go up and mess with other satellites from other people. “In 2019, Russia launched satellite Cosmos 2542, which released a second satellite, Cosmos 2543. Cosmos 2543 then began following a U.S. national security satellite and approached it multip

articles.title: Was I wrong about open models & cyber risks?
articles.snippet: Last week coined the term “ Black October “ after an onslaught of critical vulnerability disclosures, including PHP2Shell and a long-standing GitLab bug, signified the moment when the cyber risks of AI models started to materialize. It seemed like the news cycle had stabilized a bit when I started writing this, but then there was news about another major crypto security incident at Binance . The crypto industry has a very long history of hacks , so it’s not the best industry to indicate vulnerabilities translating into new societal harm. Still, we are very much still living through the implications of this transition. The best guess for what is happening in the cybersecurity space is that the behind the scenes work has only accelerated, bringing more people and resources in to try and patch the internet — the Wall Street Journal reported that cyber first responders are strained , which seems like the system working. We’re living through this plot of an exponential rise in vulnerabilities, which will take a long time to level off at the top of the sigmoid. A few weeks ago, before the rapid acceleration in vulnerability disclosures and the uptick in reported hacks, I wrote the following take. It’s been getting a pretty consistent barrage of feedback, some hopeless dunk attempts and some reasonable discussion, so I wanted to unpack where I stand. Share Open-weight Mythos in April would’ve been fine? When Claude Mythos was announced, it was previewed as if it was a new class of cyber weapon, where if it ended up in the wrong hands it would’ve caused mass societal destabilization. It seems like this was wrong. By all measures, GLM-5.3 is the model that crosses that threshold of capability, and there’s little public evidence that much has changed, and we’re over a month out of the model weight release. In fact, I would go further. If Claude Mythos was accidentally released as open-weight, it seems like the world would have been more or less fine. Yes, there would be a clear increase in cybersecurity incidents and it would be bad for society if the model leaked, but it would be a scenario that looks more like an acceleration than a step change in risk. The leading proponents of this new wave of open-weight fear mongering have effectively been making a falsifiable prediction — that the current open-weight models are going to cause substantial, not seen before AI harms by crippling our cyber infrastructure. Based on all the evidence I have, which I’ve unpacked above, they’re set up to be wrong. At least now, after so many years of debating open weight risks, we will start to get some real answers. To start the reflection, I wanted to do more due diligence and track down some receipts on the claim that the AI safety community was reacting as if open-weight Mythos would be an actual disaster, and not just a painful headache. This was distinctly my impression having lived through the online discourse. I’ve gotten criticism that the frontier AI community never said it would be a “true disaster,” but regardless of exactly what they said, it is always about how people hear and internalize your information. Here are some examples of the sort of language that I felt was too exaggerated and from prominent people, which spilled into the public and more importantly federal government perspective that this was a cyber weapon include: Rob Wiblin, host of the 80,000 hours podcast, on his own podcast (April 10, 2026): “If it fell into the hands of criminals or hostile state cyber actors, it would be an actual disaster.” Anthropic, in the Project Glasswing announcement blog (April 7, 2026): “Given the rate of AI progress, it will not be long before such capabilities proliferate, potentially beyond actors who are committed to deploying them safely. The fallout—for economies, public safety, and national security—could be severe.” For one that is actually more reasonable, to illustrate the fine lines between correct and exaggerated, from Zvi Mowshowitz (who I don’t agree with a ton of things on) on April 9, 2026: “Claude Mythos would give attackers a cornucopia of zero-day exploits for essentially all the software on Earth … It would be chaos.” To date, this chaos has been confined to those running large-scale digital products, which is good, but could change. I largely still stand by my above writing a few weeks ago, but I’m nervous about it. I’m not a cyber expert, I’m working hard to make the most educated predictions I can. It’s a fine line between “all of our tech companies need to work extra hard to keep us secure” and “public infrastructure is actually going down.” It is very clear as of writing this that there are way more critical vulnerabilities which are being found in popular tools and fixes are being built. For example, Epoch AI recently published a nice post on their internal work using GLM-5.3 to try and find vulnerabilities and chain them into what could be an attack. The actual exploit they found in Firefox is a good example of why cyber risks need multiple things to align for harm to be done: We used GLM 5.3 to create a website that, simply when visited by a Firefox user and without further interaction, gave the attacker the ability to exfiltrate files from the user’s computer. Here, the exploit is in Firefox, and a would-be hacker needs to plant a website that is looking for this exploit. This is doable, and could have serious consequences, but just finding the exploit is only one step in a multi-stage process. In the previous post, I should’ve been more specific on what “fine” is for a future of cybersecurity, and in this case it means giving more credit to some of the AI safety community that discussed this reasonably as a new era in cyber instability. Reflecting on it, I’m not sure fine is the right word to describe what is inevitably coming – a forced industry update to a new way of working with software, which will clearly be expensive and accompanied by some hard work. If you’re already som

articles.title: Confidence isn’t about having more, it’s about calibrating the right amount
articles.snippet: Joe Burrow is once again among the NFL’s elite quarterbacks. Through five weeks of the 2026 season, he ranks fourth in touchdown passes, sixth in passing yards, and leads the league in completion percentage at over 70%. Yet, what sets him apart isn’t physical. It’s mental. Burrow has a nearly perfect level of confidence, which has been calibrated over time. Calibrated? Yes, calibrated. Let me explain. When Burrow was just nine years old, his AAU basketball team was trailing by eight points with thirty seconds left. His coach thought the game was over. Burrow didn’t. He scored nine straight points, including several consecutive free throws, and somehow won the game. Afterward, Burrow’s coach, a sociology professor at Ohio University, pulled his parents aside and told them their son possessed an unusual quality. His blood pressure, he said, appeared to be the same whether he was shooting a basketball, cutting the lawn, or pulling someone out of a burning building. He was unfazed, regardless of the task. Then the coach paused before telling them he was thankful their son was using his talents for good. Otherwise, he could be the next Dexter, the fictional serial killer. Thankfully for Burrow, his parents, and Cincinnati Bengals and LSU Tigers fans alike, that confidence was channeled in the right direction. Over the past decade he has won a national championship and a Heisman Trophy, earned multiple trips to the NFL Pro Bowl, and came within minutes of winning the Super Bowl in 2022. The older I get, the more I appreciate how much confidence matters. In fact, I am now convinced it might be the most significant differentiator in many walks of life. But here’s the critical nuance: it’s not about having “a lot” or “a little”. It’s about calibrating whatever amount of confidence you have. For some people, confidence needs to be unlocked. For others, it needs to be reined in. And for people like Joe Burrow, the challenge is channeling it in the right direction. Too little confidence can prevent someone from taking risks, facing challenges, or even engaging at all. Meanwhile, too much can morph into arrogance. Taken too far, it convinces someone that the rules, the odds, or even reality itself doesn’t apply to them. The key is finding the right balance. I witness this every day with my two sons. My younger son, who is about to turn eight, thinks he can rule the world. There is absolutely no reason for him to possess this much confidence. He hasn’t earned it. He hasn’t justified it. He just has it. And, in many ways, it’s wonderful. Very few things scare him. He’s adventurous. He jumps into nearly everything he does with reckless abandon. This extreme level of confidence might be his greatest strength. Yet, it has the potential to become a material weakness if he doesn’t learn to keep it in check. My older son has confidence too, but his is more like a flame that needs oxygen. It often requires encouragement before it begins to grow. Yet when it does, you can see it. He consistently surprises me with what he is willing and capable of doing. Neither is better. They’re just different and in need of different levels of calibration. But how is someone supposed to find the right level? First, calibrating confidence starts with the people who surround you or you surround yourself with. To this point, while Burrow’s coach may have sounded like he was complimenting his star player, I actually think he was directing his comments at his parents. Burrow’s confidence was the easy part. He simply had it. The challenge was channeling it into productive use, which, as Michael Moritz of Sequoia Capital said on The Outsider podcast, is the essence of parenting. That said, we obviously can only control this to a point. Our parents are ours whether we like it or not. The same is often true of our teachers, coaches, and bosses. However, what we can do is identify those who bring out the best in us, determine what makes them unique, and seek out more people like them. Personally, I’ve had countless teachers, coaches, and bosses. Unsurprisingly, I had a lot of good, or even very good ones, but only a few were truly great. So, what made them different? For one, they didn’t treat everyone with a broad brush. Knowing that people are wired differently, they took the time to figure out what made people tick and adjusted accordingly. In many ways, it’s the same lesson I’m learning from my sons. One needs to be encouraged to take more risks. The other occasionally needs to be reminded that he isn’t invincible. Treating them the same way wouldn’t necessarily bring out the best in either of them. The best teachers, coaches, bosses, and parents understand this. In doing so, they become what are often called force multipliers. Latch on to these people. Study them. Work for them. Hire them. Second, confidence is calibrated by pursuing hard things and experiencing difficult moments. Even Joe Burrow needed this. Burrow arrived at Ohio State as a highly recruited quarterback with every expectation of becoming the starter. Instead, he spent three years as a backup, largely watching games from the sideline. In doing so, it humbled him and he said as much after being drafted by the Bengals, admitting that his confidence was really shaken as a result of his experience in Columbus and that he didn’t know if he had what it takes. Ironically, his two teammates who started over him — J.T. Barrett and Dwayne Haskins — had little-to-no success in the NFL. Yet Burrow didn’t transfer when things got difficult. He stuck it out, graduated, and then looked for a fresh start. And when he did, he didn’t seek out a lesser program where starting might be easier. He chose LSU. Two years later, he produced one of the greatest seasons in college football history, winning the national championship and Heisman Trophy. Which brings me to something former Navy SEAL commander William McRaven said he looked for in a SEAL. Intelligence mattered, but what really

For this one, you have to design a protocol-emulator ASIC that can be used to test chips outside of a live system. Jane Street will pay to fabricate their favorite submissions. The competition is open until January 18th. Get started at janestreet.com/dwarkesh Timestamps (00:00:00) – How Caro gets people to talk (00:05:03) – Does America need a little more Moses today? (00:12:42) – Moses the young idealist (00:17:57) – Watching Moses lose power (00:24:01) – Did Moses realize he was changing? (00:27:53) – Building during the Great Depression (00:32:51) – The threats and promises of Lyndon Johnson (00:36:08) – Could Kennedy have passed Johnson’s laws? (00:41:00) – Getting a book down to one sentence (00:46:21) – All the material that never made it into the books (00:52:59) – Loneliness Transcript 00:00:00 – How Caro gets people to talk Dwarkesh Patel “If you do everything, you will win.” That is the maxim by which Lyndon Johnson lived his life. My guest today is Robert Caro . Over the 50 years that he has spent writing about Lyndon Johnson , he has lived in the edges of the Texas Hill Country to understand the poverty and loneliness of Johnson’s youth. He has sifted through millions of documents in the Senate and presidential libraries of the entire nation. He has chased down for interviews everyone, from the former goon who helped Johnson steal an election to the chauffeur who drove him on his first desperate campaign . In other words, my guest today is a man who understands Johnson’s aphorism: “If you do everything, you’ll win.” Mr. Caro, it is such a huge honor to have you on the show. Robert Caro It’s great to be here. Dwarkesh Patel My first question is what I hinted at in the introduction. How much do you see yourself represented in Johnson or in Moses ? Is part of the reason you’re able to write so compellingly about them that you share some of their qualities? Robert Caro Let me say first, I think, I hope, there are qualities of both these guys that I don’t share. Among other things they’re so, I’ll use the word, ruthless. You say they’d do anything to win. That’s part of their greatness. I remember when I started learning about Robert Moses, I went to the La Guardia papers, which were kept in the Boat Basin. They were stored by the Municipal Archives , literally in the 79th Street Boat Basin on the Hudson River, three levels down. There was this row of file cabinets against the wall. I’m sitting there day after day going through these documents. Occasionally I’d come across a note that Robert Moses wrote, and I realized I’m following the same path he was. It’s fascinating, actually. Dwarkesh Patel Obviously, not all the qualities. But the quality I’m referring to here is that just like Johnson or just like Moses, you refuse to take no for an answer. If somebody says, “I won’t give you an interview,” you don’t stop there. You refuse to leave a stone unturned. So there is a relentlessness that you share with these subjects. Robert Caro I’m going to take that as a compliment. Yes. You feel there are certain people that you have to interview. If they don’t want to give you an interview, you can’t, I feel, say no. Like Lyndon Johnson’s first secretary, the one who rode in the car with him on the campaigns. I said, “There’s no other human being on earth who knows what Lyndon Johnson is doing all these hours driving back and forth across Texas. I don’t know what I have to do, but I have to get him to tell me honestly about this thing.” Dwarkesh Patel This raises another question that I wanted to ask you. You’re interviewing all these people, and in many cases, they must know that it’s not good for them to tell you what you want to know. In many cases, they tell you anyway. How do you get people to tell you things that they know they shouldn’t tell you? Robert Caro You ask terrific questions. Sometimes you’re sitting there and you know this person doesn’t want to talk to you about what you want to get out of them, like John Connally on how Johnson used money to get political power. I’m thinking, “But I’ve been through the notes. Connally collected the money and gave it out at Johnson’s instructions, so he’s the only guy who can tell me how Johnson did this, how he judged who to give money to.” Sometimes Johnson would write on a request for money. If the guy asked for $1,500, Johnson would write, “Okay, 1,500.” Sometimes he’d write 500, sometimes he’d write no, but sometimes he’d write, “No, never.” I asked Connally what that meant, and he said, “This guy was never going to get money from Lyndon Johnson.” Then when you ask why he felt this way about this particular congressman, that’s when the really fascinating stories emerge. 00:05:03 – Does America need a little more Moses today? Dwarkesh Patel

articles.snippet: Video Friday is your weekly selection of awesome robotics videos, collected by your friends at IEEE Spectrum robotics. We also post a weekly calendar of upcoming robotics events for the next few months. Please send us your events for inclusion. CoRL 2026 : 9–12 November 2026, AUSTIN Humanoids 2026 : 6–9 December 2026, SANTA CLARA, CA Enjoy today’s videos! Some top-notch whole-body manipulation here from RAI, although it’s a little hard to tell whether there’s direct torso involvement, which is something that humans do with heavy or awkward stuff all the time. “Anything that shows up as a blob in a depth image can be taken for the tire, whether a person walking past or a stray object on the floor. In a few runs the robot left the tire and went after something else.” That “something else” seems suspiciously vague, doesn’t it? [ Robotics and AI Institute ] We present a contact-centric learning framework for versatile humanoid mobility in complex and unstructured environments. Our approach bridges motion imitation and reinforcement learning by leveraging human motion data as a training prior while enabling autonomous adaptation to previously unseen terrains. [ ETH Zurich Robotic Systems Lab ] You’ve literally heard me say it a thousand times: The only things that could possibly make Reachy Mini better would be some wheels and a whole bunch of fancy hats. But of course the only way I could possibly recommend the wheels is if Reachy Mini can totally wreck Microduck in a race. [ Pollen Robotics ] Luxonis is launching OAK 4 FFC, a 70 x 53 mm vision computer that lets humanoid and drone builders put up to five cameras wherever the robot needs them. The board runs sync, stereo depth, and AI itself, and calibrates from the scene instead of a checkerboard. [ Luxonis ] Thanks, Carson! Coming soon: Mini Pupper 4! [ MangDang ] HX Friends explores different robotic hand designs powered by DYNAMIXEL, ranging from a single articulated finger and a gripper to three-, four-, and five-finger hands. The video includes motion demonstrations across the lineup and VR teleoperation of the multifinger hands. [ Robotis ] Thanks, Hyunwoo! Developed by bluZenit, monkeyBot 2.0 is an innovative robotic platform designed to navigate complex industrial piping systems. Inspired by nature, monkeyBot 2.0 uses a unique gripping and climbing mechanism to move along vertical and horizontal pipes, navigate bends, and access challenging locations within industrial facilities. [ bluZenit ] Thanks, Trevor! I understand that you need some kind of repeatable baseline or whatever for training robots to do stuff, but I would be so much more impressed with any cleaning robot at all if it would clean stuff that was actually dirty for once. [ Generalist ] Calling this a “robot” hand at this point might be a little bit premature, but this is the kind of technology we’re going to need for deployable robots that are compliant and safe. [ BruBotics Human Robotics Research Center ] Robotiq really is the OG of industrial manipulation, aren’t they? And they’ve got a new tactile sensing gripper, too. [ Robotiq ] Introducing ANYmal X, which is the least likely to explode quadruped currently available for purchase. [ ANYbotics ] For those of us who prefer to play tennis alone. [ LimX Dynamics ] At Yulong River Scenic Area in Guangxi, China, DEEPRobotics’ Lite3 quadruped robot and LYNX M20 wheeled-legged robot are working together across a range of real-world tourism scenarios. Their AI algorithm MonoRace won the AI Grand Challenge and then beat three human FPV world champions. The drone uses only a single onboard camera and an IMU for state estimation. articles.title: Weekly Dose of Optimism #217
articles.snippet: Cover Image by Runway Hi friends 👋, Happy Friday and welcome back to our 217th Weekly Dose of Optimism. And what a week it’s been! Per New York Metro Weather , we’re in the midst of the longest streak of 8/10 or higher days since the account started in 2021, and here at the Dose, we’re in the middle of a string of 9/10 or higher weeks so long that I’ve lost count. Have a great Halloween tomorrow. For now, all treats no tricks. Let’s get to it. This Week’s Weekly Dose is Brought to You By… Reducto The Document Editor Built for AI Products AI products need more than file generation. They need a fast, accurate document editor that agents can also use. Reducto Editor brings full-fidelity DOCX, PPTX, and XLSX editing into your product through an SDK and embeddable UI. Lightweight and browser-based, it gives agents the tools to revise contracts, update presentations, and edit spreadsheets while preserving formatting and all the functionality you’re used to. Users collaborate in the same file, review native Word tracked changes and comments, and make their own edits without leaving your application. Files retain their full formatting when opened in Microsoft Office. From the team behind the document infrastructure trusted by Harvey, Scale AI, Toast, and Vanta, Editor runs in the browser or on your own servers. Build with Reducto Editor → (1) Anduril Unveils American-Made BlueChip Computer Another week, another extension of Anduril’s capabilities 1 . Last week, we wrote about Warhound , Ben Lamm’s effort to (humanely) genetically engineer dogs to be used in police and military work. Anduril is providing “software and hardware enhancement for items such as dog protection vests and eye goggles.” This week, Palmer Luckey announced that Anduril would be making its very own Made in America computer, BlueChip: designed here, with components from here, with metals America can mine, refine, process, and mill at scale and at reasonable price. American batteries, too. This is cool because as Palmer says in the video, “If you don’t control your technology, you can’t control your future.” But it’s also cool because it seems as if Anduril has gotten to the point where it’s built a machine that can make machines. Assemble enough engineers, capital, manufacturing capacity, distribution, etc… and you can build almost anything. It’s very Elon Companies-esque. And as we wrote in The Electric Slide , making products that can sell a ton of units, like laptops, can create the pull to bring more of the supply chain here, too. (2) OpenAI Says Its Models Disproved the ETH (and more) Video created with Runway The race to solve everything solvable continues apace. This week, OpenAI announced “three new discoveries in mathematics, computer science, and physics about harmonic analysis, complexity theory, and quantum field theory.” In math, OpenAI’s models produced a proof of Christopher Sogge’s 1991 local smoothing conjecture in every dimension, which would also settle the Kakeya conjecture and Stein’s restriction conjecture (of course). For context, Hong Wang and Joshua Zahl proved Kakeya in three dimensions just last year, and it was one of the biggest math stories of 2025. In computer science, a model refuted the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), the widely held belief that problems like 3-SAT can’t be solved meaningfully faster than brute force. If that makes no sense to you, check out the explainer video I made with Runway , which breaks it down in claymation well enough that I could actually understand it. In physics, the models produced a rigorous proof that interacting quantum field theories, including QCD and pure Yang–Mills, exist in four dimensions. That’s half of a Millennium Prize problem. Whereas before OpenAI has just dropped a bunch of solutions on the internet’s head and walked away, leading to quasi-embarrassing situations like when they said GPT-5 had solved ten open Erdős problems but it turned out the model had mostly found solutions that were already sitting in the literature, this time, OpenAI is sharing the outputs as research data with experts they call “shepherds” in each field, who will choose what to do with the data and where/when to publish. Shepherds don’t have to sign NDAs, don’t get paid, and do get the credit for explaining the work. Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi, who proposed ETH, are leading the review of its disproof with MIT’s Ryan Williams. Nobel laureate David Gross is leading the physics group, which chose to withhold the AI material and write it up themselves. The math proof and the ETH disproof are on GitHub with Lean formalizations. Lean, a checking software, guarantees the proof proves the formal statement, but human shepherds still have to confirm that the formal statement is the right one. Big week for Lean, by the way. On Tuesday, Axiom announced a complete Lean auto-formalization of the Classification of Finite Simple Groups, the “periodic table of symmetry.” The proof runs about 15,000 pages and was written by more than 100 mathematicians over several decades. It’s so big that no single person has ever checked all of it. For a sense of scale, it took Georges Gonthier’s team six years to formalize just one piece of the classification, the Feit–Thompson theorem, back in 2012. But Axiom’s machines can do a lot of human-years quickly, and they’re going to need to to keep up with all of the math and physics coming out of the labs. Because not only did OpenAI announce those results this week, a physics neolab, Physical Superintelligence (which we covered in Dose #209 ) released results on five problems from IQOQI Vienna’s list of open quantum problems , each with a paper, a Lean formalization, and open source verification code on GitHub. For those of you who were planning to spend the weekend cracking OQP 12: Can vacuum correlations violate the CHSH Bell inequality at arbitrarily large separations? or OQP 12: Can vacuum correlations violate the CHSH Bell inequality a

articles.title: What I learned about power from LBJ and Robert Moses
articles.snippet: Thanks to Max Farrens , who paired with me in writing the script for this video essay. I recently interviewed Robert Caro. He’s spent the last 50 years writing a four volume biography of Lyndon Johnson, and he spent another 7 years before that writing the biography of Robert Moses, the master builder of New York. His books are widely regarded as the best explorations of political power that have ever been written. They also happen to be literally my favorite books ever. Whenever I meet somebody new, one of the first questions they ask me is, “Who is it that you most want to interview that you haven’t yet?” And for six years, I’ve answered the question the same way: Robert Caro. I’ve spent so much time trying to make this interview happen: chasing his agent, calling his publisher, contacting the museums that have his archives, and even sending him handwritten letters. I finally got to sit down with him, and I’m very happy with how it turned out. It’ll be out this Friday. In the meantime, as I was preparing for the interview, and rereading these biographies, I wrote down the lessons they laid out about how to accumulate and use power. Robert Moses Robert Moses was the master builder of New York. He built more of the physical city than anyone before or since: the Triborough and Verrazano bridges, the Cross Bronx Expressway, Jones Beach, Lincoln Center, Shea Stadium, two giant power dams upstate, in addition to hundreds of parks and dozens of pools. Of the 899 miles of highways completed in New York State by 1964, Moses had built 672 of them. His projects collectively cost hundreds of billions of dollars in today’s money. For more than 30 years, Robert Moses was the most powerful person in New York (more powerful than any elected mayor or governor, despite not being elected to anything). How did he get and keep that much power? Exploits in law Part of the answer is that Moses wrote the laws that governed him. He was called ‘the best bill drafter in Albany,’ and he used that skill to write himself powers that the legislators voting on his bills didn’t know they were granting. The political genius of Robert Moses is perhaps best illustrated by his use of public authorities, which are government-created corporations that build city infrastructure. Public authorities sell bonds to pay for a specific project, say a new bridge. Once the bridge is built, the authority would charge drivers a toll until it had collected enough money to pay off its bonds. Then the authority would tear down the tollbooths, hand the bridge over to the city, and go out of existence. At least, that was the idea. And that’s what Albany assumed would happen when the New York State Legislature approved the Triborough Bridge Authority Act of 1933, whose final version included - buried within pages and pages of legalese - a few seemingly minor alterations drafted by Robert Moses. Section 1 clearly stated that the authority would dissolve once the bonds were paid off. And since the bonds could run at most 40 years (and the revenues from the bridge would pay back the initial cost far sooner), it seemed like the authority had a clear, built-in expiration date. However, in a subsection of Section 9, Moses added a single sentence that said the Authority could “from time to time” pay off its old bonds by issuing new ones. And those new ones could be “for any other corporate purpose.” So just before the original bonds were about to expire, the authority now had the right to issue a totally fresh 40 year note, for a potentially totally different use. And what could the Authority build with all that money? The original act let it build two bridges and their “approaches.” Moses’ amendments also gave this authority the right to build “connecting” roads and “facilities not inconsistent with the use of the project”. These rights, when interpreted as creatively as Moses intended to, would allow Moses to alter most of the roads, parks, and housing in New York - for if a road connected to a road which connected to a road which connected to the bridge, or if a park lay along the road that connected to the road that connected to the road that connected to the bridge, surely the Triborough Authority was entitled to improve and change it. All this construction could be financed by the bridges’ enormous toll revenues and the right of the Triborough Authority to borrow against them. To give some perspective, in 1946, the entire New York City government could only borrow $150 million before hitting its legal debt limit. That very same year, Triborough could borrow $360 million. So Moses’ bridge authority had access to more than double the amount of money as the largest city in America. But what if a future governor or mayor eventually learned about all the power and revenue that had been delegated to this authority, and decided to claw back? Moses had planned for that too, and his solution was so clever that no lawyer or lawmaker in Albany saw it coming. The US Constitution says that no state shall make “any … Law impairing the Obligation of Contracts” entered into by a government entity. A bond issued by a public authority is such a contract. Moses snuck a clause into the law that allowed him to add into those bond contracts “any other matters, of like or different character, which in any way affect the security or protection of the bonds”. These “matters” included whether Triborough could charge tolls for however long they wanted, and whether they would get to keep the surplus thus generated. That is to say, Moses could now entrench his powers simply by writing them into the bonds he issued. From the moment the bonds were sold, those powers could no longer be revoked by the Legislature, the governor, or the mayor - by anything, in fact, short of a Constitutional Convention. The powers that Moses now had were guaranteed for the bonds’ entire lifetime - a lifetime which could always be extended simply by refinancing. So, with just a few minor tweaks

articles.title: The Anthropic Prospectus Arrives: My (but not the) IPO valuation!
articles.snippet: I am a dabbler, by nature, moving on from topic to topic, but this year, I have spent more time than usual on AI, but that is because it seems to be part of almost every business or economy related story. I tried to value SpaceX ahead of and after the filing of the prospectus for its initial public offering before moving on to the question of whether it and OpenAI and Anthropic should be part of the S&P 500 index . I started my analysis of how AI would affect the rest of us , from doomsday to do-nothing scenarios, largely in response to Citrini and Citadel reports on the topic. in August 2026, I took my first big picture look at AI as a business, which I titled its bar mitzvah moment, with a look at its potential market, business economics and moats. That look was a prelude to the initial public offerings in the works (then) for Anthropic and OpenAI, and I provided a simple way to reverse engineer how much investors would need in revenues from these companies to justify their sky-high pricing. In early October, I looked at how the massive investments in AI are playing out in the aggregate earnings , cashflows and invested capital at US companies, and why it is contributing to holding the market intact, in the face of rising rates. Just last week, I argued that both Anthropic and OpenAI would be priced , rather than valued, for their initial public offerings, using what I called buzzy metrics (like annualized run rates) and promised that I would try to value the company, when it filed its prospectus. On October 26, Anthropic filed its prospectus , and at the risk of being called hopelessly wrong by both bulls and bears, I will try to value the company, using what I see as its most likely pathway, while also leaving the door open for you to disagree with me, and pick your own pathways to valuing the company. The Prospectus Before I delve into the details of the S-1 filed by Anthropic, it is worth noting that at 416 pages, it is long and filled with distractions, as has become the case with almost every initial public offering in the last two decades. (I chronicled this trend in my post on the d isclosure dilemma , arguing that while filings have become longer, they have become less informative). The Anthropic IPO has useful information that both bulls and bears will spin to justify their priors, and in the section below, I look at key disclosures, broken down by valuation input into revenue growth, profitability, risk and reinvestment categories, from both an optimist (glass half full) and pessimist (glass half empty) perspective: Revenue Growth and Composition : The good news in the revenue story is that the company has grown exponentially over the last year, with revenues in the first two quarters of this year about fourteen times as high as the revenues in the first two quarters of the last year, but the sobering news is that revenue growth slowed down in the third quarter of 2026, as OpenAI increased market share, compute capacity acted as a constraint and some enterprises moved to cheaper open source models. The good news on customer composition is that the number of enterprises that spend more than $1 million a year on Claude increased to 1900 , from less than a hundred a year ago, but the bad news is that the company still has concentrated revenues , with its top five customers accounting for 25% of revenues. Operating and Net Profitability : In bad news, Anthropic reported an operating loss, corrected for non-cash and one-time charges, of over $ 8 billion, for the first six months of the year. The actual loss reported was $80 billion, but $72 billion represented a non-cash charge, expensing the conversion option of the convertible bond. The good news, though, is that not only are the trend lines working in their favor, with the company claiming that it had an operating profit in the most recent quarter. The company is also delivering its revenues more efficiently over time, with all of its expenses decreasing as a percent of revenues across the quarters, with compute costs, its biggest cost,, decreasing from more than 250% of revenues to 48% of revenues, on a quarterly basis. Reinvestment for growth : AI agents are computing power hogs, and AI companies invest immense amounts in compute power. The financial statements in Anthropic's prospectus actually do not show this investment at the moment, with neither the cap ex in the statement of cash flow nor the debt (and invested capital) in the balance sheet showing substantial investment in compute power. Before you accuse Anthropic of hiding the truth (or worse), the company is open about its future compute power commitments, reporting hundreds of billions in compute commitments in future years. The good news is that Anthropic is now catching up with OpenAI, which had the lead on compute power, but the bad news is that this catching up has not been cheap, in terms of cost commitments in future years. It i s also worth noting that compute power will need to be renewed and reinvested in, and while chip costs (a key component) may come down, data centers, facing opposition from communities, may become more expensive. Operating and Regulatory risk : Anthropic's argument is that its customers, once they adopt Claude models within their enterprises, will find that they become so integral to operations that they will not abandon them (making revenues sticky and the business less risky). That has not been fully tested yet, and it is entirely possible that spending on AI agents is cyclical and that companies will pull back in bad times. On the financing front, committing to hundreds of billons in compute, purchase and lease commitments exposes the firm to default risk (with a bond rating of BB+), but in response the company will argue that its access to new capital, as a publicly traded large market-cap company, will make this risk recede. In addition, its cash balance, already at $114 billion, and likely to be bulked up with another $100 bill

articles.title: Artificial Analysis v5 and the benchmarker's dilemma
articles.snippet: Hill-climbing is easy, knowing what to hill-climb is hard. Making scores go up is expensive , but we have a much clearer playbook for it than we do for creating meaningful benchmarks at the true frontier of AI today. Independent evaluation of language models is under-appreciated in how hard of a task it is. These groups are not just taking current models and certifying their scores, which is a technically involved task. This is their job if AI progress is slow. When AI progress is as fast as it is, the technical details of the job are the routine work part of trying to put a single number on what makes for a good AI model today. The goal is to have a single number that is representative of current models, matching vibe checks, community sentiment, and scientific analysis, while being forward looking enough so that it’s not outdated in 3 months. Everyone building a benchmark faces a sort of paradox. You need your benchmark to reduce to one single number, so that it is easy to discuss, use in reports, and compare models, but every method of aggregating scores comes with meaningful trade-offs. The best scientists need to do this, everyone does. It’s a matter of creating aggregation metrics that you think are most fair, knowing there will always be imperfections. With the amount of money in the AI ecosystem today, the weight of independent evaluation is even higher – you dictate the winners and losers of a trillion dollar market. You also influence some of the models themselves, steering the shape of progress. This is a lot of pressure! My prompt for this article is Artificial Analysis’s recent update to their Intelligence Index, v5 . The AA index is the most prominent independent intelligence metric for the latest frontier models, followed in a distant second by Epoch AI’s Capabilities Index (ECI) . To date, all of these have been incredibly useful for the community and massively flawed! Interconnects AI is a reader-supported publication. Consider becoming a subscriber. Language models are capable of so much today, and this scope of capabilities is growing quickly. Our era of singular intelligence indices should be phased out soon, but it will take a long time. A summary of AAv5 is below, from their blog post, where they describe it as “reflecting real-world usage today:” Intelligence Index v5 weights: ➤ Knowledge Work (25%): AA-Briefcase (15%), AutomationBench-AA (5%), and GDP.pdf (5%) ➤ Coding (25%): FrontierCode 2.0 (15%) and Terminal-Bench 4.0 (10%) ➤ Science (25%): Terminal-Bench-Science (15%) and CritPt v2 hard subset (10%) ➤ General (25%): AA-Omniscience v1.1 15% (10% accuracy, 5% non-hallucination) and HLE-Diamond (10%) Here’s the new ranking of models: The problem with trying to benchmark real-world usage today is that it is extremely jagged, just like the models. The most proven use-case is coding, where open models are far more competitive and likely to keep up. In knowledge work, I’m less confident in open models. At first glance, in aggregate, their model ranking definitely looks reasonable. Still, it shows signs of strain and confusion, as any benchmark will, with GPT 6.1 Terra beating Claude Fable 5.1 on AAv5. Today, some benchmarks measure the absolute frontier of capabilities, playing nicely in open-ended tasks through your favorite harness, which often does take a large model. Some other benchmarks measure certain skills that will be needed of a model in repetitive agentic tasks. I get the feeling that AA is tuning their benchmark more towards the former, a general agentic collaborator, but all of these behaviors overlap. This takes us to the plot going around that prompted me to write this, where they showed the balance of open vs. closed models on the new benchmark. This plot shows 8 closed models beating the best to-be open-weight model, Kimi K3.1 Pro (which isn’t colored blue). This benchmark is taking the opinion of trying to measure where frontier models are moving into, which grows the gap to open models. This is an okay decision to take, but over time as existing workflows of open models become key factors of the economy, it could become a benchmark that misses where the core economic engine of the industry is. Open models’ demise from this seems greatly exaggerated, but I do think the previous index was flattering the open weight models too strongly. Consider this plot from the Kimi K3.1 Pro launch — yes, the open models are strong and useful in some cases, but the best OpenAI and Anthropic models have been a major step ahead in their flexibility and reliability. Some of the evaluations in AAv5 that open models are most behind on are “science” evals like terminal-bench-science and CritPT v2 . Open models are behind, but the value proposition was never to compete truly at the frontier. The open model economy will be about Reducing domains with high market demand for inference to a commodity price of hardware. Allowing ownership of intelligence, specializing it to internal data, and controlling internal agents across many companies in the economy. Both of these will take a very long time to materialize and are partially represented in benchmarks. The supply of compute is currently so low that open model providers also are raking in solid margins – when this shrinks, we will know the system is starting to work. The same goes for diffusion into enterprises, it’s not clear what the exact ceiling on it is because of the difficult ML expertise that is needed to build evaluations and do post-training today. Share At the next major model cycle, say in 2-3 months with GLM 6 or Kimi 3.5, I expect the leading open model labs to make substantial steps on this index, again surprising many observers. This is a cycle we have been on for years now. I’ve written many times about how open models keep up with the frontier, and a summary is that: The best open models do benchmax a little. The worst open models benchmax a lot (but don’t get a ton of attention anyways). The best open mo

articles.title: Your Robot’s Safety Functions Already Work. What If the Input Lies?
articles.snippet: This article is brought to you by VicOne . A mobile robot slows for someone in a hallway. A collaborative arm eases its movement as a worker approaches. A humanoid pauses to let a person pass. Each response depends on information about the robot or its surroundings: a distance reading, a position estimate, or a stop signal. But what happens when one of those inputs is wrong, and the robot still responds exactly as designed? The mobile robot reads the hallway as clear while someone is still there. The arm estimates that the worker is farther away. The humanoid does not receive a stop signal as a person crosses its path. In each case, a fault could cause that mismatch. So could deliberate manipulation . At VicOne LAB R7 , we examine how manipulated inputs can change robot behavior — and what that means for the systems meant to keep people safe. How an untrusted input can change a robot’s behavior A robot does more than measure its surroundings. It may interpret what it sees and hears to decide what to do next. Information placed in its environment can therefore influence its actions. Published research shows how this can happen. In a study of vision-language-action (VLA) models , a patch in a camera’s view reduced task success in simulated robot tests. FreezeVLA found that an adversarial image could cause tested models to ignore later instructions. Although the studies used different methods, both demonstrate how visual input can interfere with a robot’s intended task. In a robot-dog test using Gemma 4 E4B, text on a poster was treated as an instruction and changed the robot’s movement. VicOne LAB R7 also tested how untrusted inputs could change robot behavior. In a robot-dog test using Gemma 4 E4B, text on a poster was treated as an instruction and changed the robot’s movement. In a separate hospital-service-robot simulation using Nemotron on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, crafted audio that is inaudible to people changed the robot’s simulated behavior. The assigned tasks did not change; the inputs did. In a VicOne LAB R7 test, text on a poster changed a robot dog’s movement, illustrating how a crafted input can turn an unlikely outcome into a repeatable attack. VicOne Safety-related decisions have inputs too An independent protective system may still stop a dangerous action. But that system also depends on information: readings, estimates, and messages that tell it when to intervene. What happens if one of those inputs is manipulated? At a robotics bug bounty event, VicOne LAB R7 researchers injected a ROS 2/DDS message into a robot that organizers expected to remain still under a safe-control setting. The robot moved. A humanoid’s balance controller offers another example. If it relies on a vulnerable gyroscope, sound at the sensor’s resonant frequency could distort its reported rotation. The controller might correct for a tilt that never occurred. Researchers demonstrated the underlying acoustic attack against drones with vulnerable gyroscopes. The research did not demonstrate the same attack chain causing a humanoid to fall. Other protections could interrupt either chain. The question for safety and security teams is whether those protections detect the danger independently or depend on the same manipulated information. Figure 1. VicOne maps how accidental faults and deliberate cyber manipulation can lead to similar robot safety outcomes, from loss of control to physical harm. VicOne Deliberate attacks challenge safety assumptions A safety assessment may treat a combination of accidental faults as unlikely. Deliberate manipulation changes that assumption. An attacker can choose when to introduce a false input and repeat the same trigger. That does not make harm inevitable, but it may change how cyber risks should be assessed. Redundant sensors also need an adversarial test. If one action can affect both inputs, their agreement may offer less reassurance than expected. In autonomous driving research , a crafted physical object misled a system combining camera and LiDAR perception. The study does not establish a weakness in a particular robot, but it shows why teams should test whether one manipulation can affect several checks at once. Cyber threats add intent to the safety equation, so risk assessments based on accidental faults must be revisited to account for attacks that can be timed and repeated. Security testing strengthens robot safety evidence Safety teams set limits for speed, protective distances, and permitted operating areas. The evidence behind those limits should also show what happens when the information used to enforce them is deliberately manipulated. That evidence can also support assessments against applicable requirements. China’s GB/T 45502-2025 addresses information security for service robots. IEC TS 63074 examines security threats that could affect safety-related control systems. The EU Machinery Regulation , which applies from January 20, 2027, includes requirements to protect safety-relevant systems and data against corruption. Each has its own scope, and teams still need evidence for their robot’s design and operating conditions. Figure 2. Cybersecurity strengthens robot safety evidence throughout the lifecycle. VicOne helps teams test safety limits against manipulation before deployment and monitor the conditions behind safe behavior in operation. VicOne Before deployment, safety and security engineers can compare normal and adversarial scenarios against the same safety limits. During operation, they can monitor for changes to software, models, sensor signals, or behavior that may call earlier results into question. Any response to suspicious behaviors should follow policies approved by the safety team. VicOne supports that work across the robot lifecycle. Through the Robotic Hacking Community , VicOne LAB R7 works with researchers to investigate how cyber threats can change robot behavior. articles.title: A Field Guide to Getting Lost - by Rebecca Solnit
articles.snippet: summary: Really beautiful writing. Wonderful semi-poetic words around the subject of exploring, venturing into the unknown, and identity. Only downside is the subjects became just memoir for the second half of the book, instead of sticking to the theme. recommend: 6/10 my notes: Transformative, extending the boundaries of the self into unknown territory, about becoming someone else. Capable of being in uncertainties, mysteries, doubts, without any irritable reaching after fact and reason. To be lost is to be fully present. It is a conscious choice, a chosen surrender, a psychic state. Being at home in the unknown, so that being in its midst isn’t cause for panic or suffering. “Lost” comes from the Old Norse los, meaning the disbanding of an army. Explorers were always lost, because they’d never been to these places before. They never expected to know exactly where they were. A Hawaiian biologist discovers new species by getting intentionally lost in the rainforest. She need not think about anybody. She could be herself, by herself. To be silent; to be alone. A need to become no one and anyone, to shake off the shackles that remind you who you are, who others think you are. Some questions are more significant than their answers. Art: Does the work mean what the artist intended it to mean, or is it larger than they intended? We treat desire as a problem to be solved. Rather than on the nature and the sensation of desire, cherished as a sensation on its own. Look across the distance without wanting to close it up. Love this distance. Distance ceases when we arrive in it. The far becomes the near, and they are not the same place. Adults scan the landscape for picturesque panoramas. Kids on their hands and knees, engaged with what was immediately before them. Adults travel by abstraction. There is no distance in childhood. Distance comes with time, with the discovery of melancholy, of loss, the texture of longing, A desire to be lost, to be far away, a desire for that melancholy wonder that is the blue of distance. Yiddish insults can describe defects of character with the precision that Inuit describes ice. The place they were exiled from no longer existed, and they were no longer the people who had left it. A man galloping by a monk who asks, “Where are you going?” “Ask my horse”, says the man. The ethnic past was regarded as unnecessary baggage. The old longings had become little more than habit. Some people receive as birthright a sense of self that those who set out to reinvent themselves, for survival or for satisfaction, travel far. Some people inherit values and practices as a house they inhabit. Some of us have to burn down that house, and build from scratch. Vacant lots like missing teeth gave a rough grin to the streets. Places gave punk part of its aesthetic. Like most aesthetics this one contained an ethic, a worldview with a mandate on how to act, how to live. Nature is allowed to take over when maintenance is withdrawn. Solitude in the city is about the distance of other people. But in remote places solitude seems natural. Writing is an opening statement in a conversation that takes place long afterward without the author. Male hermit crabs often drag a female around by her claw, fighting off rival suitors, until she molts. Only when she is between shells can they mate. Nonfiction seems photographic, finding form and pattern in the stuff already out there. Fiction lets you start with a blank canvas. Romance once meant heroic, adventurous, or mysterious. A poet so perfectly describes the emperor’s vast and intricate palace. The palace disappears when the poem replaces it. To destroy false notions, without even going any further, is one of the ways to advance knowledge.

articles.title: Import AI 478: Math for alignment; ProgramBench; and Mirendil shows what RSI means
articles.snippet: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now How math could help alignment: …What the “industrialization of mathematics” means for safety… AI safety startup Resolution (formerly known as Sequent, Import AI 461 ) has published work on how it has automatically formalized some mathematical statements related to statistical learning theory. Specifically, the team has autoformalized the resolution of singularities, which they believe “lays the groundwork for further automated research into the relationship between loss landscape geometry and generalization.” How they did it: I’ll skip over the math and concentrate on how they did it, which gives us some broader lessons for how people are using AI systems to push on the frontier of knowledge. A Resolution researcher “started by working with agents to develop two plans: a high-level, human-interpretable version and a detailed (112-page) plan divided into atomic steps that closely followed the existing literature,” they write. The researcher “then deputized an orchestrator agent to carry out the plan, spinning up agents to do pen-and-paper math, write Lean, and handle support functions like checking that things were staying on track… the execution phase required little scaffolding beyond the initial plan and some agent skills distilled from earlier internal autoformalization efforts.” $135k for math formalization: The work took about a week, taking “on the order of 100B input tokens (90% cache reads) and about 300 million output tokens (totaling an estimated $135,000 in token spend), and produced about 600k lines of Lean.” Now that they’ve done this, they’ve been able to accelerate some other aspects of their research: “We have already seen both benefits from autoformalization in using this library to extend parts of singular learning theory. Formalizing resolution of singularities lets us automate more of the theory, for example, to better understand sampling, and that understanding is what lets us shape how models learn, which is the goal of what we call patterning”. Why this matters – perhaps the math boom will help us make safe AI: Though frontier mathematics often seems disconnected from immediate advances in other fields, posts like this highlight how the two might converge. The key point here is that AI is making it possible to do things that were previously so unbelievably expensive and human-time-intensive that very few people did them and you couldn’t easily integrate them into the research roadmap of a startup – but that has now changed. “We expect the coming industrialization of mathematics to make possible a new, rigorous science of research automation,” Resolution writes. Read more: Formalizing Hironaka’s Resolution of Singularities (Resolution) . *** Agents can build programs from scratch: …ProgramBench goes from 0% to 18.5% performance in a few months… In a reminder of the blistering pace of AI progress, Claude Opus 5.5 (xhigh) has got a score of 18.5% on ProgramBench, a very hard benchmark that came out in May of this year – and when it came out, every tested model scored 0%. What ProgramBench is: ProgramBench tests out how well AI systems can rebuild software programs based on being given a compiled program and its documentation. Tasks include building things like language interpreters (PHP, Lua, tinycc), databases (DuckDB, SQLite), media and compression utilities (FFmpeg, zstd, xz), and developer tools (ripgrep, fzf, jq). It was very hard until it wasn’t: When it came out, the best scoring system was Claude Opus 4.7 with 0% resolved (fraction of the 200 tasks where all tests passed), and 3% almost (fraction of the 200 tasks where >95% of tests pass). Compare that to today, when Claude Opus 5.5 gets 18.5% resolved and 70.5% (!!!) almost. Why this matters – the era of ephemeral software cometh: In 2027, huge amounts of software will be built via AI systems end-to-end autonomously developing whatever they need to do for whatever tasks they’re being put to. Evals like ProgramBench give us a sense of how rapid the pace of progress is here, given we went from 0% earlier this year to 20% now. My expectation is ProgramBench is saturated by the end of 2027 (where I define saturated as some very high score on resolved, though as with most benchmarks it’s likely there’s some kind of noise ceiling here, so it might not strictly be 100%). Read more: ProgramBench: Can Language Models Rebuild Programs From Scratch? (arXiv) . *** OpenAI illustrates why locking down AI systems is harder than you think: …Securing smart agents is like catching greased pigs… Here’s a nice post from OpenAI going over some of the things they discovered when they recently used their AI systems to ‘red team’ their own internal controls. The post goes over a number of the escapes and vulnerabilities that OpenAI’s agents found. There’s one particular example about communicating which is worth studying in detail because it tells us something about the wild cunning complexity of these systems. What they did and what they found: OpenAI “asked agents in separate microVMs, created and managed by OpenAI’s sandboxing software on shared host machines, to exchange synthetic secrets without the use of network connections or shared writable files—something that our systems are meant to prevent,” the company wrote. “The agents found a way to communicate using the processor’s cache: a small, fast memory that holds copies of data that applications have recently accessed. Reading data from the cache is faster than retrieving it from main memory, and the agents used this timing difference to communicate. One agent encoded information by evicting selected data from the cache. Another timed how long it took to reload that data, using the difference between fast and slow reads to recover the message.
